chapters.title: Defending the complete system
chapters.subtitle: From a two minute explanation to a whiteboard defense
intro: The strongest project discussion starts with the user problem and then names the authority that owns each fact. The Continuity Ecosystem explores what happens when a voice interaction ends before the business work does. Three libraries separate execution, channels and delegation; a local travel support application composes their public interfaces.

These questions are inferred preparation prompts, not reported LiveKit interview questions. Model answers explain the repository snapshot. Replace statements about personal decisions, effort and experience with your own account. A source citation shows where to inspect behavior; it does not mean this book reran the associated gate.

concepts.title: The central boundary
concepts.body: A room carries a conversation. A case owns business truth. Accepted work, an external effect, result applicability, delivery evidence and a human acknowledgment each have a different meaning.

concepts.title: A defensible answer
concepts.body: State the contract, identify its commit point, walk through one failure, show a source or test, and finish with the limitation.

questions.title: The project in two minutes
questions.question: What did you build, and why does a LiveKit agent need it?
answer: The project is a local reference implementation of application continuity around LiveKit Agents. P1 persists cases, accepted work, exact confirmation and execution state. P2 retains verified inputs across voice, chat and simulated SMS and connects them to the same case. P3 coordinates bounded specialist checks and keeps result truth separate from whether the result can still be used.

For example, a caller asks about changing dates, leaves, follows up by SMS and later rejoins a fresh room. The system should retain the original work and explain the current result without repeating an uncertain supplier mutation. LiveKit handles realtime transport and the conversational runtime; the application supplies these durable business contracts. This is a local POC with selected evidence, not a claim of production or multi region readiness.

followups.question: Why three libraries?
followups.answer: Their state changes at different boundaries. Channel acceptance, case intent and specialist interpretation need separate APIs and tests. The reference application proves composition without giving every library direct access to sibling storage.

followups.question: What is the most important invariant?
followups.answer: Accepted business work has one durable execution owner. Model output, a new room, a specialist response or a delivery badge cannot independently create mutation authority.

questions.watch_for: Do not present a distributed media platform or a general workflow engine as an implemented feature.

questions.title: Draw the authority map
questions.question: Which component owns each kind of state?
answer: P1 owns current case revision, confirmation and intent, execution attempts, leases, effects and authoritative work results. P2 owns retained channel input, channel associations, outbound operation identities and communication observations. P3 owns contracts, applicability and derived projection or processing metadata while using public P1 execution authority.

The application supplies trusted scope and adapters. A browser can display a projection but cannot promote it into a permission. A specialist can return facts but cannot revise the case. A room lifecycle can stop conversational output while accepted business work remains durable. I would draw each database ownership boundary before drawing network arrows, because the dangerous bugs occur when two components think they own the same transition.

followups.question: Can P3 keep a cache?
followups.answer: Yes, as derived as of metadata with source identity and retention rules. Cache contents cannot become a recovering accepted work queue or authorize delivery or action.

followups.question: Can one PostgreSQL instance hold everything?
followups.answer: Yes. Logical ownership, credentials, schemas and public interfaces still matter. Co location enables selected atomic guards but does not make every P2 and P1 observation a single transaction.

questions.watch_for: Shared infrastructure is not shared authority.

questions.title: Trace one input end to end
questions.question: Walk through text input, background policy work and a later SMS follow up.
answer: A trusted construction binds the native participant, conversation, case and account. P2 durably accepts the input and preserves its original operation identity before generation. Dispatch uses that accepted input to submit P1 work through the original input bridge. P3 runs the policy specialist only under a new P1 issuance and retains its validated result through P1.

The stable receiver stores its own fixed notice while preserving original result bytes and identity. A subsequent channel read can load P2 history and public P1 state as separately timed observations, then recheck disclosure permission. A verified simulated SMS is a new input on the same case, not a continuation of an old RTC transport packet. Rejoining creates fresh session context; it does not recreate accepted work.

followups.question: Which ID survives the room?
followups.answer: The case and original input or operation identity survive. Room and participant IDs identify a transport session and must not select replacement durable work keys.

followups.question: Where does the LLM choose dispatch?
followups.answer: The joined showcase keeps the persisted investigation dispatch rule deterministic in every inference mode. Provider generated wording does not choose business authority.

questions.watch_for: A fresh room must not turn an ambiguous original submission into a new logical operation.

questions.title: The hardest boundary
questions.question: Why is exactly once the wrong overall promise?
answer: A database can make one scoped acceptance identity unique and commit a transition atomically. It cannot, by itself, prove whether a remote supplier applied a request whose acknowledgment was lost. The project uses stable identities, conditional admission, immutable possible send markers and reconciliation instead of equating one stored row with one external effect.

At the boundary I enumerate the cases: failure before reservation, reservation with no known result, known supplier success, and success with lost local acknowledgment. The recovery action depends on the supplier contract. A cooperating idempotent supplier can safely reconcile an original key; an ordinary ambiguous request can remain unknown. That uncertainty is visible rather than erased by a retry or deadline.

followups.question: Why not retry with a new UUID?
followups.answer: That creates a second operation from one unresolved intention. A new attempt ID may be legitimate only under the original operation contract; a new business identity cannot conceal the first possible effect.

followups.question: Does a lease solve this?
followups.answer: A lease fences protected database writes by owner and epoch. Unless the supplier checks an appropriate fence, an old worker can still have an external request in flight.

questions.watch_for: Name the boundary where a guarantee holds instead of saying the whole system is exactly once.

questions.title: Prove the demo
questions.question: What would you demonstrate in a ten minute interview?
answer: I would show one happy journey and one failure boundary. First, accept text, show the linked durable work and policy result, leave, accept a simulated SMS, and rejoin into the same case. Then show a P1 investigation and a separate authenticated approval of the exact quote before mutation. Each displayed state should be read from its authority.

For the failure demonstration I would use an existing isolated crash or ACK loss scenario and explain the durable record that remains. I would prepare the exact source and retained evidence in advance, keep synthetic identities and avoid paid provider calls unless explicitly intended. A recorded provider showcase can support media discussion, but it does not qualify every later code change.

followups.question: What if the live demo fails?
followups.answer: Explain the failing layer and show retained evidence tied to the same source snapshot. Do not treat a video from an older snapshot as proof that the current failing path passed.

followups.question: Which screen proves human consent?
followups.answer: Only the authenticated controller action bound to the exact quote and revision establishes that permission. The transcript, audio waveform and result badge establish different observations.

questions.watch_for: Do not demonstrate only UI animations while describing durable recovery.

questions.title: Discuss the current gaps
questions.question: Is the complete portfolio finished?
answer: The evidence is mixed by scope and snapshot. The catalog has 55 cases with 24 registered runners: the baseline, all 20 P1 rows and three P3 rows. P2 and P3 have many qualified selected slices, but the complete P2 charter rows and remaining P3 rows are not thereby complete. local_real remains unqualified.

The historical P1 provider_real v2 qualification is also narrower than an unconditional current pass. Later v5 changes require affected requalification; the latest audit records an open provider rerun and a full PostgreSQL run with five errors under host load followed by passing targeted reruns. The audit also identifies unresolved shutdown and gateway lifecycle risks. I would state these before making a readiness claim.

followups.question: Do many passing tests prove release readiness?
followups.answer: They support the assertions they actually executed. Missing setup, skipped requirements, old evidence, and unresolved full lane errors stay visible; counts do not aggregate into a stronger contract.

followups.question: What would you fix first?
followups.answer: I would prioritize the high severity normal stop input exhaustion and final input lifecycle issue, then cleanup ownership and affected gates. That ordering is a proposed next step, not a completed fix.

questions.watch_for: Do not turn selected phase qualification into a current whole system pass.

questions.title: Why these tools
questions.question: Why PostgreSQL, Python and TypeScript rather than a broker plus a workflow product?
answer: The POC needs explicit state transitions and race evidence more than broad infrastructure. PostgreSQL provides durable scoped identities, short transactions, CAS and database time for leases. Python integrates the native Agents runtime and public authority; TypeScript supplies channel adapters, a specialist boundary and browser interfaces. The selected boundary is useful to a real installed consumer.

A workflow product could supply timers, execution history and operational tooling, but would still need exact business confirmation and an external effect contract. A broker could move notifications without owning the case. These are tradeoffs to revisit with operational scale and team needs. The repository intentionally keeps Redis, NATS and a general workflow platform out of its application V1.

followups.question: Would you use this instead of Temporal everywhere?
followups.answer: No universal claim follows from a POC. I would compare workflow duration, supported languages, determinism, operational burden, visibility and integration needs against concrete requirements.

followups.question: Why preserve SQLite?
followups.answer: It preserves the original M1 investigation subset and its compatibility evidence. Multi worker V1 authority is PostgreSQL; the subset must not be mistaken for full feature parity.

questions.watch_for: Do not justify a technology choice with a benchmark this repository has not measured.

questions.title: Adversarial data and authority
questions.question: What if an SMS, screenshot or specialist result tells the agent to approve a change?
answer: The content is data. It cannot grant a tool permission, change tenant scope or authorize an external mutation. Trusted construction binds identities and capabilities before interpreting input. Strict contracts bound what can be accepted, and the authenticated controller still has to approve the exact quote against the current case guard.

I would test a syntactically valid policy fact or image containing instructions to ignore confirmation. Its text may appear as evidence or be rejected for factual reasons, but it cannot become an instruction to the control plane. Runtime validation and factual validation also remain separate: a schema valid result can be unsupported, stale or unauthorized for action.

followups.question: Does prompting solve injection?
followups.answer: Prompts help conversational behavior, but authority must be enforced outside model text. The mutation path must reject a malicious recommendation even if every model follows it.

followups.question: What about secret diagnostics?
followups.answer: Use stable error codes and bounded identifiers, exclude raw credentials and private transcripts, and keep provider credentials confined to the explicit native provider runtime.

questions.watch_for: Never describe schema validation as proof of truth or consent.

chapters.title: P1 Agent continuity and durable execution
chapters.subtitle: Durable authority beyond the LiveKit session
intro: P1 is the portfolio's durable case and execution boundary. The interview discussion should start with the acknowledged command, exact consent and external uncertainty, then explain leases, persistence and packaging as mechanisms that preserve those contracts.

The implementation has two deliberately different storage lines: the preserved SQLite investigation subset and full PostgreSQL booking lifecycle, plus a separate opt-in P1-owned work profile used by delegation. Booking versions v1 to v5 and work versions v1 to v4 are independent.

The source and test references below are verified against the reviewed checkout. Answers are preparation guidance rather than claims about personal authorship. The review did not rerun paid-provider, browser or database qualification gates.

concepts.title: Acceptance before acknowledgement
concepts.body: An accepted command exists durably before the caller receives success. A lost response requires exact original-identity reconciliation, not a new command key.

concepts.title: Commit authority once
concepts.body: Case revision, exact published quote, explicit confirmation and immutable action intent share one protected transaction. Neither a model reply nor a worker lease supplies that consent.

concepts.title: Preserve external uncertainty
concepts.body: A local fence can reject a stale database write, while an old reserved supplier call can still land. Provider cooperation or an explicit uncertain outcome closes that boundary honestly.

concepts.title: Truth and permission differ
concepts.body: A known result or receipt survives later cancellation and expiry. Retained history does not grant new execution, delivery or action permission.

concepts.title: Actual work owns resources
concepts.body: Cancelled waiters do not stop threads, child processes or remote work. Keep actual tasks and process groups owned until closure is observed.

questions.title: The boundary that survives the call
questions.question: Explain Agent Continuity in two minutes. What survives when the LiveKit room and agent process disappear?
answer: P1 makes accepted business work independent of a conversational process. A LiveKit session can collect a request and invoke a narrow application API, but it does not own the authoritative booking case or its execution lifetime. The PostgreSQL path persists the original investigation, a distinct case identity, its current revision, managed continuation state, effect attempts, cancellation receipts and completion delivery. A new process can read those records and select eligible work without reconstructing an old coroutine stack.

The managed acceptance implementation is a useful concrete example: one protected transaction creates the inquiry, case owner and absolute continuation deadline. Its acknowledgement comes after that transaction; replay returns the original records. Later workers pull due steps from the same authority. An unsignalled wait occupies durable rows rather than a sleeping room or child process.

I would demonstrate this with an acknowledged request, an independent-process loss, a fresh-process read and useful resumed progress. I would distinguish the preserved SQLite investigation subset from the full PostgreSQL lifecycle, and distinguish historical qualified P1 V1 evidence from the still-open post-v5 provider requalification. This is explicit persisted state, not automatic checkpointing of arbitrary Python code.

followups.question: Why not keep AgentSession or chat history alive?
followups.answer: A conversation object is useful working context, but its lifetime and availability do not establish durable acceptance, exact consent or external effect truth. Keeping it alive also consumes resources while a case waits. The new session rehydrates from authoritative records.

followups.question: What would you draw first on a whiteboard?
followups.answer: Draw the session and controller as clients, one case and execution authority over PostgreSQL, and independent supplier and receiver stores. Mark the acceptance commit, exact-consent commit and external-call boundary before adding workers, models or channels.

questions.watch_for: Do not describe a room identifier, model memory or a running task as the durable business authority.

questions.title: Acceptance and acknowledgement loss
questions.question: A submit call times out. How can the caller discover whether the investigation was accepted without creating a duplicate?
answer: The caller must retain its original scoped idempotency key and canonical request. It replays that exact command or performs the documented lookup; it does not invent a new key because the response was lost. The store looks for the existing identity within its protected write transaction. Identical content returns the original task, while different canonical content is a conflict. The failure can occur after the database committed, so a timeout alone cannot mean rejection.

The SQLite execution path makes the distinction visible with before-commit and after-commit failpoints. Its returned created flag concerns the original intake task, while enrolled concerns creation of the execution row. The managed PostgreSQL facade additionally requires the existing case and continuation records, checks original ownership and preserves the first deadline. It does not silently enroll an arbitrary legacy task during a retry.

A strong test covers concurrent identical submits, a process lost after commit but before acknowledgement, and fresh-process recovery of the same identity. It also proves a changed request conflicts and that a different scope can independently reuse the textual key. The guarantee is one accepted logical identity within this contract, not one network transmission or unconditional exactly-once execution.

followups.question: Should a client retry a changed date under the same key?
followups.answer: No. A key identifies an immutable command. A changed date needs an explicit revision contract or a new logical request. Reusing the key with changed content must fail so that an ambiguous original acceptance is not silently overwritten.

followups.question: Does a successful lookup authorize execution?
followups.answer: No. Lookup establishes retained acceptance. Execution needs the relevant worker lease or newly issued execution grant. The accepted-work profile deliberately separates acceptance, invocation and result recording so that transport retries do not become permission to invoke again.

questions.watch_for: A retry with a new identity can turn a lost acknowledgement into duplicate business work.

evidence.label: Original owner and deadline on replay

questions.title: Canonical content and identity conflicts
questions.question: What exactly is idempotent here, and why is comparing only an idempotency key insufficient?
answer: The identity is scoped and bound to immutable semantics. The inquiry store canonicalizes a validated BookingChange into sorted compact JSON, then compares that canonical payload when an existing scope/key is found. A repeated key with different dates is an explicit IdempotencyConflict. The public accepted-work profile preserves operation, exact bytes, digest and original absolute deadline; changing the deadline is also a semantic conflict. Reconstructing a WorkPayload prevents trusted callers from supplying a modified digest alongside inconsistent bytes.

Canonicalization solves representational ambiguity only within the declared contract. P1 does not guess that two different texts mean the same user intent, nor does it ask the LLM to resolve conflicting commands. Typed schemas, bounded identifiers and exact comparison keep the behavior deterministic. Different scopes may reuse the same visible key without sharing records.

In an interview I would explain why deadline replay occurs before new-work expiry and capacity checks. An old accepted command remains discoverable even after its original deadline passes or the store reaches capacity. That does not renew its deadline or grant new execution. Tests should assert immutable original bytes and IDs, altered-content conflicts, cross-scope isolation and unchanged retained counts on replay.

followups.question: Why compare stored bytes if a SHA-256 digest exists?
followups.answer: The digest is a useful stable integrity and correlation value, but the API contract still binds the actual stored payload. Reconstructing validated values and comparing exact semantics prevents inconsistent object fields or accidental changes to the canonicalization path.

followups.question: Could semantic deduplication improve the product?
followups.answer: It could suggest likely duplicates to a user, but it should be an advisory layer. Authoritative command deduplication needs a stable explicit identity and precise conflict rules. Fuzzy matching cannot safely decide whether two booking changes authorize one effect.

questions.watch_for: Do not silently normalize a changed deadline into a replay or infer identity from similar natural language.

questions.title: Keep identities separate
questions.question: Why does the implementation distinguish case, workflow, effect, attempt, command and delivery identities?
answer: Each identity answers a different question. The case identifies the evolving business request; the workflow identifies accepted execution; an effect identifies the immutable supplier operation; an attempt identifies one invocation observation; a command ID deduplicates a controller action; and an event or delivery ID identifies notification work. A room or conversation can end while all of these remain meaningful. Combining them would make revision, replay and recovery ambiguous.

The case store explicitly rejects a case UUID equal to its task ID and checks that the current quote belongs to the same task, revision and requested booking. A v2 proposal additionally binds the immutable case UUID. The committed ActionIntent carries its own intent, effect and dispatch event IDs. A new lease epoch is neither a new business effect nor a revision of the user's request.

This separation also constrains observability and recovery. A correlation ID can connect evidence across processes but grants no mutation authority. An attempt from an old epoch cannot acknowledge current work, yet its supplier effect may still be a fact needing reconciliation. I would follow the exact original identities through a crash timeline rather than say that every retry creates a new job.

followups.question: When does a changed user request get a new identity?
followups.answer: Before commitment the case can advance through expected-revision CAS while keeping its stable case identity. After an intent is committed, revise rejects the edit; a new request or explicit reconciliation flow is needed because the original effect must remain immutable.

followups.question: Can a lease owner UUID double as a confirmation command ID?
followups.answer: They belong to different contracts and authority boundaries. A lease owner identifies one worker invocation; a confirmation command represents a trusted controller decision with replay semantics. Reusing their textual values obscures provenance and is explicitly discouraged by the repository rules.

questions.watch_for: A new worker epoch must never create a new supplier effect identity merely because ownership changed.

evidence.label: Independent intent effect and dispatch IDs

questions.title: Investigation is not mutation consent
questions.question: What prevents a model from booking a change after hearing a general yes?
answer: Investigation intake and booking mutation are separate contracts. BookingChange carries investigation consent only. A trusted proposal is published as an immutable QuoteSnapshot. The authenticated controller must provide an explicit Confirmation of that exact proposal, including its case revision, booking, dates, amount, currency and expiry. For v2 it also includes the case UUID, supplier identity and expected supplier revision. The model cannot manufacture the authority merely by emitting those fields.

The database authority validates the current case and exact published quote under locks in the transaction that records confirmation, action intent and dispatch event. It checks cancellation, managed state and deadlines at that point. Native conversational tools are limited to submit, inspect and request cancellation; quote preparation and confirmation remain in trusted controller composition. This is an application authorization boundary above SDK tool invocation.

I would show the controller path, then run through missing consent, changed amount, stale revision, expired quote and wrong supplier binding. Every negative case must produce zero mutation intent and zero apply calls while a separately valid case still progresses. A syntactically valid model tool call is not sufficient evidence that a human approved the exact business change.

followups.question: Could the model call a confirm tool with explicit=true?
followups.answer: That would collapse the trust boundary. The boolean is a validated contract value, not evidence of human authorization by itself. Only the authenticated controller route should construct and submit the exact confirmation; the native model must not receive that capability.

followups.question: What if the user interrupts speech after approval?
followups.answer: Speech interruption changes media generation or playback. It does not erase a committed business intent. The user can separately request business cancellation, whose disposition depends on whether an external dispatch may already have occurred.

questions.watch_for: Never claim that model confidence, an SDK tool schema or physical playback establishes exact human consent.

questions.title: One atomic commitment point
questions.question: Walk through the exact transaction that turns confirmation into an immutable action intent.
answer: The protected transaction first takes the shared booking admission lock and then loads the authorized case row for update. It looks up the confirmation command receipt before attempting a new commitment. An exact replay returns the original intent; a changed actor, task or payload conflicts. For a new command it locks continuation and pending wait rows, then samples time after the required locks. That timing matters because waiting for a lock can cross quote or business expiry.

The authority validates managed state, original business deadline, matching wait deadline and the exact current quote. It then inserts the immutable confirmation. If no intent exists, it inserts one ActionIntent with stable effect and dispatch IDs and an intent-dispatch event in the same transaction. It moves managed control to intent_committed and consumes the matching wait while expiring unrelated pending waits.

There is no supplier call in this transaction. The commit establishes authorization and durable work, not the supplier's outcome. A rollback must leave none of the partial consent, intent or dispatch evidence. A lost commit acknowledgement is reconciled through the original command receipt. Tests kill an independent process both before commit and after commit acknowledgement loss.

followups.question: Why not validate first and insert the intent in a second transaction?
followups.answer: Another revision, cancellation or expiry can intervene between validation and commitment. The transaction must protect the preconditions and the intent together. A preceding read can prepare UI context, but only the guarded commit decides whether the action is admitted.

followups.question: Why replay before checking current expiry?
followups.answer: The original command may already have committed while valid. Replaying it later should return that historical fact, even when a fresh commitment would be expired. Replay must not create another effect or reinterpret the old authorization under new state.

questions.watch_for: An intent-dispatch row means durable authorization to execute; it is not proof that the supplier was called.

questions.title: Revision and confirmation races
questions.question: A user changes dates while another controller confirms the old quote. Who wins?
answer: The database serialization point determines the winner. revise requires the expected current revision, rejects any existing committed intent and cancellation, updates the request under CAS, clears the current quote and expires pending waits. A later attempt to confirm the old quote fails because its revision or published proposal is no longer current. This is the revision-first outcome.

If confirmation commits first, the immutable intent is already bound to the exact proposal. A later revise sees the committed intent and raises intent_committed rather than rewriting the action. This is the intent-first outcome. The API does not decide the winner from client timestamps or from whichever response the UI receives first. Both races use the same protected authority and lock order.

The meaningful test proves each order deliberately using barriers and independent contenders, then checks both the rejected stale operation and useful valid progress. The case revision is an application precondition, not a claim that all supplier or workflow facts were read atomically. A lost acknowledgement from revise is particularly different from a receipted confirmation: matching later state does not identify who won a CAS update.

followups.question: Can the UI automatically rebase the rejected change?
followups.answer: Not safely as the same command. The user must see current state and make a new explicit choice. Automatic rebasing could authorize a different amount, revision or supplier state from the one the user intended.

followups.question: Why not use last-write-wins timestamps?
followups.answer: Client clocks can skew and responses can reorder. More fundamentally, a committed supplier intent cannot be silently superseded by a later edit. Expected-revision CAS and a single protected commitment define a defensible business ordering.

questions.watch_for: Do not infer the winning command from matching request content or response arrival order.

questions.title: Legacy consent and proposal evolution
questions.question: Why does quote v2 add supplier and case bindings instead of filling those values into old quotes?
answer: Old consent must preserve what was actually approved. A legacy v1 quote does not bind an immutable case UUID, supplier identity or expected supplier revision. Filling those fields later from mutable current state would retroactively expand the authority of old consent. The versioned parser therefore preserves v1 read and replay, while schemas supporting mutation require a new supplier-bound v2 proposal for new mutation commitment.

QuoteSnapshot treats the three extra bindings as an all-or-none set. It validates UUIDs and the supplier revision, keeps case and workflow IDs distinct, and emits exact versioned fields. The case authority rejects new proposals of the wrong version and checks that a v2 quote belongs to the case. MutationWorker also verifies that the configured supplier's provider identity matches the committed proposal before lookup or apply.

This is a useful SDK evolution example: compatibility does not mean assigning new authority to old bytes. An explicit owner upgrade can add storage for new behavior while old payloads and receipts retain their original meaning. The test plan must include old data, replay, changed provider configuration and a valid new proposal that makes progress.

followups.question: What happens if deployment config points to a new supplier?
followups.answer: Existing committed work stays bound to its original supplier. The worker rejects a mismatched configured provider; it cannot redirect an old authorized operation by changing configuration. A separate migration or new explicitly confirmed request would need its own contract.

followups.question: Can v1 confirmation replay still return an old receipt?
followups.answer: Yes, preserving original history is different from permitting a new mutation. Exact old replay can remain readable and idempotent. A new mutation proposal requires v2 and cannot derive missing bindings from later state.

questions.watch_for: Backward compatibility must preserve old semantics rather than invent new consent.

questions.title: Persisted waits and early signals
questions.question: How can a workflow wait hours without keeping a Python coroutine or LiveKit room alive?
answer: The wait is persisted data: its identity, exact quote snapshot, deadline and pending state live in PostgreSQL. Signal acceptance is separate and retains an immutable scoped event identity and canonical payload. Signals can arrive before the matching wait exists, and later advancement examines unconsumed matching signals. Replayed signal content deduplicates; changed content under the same event ID conflicts; unrelated signals cannot advance the case.

Advancement occurs through the same case authority transaction as exact intent commitment and signal consumption. It checks current quote and case state, original business and wait deadlines, then consumes a matching signal once logically. Revision or replacement of a proposal expires obsolete waits. No process-memory future or sleeping worker owns the accepted decision.

The selector only chooses a waiting task when an expiry or matching signal makes it useful to advance. That preserves finite worker capacity for other cases. A good demonstration stops all original processes, accepts a signal using the original identity, restarts a worker and observes one matching advancement. It should also show a stale or unrelated signal remains inert and a current independent request succeeds.

followups.question: What if a confirmation arrives before the quote wait is armed?
followups.answer: Retain the authenticated signal under its exact original identity and payload. Arming or advancing the matching wait can later correlate it. Do not reinterpret arbitrary early text as consent, and do not drop a valid event merely because no process is currently waiting.

followups.question: Can revising dates extend the original business deadline?
followups.answer: No. A revision changes the request and invalidates stale wait context, but the original managed deadline remains. Otherwise repeated edits could bypass bounded execution and preserve an indefinitely live task.

questions.watch_for: A durable wait is not an in-memory Event with a periodic database backup.

questions.title: Supplier success before the crash
questions.question: The supplier changes the booking, then the worker dies before recording success. What happens next?
answer: P1 persists an immutable intent and a possible-dispatch reservation before calling the supplier. The effect has a stable supplier key, and its dispatch_count remains greater than zero across worker epochs. A replacement worker must therefore treat the outcome as potentially executed. It first verifies the original provider binding and reconciles through the supplier's declared lookup and idempotency contract rather than inventing a fresh effect.

With the cooperating fake supplier, lookup finds the original result, validates its binding to the exact intent and records known success. If lookup is temporarily unavailable, the reservation remains recoverable; this is not proof of failure. If the supplier lacks the required cooperation, ambiguity becomes a durable uncertain outcome with no unsafe automatic resend. The absence of a response or a revision mismatch alone cannot identify this particular effect's outcome.

The evidence must inspect an independent persisted supplier ledger after an actual worker kill. It should prove the exact booking revision, one logical cooperating effect and useful recovered progress. Reopening the application database in the same process would not exercise the external success-before-acknowledgement window.

followups.question: Why require idempotency as well as lookup for a possible prior call?
followups.answer: A paused old call can still arrive after a lookup reports absence. Lookup alone cannot prevent a later duplicate. A stable idempotent key makes a same-operation retry safe under the declared supplier contract; without that cooperation the result stays uncertain.

followups.question: Does retrying the same key mean exactly one HTTP request?
followups.answer: No. Several transport attempts may reach a cooperating supplier, which deduplicates them into one logical effect. The claim must name that contract and the tested schedules rather than promise universal exactly-once external execution.

questions.watch_for: A database lease cannot retroactively cancel a request that was already admitted outside the database.

questions.title: An honest unknown outcome
questions.question: When does P1 deliberately return uncertain instead of failed or cancelled?
answer: Uncertainty is required when an external effect may have happened and available evidence cannot safely establish its outcome. The important distinction is a claim before reservation versus a possible prior dispatch. A claimed effect with dispatch_count equal to zero can still be prevented definitively; any retained reservation means an older paused request could land. Recovered state must preserve that distinction across generations and leases.

MutationWorker refuses an unsafe resend when a possible previous call lacks both lookup and idempotency. prepare_dispatch also refuses to label cancellation or expiry as definite prevention when an earlier reservation exists. Even a current lookup miss does not erase that history. It records ambiguous_outcome and an uncertain effect, preserving cancellation requested as a separate disposition when applicable.

This boundary was important enough to receive a concrete audit fix: a takeover worker could previously mislabel a cancelled or expired paused call as prevented. The regression tests resume the old external call after takeover and assert uncertainty. In an interview I would use this as an example of strengthening a claimed guarantee by modeling what the external world can still do.

followups.question: Is unknown a transient technical error or a business state?
followups.answer: Here it is persisted business truth about insufficient evidence. A UI should explain that the outcome needs reconciliation rather than invite a blind retry. A transport error can cause that state, but the state must survive the transport and process.

followups.question: What if the booking currently shows the requested date?
followups.answer: Matching current state does not prove which command changed it, whether this effect happened, or whether it happened once. Only evidence bound to the original supplier operation can support that claim.

questions.watch_for: Do not turn lookup absence, timeout or cancellation into proof that a reserved external operation never ran.

questions.title: Cancellation across three boundaries
questions.question: How would you explain cancellation before commitment, after commitment and after dispatch to a user and interviewer?
answer: Before commitment, cancellation wins through the same protected case authority and prevents a new mutation intent. After commitment but before any dispatch reservation, the effect can still be positively stopped: zero prior reservations establish that no apply call was admitted. After a reservation, cancellation is best effort because a paused or in-flight request may still change the booking. The cancellation request and its disposition remain separate from the effect result.

The store records an immutable cancellation command receipt and preserves known supplier success. A late cancellation cannot rewrite success into cancelled, and deadline expiry cannot erase the result. prepare_dispatch checks current cancellation and time in the protected transaction, but that fence cannot stop an earlier externally admitted call. A UI should display requested, prevented before dispatch, uncertain, or known completed according to evidence rather than a single optimistic cancelled badge.

There is also a separate media action: interrupting the agent's speech. That stops or changes output generation and playback; it does not business-cancel accepted work. Native tools can request cancellation explicitly without owning a worker lease. The test should prove both race orders and continued service for an unrelated case.

followups.question: Why should controller cancellation work while the supplier is slow?
followups.answer: The supplier call is outside protected SQL, and controller commands use authenticated case authority rather than waiting for worker lease ownership. If cancellation had to wait for that I/O, it could miss the only safe prevention window.

followups.question: Can a timeout automatically request business cancellation?
followups.answer: Only if the public contract explicitly makes that policy choice. Abandoning a waiter or expiring a UI request is not itself consent to cancel accepted business work, and it cannot prove the remote operation stopped.

questions.watch_for: Keep cancellation request, cancellation disposition, business outcome and speech interruption as separate facts.

questions.title: Atomic completion and the outbox
questions.question: Why store a completion event in the same transaction as the final business outcome?
answer: This is the booking completion outbox, separate from work-profile delegation delivery. If outcome commit and event creation were separate, a crash between them could leave successful work with no notification intent, or a notification could describe an outcome that never committed. P1 inserts the immutable business outcome, one stable completion event and initial pending-delivery state together. It also moves the managed continuation to its final state in that protected transaction.

Delivery then occurs outside SQL under a separate bounded worker step. The receiver is bound before I/O, and repeated delivery uses the original event and receiver. A cooperating receiver retains deduplication receipts so a crash after receiver acceptance but before local acknowledgement can recover one logical receipt. Delivery retry does not modify the business result, and exhausted delivery does not turn supplier success into a business failure.

I would demonstrate a completed mutation, kill delivery after sink success, restart with the same receiver and compare the original event identity and independent receiver ledger. I would also verify a conflicting receiver configuration cannot retarget an ambiguous delivery. This is at-least-once event transport with stable deduplication, not evidence that a person read or accepted the result.

followups.question: Could you publish directly to a broker inside the SQL transaction?
followups.answer: Holding locks across remote publish would lengthen the critical section without making a cross-system atomic commit. Persist the event intent in the authority transaction and publish afterward under a documented reconciliation and deduplication contract.

followups.question: What can be deleted from the receiver?
followups.answer: A separate diagnostic display projection may be pruned under its contract. Core event and deduplication receipts must remain for the replay horizon; deleting them merely because the UI no longer shows the event could allow duplicate acceptance.

questions.watch_for: A delivered completion message is neither a different business outcome nor human acknowledgement.

evidence.label: Outcome event and delivery atomic insertion
External receiver call before local receipt

questions.title: Database leases and stale writers
questions.question: Two workers believe they own the same task. How does P1 reject stale database writes?
answer: The v4 path grants an explicit lease bound to task, scope, owner UUID and monotonically retained epoch. Acquisition, renewal, release and worker write validation use the shared admission transaction. After acquiring the relevant locks, PostgreSQL clock_timestamp decides whether the grant is still live. An expired or released epoch cannot be revived, and a new owner receives a later epoch.

Each worker mutation checks the exact stored grant in the same transaction as its write. Checking a cached expires_at before opening the transaction would permit a stale commit after a lock wait or takeover. Attempt generation remains a different mechanism for identifying an effect attempt; it is not a substitute for the lease epoch. Authenticated controller reads, confirmation and cancellation remain distinct from worker authority.

This fencing protects local state. A stale process can still resume a supplier call it reserved earlier, so the independent supplier's stable identity and idempotency or explicit uncertainty remain necessary. Tests need separate processes, a real database-time expiry, a paused old owner and a new owner that makes useful progress, then rejection of the old acknowledgement.

followups.question: Why clock_timestamp rather than transaction_timestamp?
followups.answer: A transaction can start before waiting a long time for locks. transaction_timestamp would retain that old start time and might authorize a now-expired grant. Sampling the database clock after lock admission evaluates authority at the protected write boundary.

followups.question: What if the same owner acquires again while its lease is live?
followups.answer: The store can return the existing live grant for that owner. That is replay of current authority, not an epoch reset. Expired or released ownership must still follow the retained epoch rules and cannot silently renew itself.

questions.watch_for: Lease fencing prevents stale database commits; it does not independently fence supplier I/O.

questions.title: Worker lifetime and owned children
questions.question: Why does the worker parent kill and reap its child before releasing the lease?
answer: Releasing a lease while an owned child can still execute would invite overlap: another worker could acquire the task while the old child continues database or supplier activity. The parent therefore owns at most one bounded step subprocess, caps output and monotonic occupancy, stops acquisition on shutdown, and observes child cleanup before releasing the grant. A stopped waiter is not evidence of a stopped process group.

The runtime computes a step deadline using the configured ceiling and half the lease duration, drains bounded output and kills and reaps the group on timeout or shutdown. The finally path closes the child; only when the child reference is cleared does the parent release the lease. If reaping fails, cleanup remains visibly incomplete and the grant is left to expire rather than pretending the child disappeared.

This does not prove an external supplier stopped. A remote request can outlive the local process, so reconciliation remains mandatory. The meaningful evidence includes actual descendant and process-group observations, preserved private failure artifacts, and a subsequent current worker making progress. A health file or a parent exit code alone is insufficient.

followups.question: Why not just cancel an asyncio Task running the child?
followups.answer: Task cancellation abandons a waiter; it does not guarantee the operating system process or its descendants exited. Ownership must track the actual child and process group until exit and reaping are observed, then release dependent resources.

followups.question: What should happen if shutdown exceeds its deadline?
followups.answer: Report cleanup incomplete and retain ownership evidence and private files. Do not release authority or delete backing fixtures while owned activity is unresolved. A later observer can complete cleanup, but the earlier timeout remains a failed closure observation.

questions.watch_for: Never equate a cancelled await, timed-out subprocess call or SIGTERM request with a reaped process group.

questions.title: Responsive async boundaries
questions.question: What is the subtle resource leak in wrapping blocking database work with asyncio.to_thread and a timeout?
answer: Cancelling or timing out the coroutine waiting on to_thread does not stop the actual thread. If the semaphore slot is released when the waiter stops, repeated cancellations can start more threads while old writes still run. Apparent bounded concurrency then becomes unbounded actual I/O, and shutdown can close shared state while those operations remain active.

BoundedAsyncIO acquires a slot with a short admission timeout, creates and retains the actual offload task, and awaits it through shield. The completion callback releases the slot only when the underlying task finishes and observes an orphaned exception without logging private text. close rejects new work and waits for retained tasks; cancelling close does not cancel the threads. An incomplete close can be observed again later.

For conversational code this is both a latency and correctness boundary. Blocking schema validation or connection work belongs in controlled startup or the bounded offload, not on the media loop. The tests hold real underlying work, cancel its caller, assert the slot stays occupied, attempt another call, then release the operation and verify the original result and clean closure.

followups.question: Does asyncio.shield make the database write cancellable?
followups.answer: No. Shield protects ownership of the underlying task from the waiter's cancellation. The caller can still receive cancellation promptly, but the operation may commit later. Reconciliation must use the original identity, and cleanup must continue observing actual work.

followups.question: What if close fails while the body already raised?
followups.answer: Preserve the primary body failure or cancellation and attach a safe cleanup-incomplete note. Replacing it with a generic close timeout would hide the useful failure. The outstanding resource still needs ownership and a later closure observation.

questions.watch_for: A finally block that releases capacity on waiter cancellation can violate the actual I/O bound.

questions.title: Admission and useful progress at capacity
questions.question: Why are pending, active and retained-record limits separate, and what must still work when they are full?
answer: They bound different resources. Pending capacity bounds accepted unfinished work, including durable waits and committed-but-unfinished intents. Active capacity bounds current invocation leases, not all remote physical computation. Retained-record capacity bounds protected identities that must remain available for replay and deduplication. A completed workflow can free pending capacity while still consuming retained identity capacity.

The limits are persisted and enforced under shared admission so competing processes cannot each admit up to an independent in-memory cap. The due selector skips unsignalled waits, exhausted epochs and terminal state, and acquires the selected lease within the same transaction. It treats global active saturation as backpressure rather than an acknowledgement that work ran.

Known replay and authorized reads must remain useful at capacity. Rejecting an old request merely because the queue is now full would make acknowledgement-loss recovery unsafe. Tests need both negative admission assertions and positive replay, cancellation, read and useful second-work progress. The documented defaults are local safety ceilings, not measured production throughput or a promise that four leased invocations imply four total remote computations.

followups.question: Why count a waiting case as pending when it uses no child?
followups.answer: It still consumes accepted responsibility, retained continuation and future service capacity. Excluding waits would let callers bypass the backlog bound by creating many long-lived waiting cases, even though active process occupancy remains low.

followups.question: Can deleting UI history free admission capacity?
followups.answer: Not for protected identities. Display retention and business identity retention have different purposes. Any capacity reclamation needs an explicit replay horizon and tombstone contract; hiding an event does not make its original command safe to accept again.

questions.watch_for: Do not report a semaphore limit as a cross-process durable admission guarantee.

evidence.label: Waits and committed intents consume pending

questions.title: Persisted retry pacing and its limit
questions.question: What does booking schema v5 change, and what retry problem remains open?
answer: Version 5 adds mutation_effects.next_attempt_at as persisted due state. For a known dependency_unavailable failure before any dispatch reservation, with attempts and deadline remaining and no cancellation, finish_failure closes the attempt and returns the effect to pending. The retry delay doubles from one second up to thirty seconds and is capped by the original deadline. The selector leaves that pending effect alone until due, so restart does not reset the wait.

Compatibility is deliberate: v4 retains its immediate-due behavior, and old rows upgraded to v5 have a NULL due value and remain eligible at once. Cancellation bypasses a paced wait so that safety commands are not delayed behind backoff. The owner-only upgrade preserves original payloads and identities; serving code performs no DDL.

The current audit records a real limitation: pacing does not cover outages after a dispatch reservation. MutationWorker can raise while a cooperating lookup remains unavailable, preserving the possible call but not passing through the pre-dispatch pending-pacing branch. I would describe this as an open reliability improvement, not claim that every dependency outage is exponentially backed off. Repeated physical remote work also remains governed by its supplier contract.

followups.question: Would you add jitter?
followups.answer: For many deployed workers, jitter can reduce synchronized retries, but it must fit the persisted scheduling contract and be testable. I would first preserve original identity, finite attempts, deadline and cancellation priority, then define and freeze the jitter policy before measurement.

followups.question: Why persist the due time rather than sleep in the worker?
followups.answer: A sleeping worker consumes occupancy and loses its schedule on restart. Persisted due state lets the worker release its child and lease, serve other tasks, and recover the original schedule from the authority after process loss.

questions.watch_for: The implemented v5 branch is pre-dispatch pacing; do not generalize it to all ambiguous post-dispatch outages.

questions.title: Safe migration without runtime repair
questions.question: How do you upgrade the store without silently changing old work or requiring the application to own DDL rights?
answer: Schema creation, controlled cutover and upgrades belong to explicit owner commands. Runtime roles validate an already active supported catalog and its grants, then fail closed on drift; they do not repair tables or initialize missing consent at startup. The booking schema and opt-in work schema are separate version lines, so booking v5 is not work-profile v5.

The booking sequence is additive and ordered. In particular, the v3-to-v4 coordination upgrade refuses an unmanaged running inquiry before DDL, because that work must first be reconciled using the old authority. Managed work can subsequently recover through explicit v4 leases. The v4-to-v5 upgrade adds due metadata while preserving existing rows as immediately due. Older upgrade entry points do not downgrade newer catalogs.

The evidence must go beyond an empty-database migration: use populated prior schemas, original payload and receipt comparisons, precommit failure rollback, lost upgrade acknowledgement, exact backup restore and runtime privilege rejection. Serving should not need migration credentials. A migration that changes the meaning of old consent or drops deduplication history is a correctness change even if every table can still be read.

followups.question: Why reject a drifted catalog instead of adopting it?
followups.answer: Unexpected tables, views, grants or constraints can change behavior and even trigger side effects during inspection. Automatic adoption would turn an unknown deployment into an asserted guarantee. An explicit owner diagnosis and controlled upgrade preserves a reviewable authority boundary.

followups.question: What does a backup test need to prove?
followups.answer: Restore the actual pre-upgrade state into an isolated target, verify original bytes and identities, then run the documented upgrade again and make useful progress. Merely producing a nonempty backup file does not prove recovery works.

questions.watch_for: Do not let application startup quietly upgrade, activate an unfinished import or restore missing consent bindings.

evidence.label: Reject unmanaged running inquiry before DDL

questions.title: The separate accepted-work profile
questions.question: Why introduce work_api instead of letting P3 maintain a second durable delegation queue?
answer: P1 remains the single durable execution owner. The opt-in work profile accepts opaque immutable read-only delegation bytes, scoped to a verified tenant and account and a stable command key. It preserves the original operation, digest and deadline and records requested cancellation. P3 can interpret specialist contracts and derived applicability, but it must not duplicate accepted work into a competing recovery ledger.

The profile is explicitly installed in a marked p1_work_ schema, separate from the booking lifecycle. Version 1 is acceptance only. WorkClient exposes submit, find, get and cancel; it binds scope through its credential directory and supplies no per-call scope override. New payload admission checks its bounded deadline and caps, while exact replay is handled before expiry or capacity checks. Acceptance does not grant invocation, mutation or delivery authority.

This separation keeps the reusable boundary small and allows later versions to add issued execution and result delivery without turning P1 into a general coroutine engine. A developer can reason about one original accepted identity, inspect it after a crash and compose the next capability explicitly. Tests verify concurrency, uncertain acknowledgement, retained caps, role drift and useful progression even when telemetry fails.

followups.question: Are opaque bytes an excuse to skip schema validation?
followups.answer: No. P1 validates its transport and ownership envelope and preserves exact bytes; P3 validates the specialist's versioned semantic schema. Each layer owns the validation needed for its contract, and neither should invent authority from untrusted request-body scope labels.

followups.question: Why not use a broker message as the accepted work record?
followups.answer: A broker can transport notifications, but accepted business identity, original bytes, cancellation and execution eligibility still need one authority. Introducing a second durable owner would require a new atomicity and reconciliation design that this local POC deliberately avoids.

questions.watch_for: Accepted is not running, completed, delivered or permitted to mutate a booking.

evidence.label: Runtime cannot DDL or rewrite identity

questions.title: Issue once and reconcile the original grant
questions.question: Why does execution_api return both an issued grant and created?
answer: Only created=true permits the caller to invoke the specialist. The issue command persists an immutable grant with accepted work, original command, owner, attempt UUID, number, epoch and lease. Concurrent or repeated calls for the same command can return that exact existing grant with created=false. If every caller invoked whenever it received a grant, an acknowledgement retry would become a duplicate remote invocation.

After an unknown issue acknowledgement, the caller reconciles through find_issue using the original command identity and must not automatically invoke the found grant. A new grant can be issued only through a distinct explicit eligible operation subject to cancellation, original deadline, active capacity and finite attempt bounds. Lease capacity bounds logical permission, not remote physical computation; an abandoned HTTP waiter might leave the old specialist running.

This is a useful API design pattern: make fresh authority explicit in the return type instead of forcing a developer to infer it from timestamps or status. The tests cover concurrent same-command issuance, global active caps across scopes, after-commit uncertainty, exact grant tampering and later useful execution. The runtime does not add an implicit scheduler, renewal loop or remote-stop guarantee.

followups.question: What if created=true is returned but the caller crashes before invoking?
followups.answer: That grant may represent unused authority, but replay must still not assume it was unused. Recovery follows the explicit contract and lease expiry before a new eligible issuance. Conservative uncertainty is safer than a duplicate invocation triggered by guessing.

followups.question: Can the specialist send back its own attempt ID?
followups.answer: It can echo correlation, but accepted result authority must match the exact P1-issued stored grant. The producer cannot create a valid execution attempt by inventing a wire identifier or claiming a scope in its payload.

questions.watch_for: Finding an old grant after acknowledgement loss is not fresh permission to call the specialist.

questions.title: Result truth and eligibility
questions.question: A specialist finishes after lease expiry or cancellation. Should P1 discard its answer?
answer: No. A known result is historical truth and should be retained under the exact original issued attempt. complete checks the stored grant for an exact match, rejects a changed replay body, and persists one immutable result per attempt. It classifies the result at the protected database commit as superseded, cancelled, expired, lease_expired or eligible_at_commit. The producer's completion timestamp cannot override the authority's post-lock time.

eligible_at_commit is deliberately narrow. It means the P1 lease, cancellation and time conditions held for that attempt when recorded. It does not establish factual correctness, semantic applicability to the current case, delivery permission or human consent. P3 validates meaning and case applicability separately; guarded action later rechecks current eligibility and exact confirmation. A later cancellation does not rewrite an already eligible result into a different historical disposition.

I would present a timeline with remote running, waiter abandoned, result received and result stored as separate observations. Tests should cover late bytes, changed bodies, superseded attempts, cancellation races and deadline passage while waiting for an actual SQL admission lock. Useful current work should progress alongside retained obsolete output.

followups.question: Why not trust the specialist timestamp if it completed before expiry?
followups.answer: A producer timestamp is an observation from another clock and does not prove the result was committed while P1 authority was live. The authority evaluates eligibility at its own protected commit; historical producer timing can remain diagnostic evidence.

followups.question: What should the UI call a late result?
followups.answer: Show it as a retained historical result with its disposition and observation time. Avoid language implying it is currently actionable. A current result view can separately explain whether it applies to the latest case and what further authorization is required.

questions.watch_for: Do not equate eligible_at_commit with factually valid, current-case applicable or authorized to act.

questions.title: Receiver binding and possible delivery
questions.question: How does result delivery avoid retargeting a possible send after a lost acknowledgement?
answer: The work v3 profile separates preparation, begin and receipt recording. prepare binds one eligible result digest to one immutable receiver and logical recipient for the original work. begin revalidates eligibility and inserts a possible-delivery marker. Only begin.created=true permits a fresh receiver accept call. A repeated possible delivery does not authorize another accept; recovery uses lookup at the originally bound receiver.

This design preserves ambiguity. If a call may have occurred, a missing receipt or reliable absence does not become permission to redirect the result to a new endpoint or person. When a known receipt arrives, record_receipt matches exact delivery, receiver, recipient and result digest and requires the possible marker. A known exact receipt remains a fact even after cancellation or deadline expiry, though no new delivery is permitted on that basis.

The standalone cooperating receiver uses retained identities and explicit initialization rather than runtime DDL. Tests cover immutable target conflicts, concurrent begin, forged receipts, cancelled-before-begin and known late receipts. Receiver acceptance is a machine receipt; neither it nor a P3 processing ACK means that a human acknowledged the result.

followups.question: Why recheck eligibility at begin after prepare already checked?
followups.answer: Preparation may be followed by cancellation, expiry or a newer result before external I/O. Begin is the admission point for a fresh possible call. Once it commits, later changes cannot retroactively prove that the admitted request never reached the receiver.

followups.question: Can a new receiver be used after a timeout?
followups.answer: Not for the same possible delivery. That could disclose the result to a different recipient and duplicate acceptance. Any new routing contract must explicitly resolve the original possibility rather than mutate its immutable receiver binding.

questions.watch_for: Possible delivery, known receipt, consumer processing ACK and human acknowledgement are distinct.

evidence.label: Fresh begin marker is call permission

questions.title: Guarded action across work and case state
questions.question: How can a specialist result influence a booking without giving the specialist mutation authority?
answer: The application uses P1's public action_api with separately trusted work and case credential bindings on the same PostgreSQL target. The lock order is booking admission, then work admission, then case and control locks. An existing action command receipt replays its original semantics. A new action must reference the exact latest stored eligible result and digest, an uncancelled work record, a live original deadline and an explicit v2 confirmation for the expected case revision.

The action store delegates exact commitment to the existing PostgresCaseAuthority inside that same transaction. A guarded clock rechecks database time after case locks, so a lock wait cannot bypass the original work deadline. The new action receipt and immutable case intent commit together. P1 does not parse the specialist's policy semantics; trusted P3 composition must validate factual support and applicability before asking for this guard.

No supplier I/O occurs inside the transaction, and no model output constructs consent. Tests deliberately make cancellation win before the locks or commitment win while both authorities are locked, then verify original receipts and useful separate work. An already committed unrelated case intent cannot be retroactively claimed as the result's action.

followups.question: Why must work and case profiles share a PostgreSQL target?
followups.answer: This implementation relies on one transaction protecting both authorities and their receipt. Splitting them across databases would remove that atomic commitment and require a different distributed protocol; a read-then-call sequence would not preserve the same guarantee.

followups.question: Does historical eligible result truth permit a new action after cancellation?
followups.answer: No. The old result remains factual history, but a new guarded action checks current work cancellation and deadline as well as exact case confirmation. Preserving truth and granting fresh authority are separate decisions.

questions.watch_for: Do not describe a P3 current badge or result digest as consent; the guarded exact controller commitment is still required.

evidence.label: Atomic work and case action guard

questions.title: A feed cursor that cannot skip a commit
questions.question: Why does the work v4 result feed allocate sequence numbers inside the result transaction?
answer: A global sequence allocated before commit can produce a cursor bug: transaction A reserves a lower number and stalls, B commits a higher number, and a consumer advances past B before A becomes visible. A's later commit is then skipped forever. The result feed avoids that by allocating a scope-local sequence under the existing admission guard and appending the event in the same transaction as result insertion.

The feed has a stable profile source UUID, immutable event IDs and cursors bound to source and tenant/account scope. Reads use a coherent repeatable-read, read-only transaction, reject a foreign source or scope and reject a cursor ahead of the current head. Exact completion replay emits no additional event. Existing results are backfilled once as adopted_history, preserving their original result bytes and timestamps while admitting that feed adoption order is historical reconstruction.

The feed is result-only and carries no source ACK or execution authority. P3 owns derived as-of projections and checkpoints. Tests use a deliberately uncommitted lower event and a competing completion, verify no skip, then reopen clients and check stable IDs. Restored divergent source incarnation rotation remains a separate unqualified recovery question.

followups.question: Why not use recorded_at_ms as the cursor?
followups.answer: Timestamps can tie and reflect a result observation rather than a safe committed ordering. A scope-local sequence allocated under the transaction guard provides an explicit bounded order; timestamp fields remain useful evidence without being the pagination arbitration rule.

followups.question: What does adopted_history mean to a consumer?
followups.answer: The event was created during upgrade for an already retained result. Its ordering is an adoption order, not proof that the original results committed in that sequence. Consumers must preserve original timestamps and avoid inventing a historical total order.

questions.watch_for: Do not use a global pre-commit sequence or a timestamp as proof that all earlier results are visible.

evidence.label: Event and sequence inside result transaction
Lower uncommitted event cannot be skipped

questions.title: Trusted scope and safe diagnostics
questions.question: Where does P1 obtain authority, and what prevents a tenant label or exception message from leaking data?
answer: The reusable store accepts trusted scope from application composition; an untrusted caller should receive a credential-bound public facade. TokenDirectory authenticates bounded opaque tokens against a finite trusted directory of digests and returns an immutable actor and scope. Public methods bind that context before accessing state and provide no caller-controlled actor or scope override. The accepted-work directory similarly binds tenant and account.

This is a local synthetic authentication mechanism, not production IAM. The directory deliberately has no self-registration, password login or general expiry service. A request body containing another tenant label cannot grant access. The case read checks scope and actor before disclosing detailed state or semantic conflicts. Worker grants add execution authority but do not authorize a controller confirmation.

Diagnostics use fixed allowlisted event and error codes rather than raw exception strings, request payloads or credentials. Even a malicious or broken exception code property must not replace the original failure. Telemetry errors must not change a committed result or make accepted work disappear. A production extension would add an explicit identity and secret-management design while preserving these narrow authority boundaries.

followups.question: Why hide the BearerToken value from repr?
followups.answer: Credentials can otherwise leak through object logging, trace attributes or debugging output. repr=False reduces accidental disclosure, but it is not complete sanitization; public diagnostics must still avoid serializing exception arguments, causes, environment values and request bodies.

followups.question: Would you log tenant and task IDs on every metric?
followups.answer: High-cardinality identifiers can overwhelm metrics and disclose context. Use bounded operation and outcome labels, and correlate detailed private traces under an explicit policy. Numeric process observations should not be mislabeled as durable global totals.

questions.watch_for: Body scope is data; only verified local principal bindings create authority.

evidence.label: No per-call actor or scope override

questions.title: A package a real consumer can install
questions.question: How do you prove this is a reusable library rather than a demo that only works inside its repository?
answer: P1 has one canonical src-layout distribution named agent-continuity with import namespace continuity_lab and a py.typed marker. The root application depends on the locked workspace member instead of duplicating a shadow package. The base package has no dependencies; PostgreSQL and telemetry are explicit extras. Public modules expose supported types and factories without starting services or running migrations at import time.

The important evidence is a built wheel and source distribution installed into isolated environments outside checkout import paths, plus installed examples and entry points. Source-tree unit tests can accidentally pass because undeclared sibling files are importable. Artifact checks examine archive paths, metadata, allowed payload and entry points, reject traversal or symlink surprises, and verify the root package does not accidentally ship services or harness code.

The declared Python support is 3.14 only. I would not claim broad interpreter support merely because most syntax looks portable. A real consumer example should construct credentials and adapters explicitly, run one useful normal and failure path, close resources and explain migration prerequisites. Public API review should test whether types make invalid authority combinations difficult to express.

followups.question: Why keep live inference dependencies out of the core library?
followups.answer: Case authority and durable execution should not require provider credentials or model SDKs. Native application composition selects inference. This keeps installation smaller, offline tests deterministic and business invariants identical across scripted and real-provider modes.

followups.question: What packaging bug could unit tests miss?
followups.answer: An example might import a private sibling module available only from the checkout, or the wheel might omit py.typed or an entry point. Only isolated installed-artifact execution proves the declared distribution contains and depends on what a consumer needs.

questions.watch_for: A passing editable install is not an isolated built-artifact qualification.

evidence.label: Import has no startup or migration

questions.title: Evidence you can defend
questions.question: Which claims about P1 are supported today, and how would you present limitations without understating the work?
answer: The charter records P1 V1 as locally qualified across all twenty acceptance rows for the explicitly selected provider_real v2 profile. That historical release includes independent supplier and receiver crash schedules, real PostgreSQL coordination, installed host and Linux artifacts, scripted media and selected real-provider evidence. It does not qualify the independent local_real profile, production-scale capacity or the complete three-project integrated release.

Current maintenance status adds a crucial qualification: after the v5 changes, the P1-20 provider deep-gate rerun remains open. The latest audit also records that the final full PostgreSQL run had five errors under host load, while targeted coordination and delivery reruns passed. I would report both facts and name the exact source snapshot and scope rather than flatten them into either everything passed or nothing works.

For interview preparation, reading tests and retained work-item evidence is different from executing those gates in this book task. I would demonstrate one reproducible normal path, one actual crash window and one negative authority case, then show the report and independent ledger checks. Counts and registration alone cannot replace applicable assertions; skipped, timed-out or missing setup remains non-passing.

followups.question: What is the difference between implemented and qualified?
followups.answer: Implemented means the behavior and its code path exist. Qualified means a declared gate executed and retained evidence for its specific scope and snapshot. A later code change can require requalification without erasing the historical result.

followups.question: Can the demo video prove reliability?
followups.answer: It is useful product evidence that a selected journey worked. It does not replace deterministic race schedules, independent supplier counts, actual process recovery or measured workload gates. A video should accompany a precise capability table and explicit open findings.

questions.watch_for: Do not relabel historical passed evidence as a fresh run after code changes, or treat a registered runner as a pass.

questions.title: Why this architecture instead of a workflow platform
questions.question: Why use a small PostgreSQL state machine rather than Temporal, Kafka or a general workflow engine?
