answer: The local POC needs a narrow accepted-work and exact-consent contract, not arbitrary coroutine replay. PostgreSQL already owns the case and immutable intent, so keeping persisted steps, waits, effects and short guarded transitions there makes the commitment boundary explicit. The worker pulls existing eligible state rather than introducing another accepted-work queue. The opt-in work profile similarly centralizes delegation ownership while leaving semantic interpretation to P3.

The trade-off is real: the project must implement and test leases, admission, retry pacing, schema upgrades, process cleanup and observability itself. A mature workflow platform could supply operational capabilities and broader orchestration, but it would not automatically solve exact human consent or an uncooperative supplier's ambiguous side effect. Kafka or NATS could transport events, but transporting an event is not the same as authorizing a business mutation.

I would choose the current boundary for the declared local scope and evaluate a workflow platform if product needs grow to many workflow types, long histories or larger operational teams. The comparison should use measured workload, failure contracts and developer ergonomics. I would preserve the public authority interface so infrastructure can evolve without changing what an acknowledged command means.

followups.question: Is the shared admission lock a scalability bottleneck?
followups.answer: It serializes important invariants and is defensible at the measured local scope, but it can become a contention limit. Before sharding it, measure lock wait and transaction occupancy, then preserve cross-capacity and action lock ordering through an explicit revised design.

followups.question: Would adding a message broker improve durability immediately?
followups.answer: Only after specifying what it owns and how its publish and consumer acknowledgements relate to the database commit. Adding infrastructure without that contract can create two recovering queues and more ambiguity rather than strengthen accepted-work guarantees.

questions.watch_for: Do not claim this local design is universally better than a workflow platform or already production-scale.

questions.title: A code review under changed constraints
questions.question: An interviewer asks you to simplify prepare_dispatch by removing dispatch_count because the new worker owns a fresh lease. How do you respond?
answer: I would preserve the distinction and draw a counterexample. Worker A commits a dispatch reservation, pauses before supplier I/O and loses its lease. Worker B acquires a new epoch and performs a lookup that finds nothing. The user cancels. If B treats its fresh claim as never dispatched, it records cancelled_before_dispatch. A then resumes and changes the booking. The database state has made a false prevention claim even though stale database writes are correctly fenced.

dispatch_count retains the possibility of A's external call across worker generations. The current prepare_dispatch branch records uncertainty when an earlier reservation exists and cancellation or deadline prevents a new call, rather than erasing that possibility. A cooperating supplier can deduplicate or expose a known result; a local lease cannot independently supply that cooperation.

To review the proposed simplification, I would write the timeline and expected invariant first, point to the existing independent-process regression tests, then require both negative truthfulness and useful recovery assertions. The strongest answer explains what the field protects, where its authority stops and which evidence would fail if it were removed. It does not defend complexity merely because the field already exists.

followups.question: What minimal test would catch the regression?
followups.answer: Pause an old worker after reservation but before external I/O, expire its lease, run a takeover lookup miss, cancel or expire the case, then resume the old call. Assert the takeover did not claim prevention, inspect supplier state and reject the old acknowledgement.

followups.question: What does this example show about framework API design?
followups.answer: Expose states that preserve real uncertainty even when they are less convenient for the happy path. A clean API should simplify correct composition, not compress distinct external realities into a misleading success, failure or cancelled enum.

questions.watch_for: Fresh local ownership never proves there was no earlier externally admitted call.

walkthrough.detail: Use the scoped public boundary and freeze the original request and key. Show one task, distinct case and original managed deadline after the acceptance commit.

walkthrough.step: Produce and confirm the exact proposal
walkthrough.detail: Read the current case and publish a supplier-bound v2 proposal. Use the authenticated controller to confirm its exact bytes and revision; show immutable confirmation, intent and dispatch event.
Use the declared isolated crash harness rather than killing arbitrary services. Preserve the original application and supplier stores after the failpoint.
A new leased worker reconciles the same supplier key, records known success and rejects a stale acknowledgement. Inspect the independent supplier count and exact booking revision.
Show the atomic final outcome and event, stable receiver binding and deduplication receipt. Keep delivery state separate from business success and from human acknowledgement.
Name the tested source snapshot and selected local gates, then explain unqualified local_real, pending post-v5 provider rerun and production-scale work.

limits: Historical P1 V1 qualification is for the selected local provider_real v2 scope. The post-v5 P1-20 provider deep-gate rerun remains open in the current work items.
local_real, production IAM, real supplier mutations, production capacity and multi-region failover are not established by the local POC.
The latest audit records a full PostgreSQL run with five errors under host load, followed by passing targeted coordination and delivery reruns. This review does not relabel it a clean full run.
v5 retry pacing covers a known pre-dispatch dependency-unavailable branch; postreservation outage pacing is an open finding.
Work-feed restored-branch source-incarnation rotation is not qualified. Retained identities have profile-lifetime protection until an explicit replay-horizon cleanup contract exists.
The book review reads implementation and tests; it does not claim to have executed the acceptance, media or provider gates.

chapters.title: P1 Code decisions under the transaction boundary
chapters.subtitle: Read the exact branch and defend its consequences
intro: These sixteen decision cards are a second source-first pass through P1. Each starts from a continuous excerpt of actual implementation, ties it to a named existing test and asks what changes if a small line-ordering or validation decision is removed.

The earlier Q-P1 answers establish system contracts. These cards examine local implementation choices: primitive validation before equality, disclosure precedence, conditional write assertions, retained evidence, commit uncertainty, actual task ownership and catalog preflight. Related question IDs connect both reading levels.

Code and test references describe the reviewed checkout. Test assertions are read from source and were not executed for this book. Alternatives are explicitly identified as inferred tradeoffs unless the implementation comment or repository history documents the reason.

concepts.title: Read the ordering
concepts.body: Ask what must be validated before comparison, before a detailed error, before a temporal check, before commit and before cleanup. Reordering two individually sensible lines can change the contract.

concepts.title: Find the owning object
concepts.body: A waiter, a retained task, a database row and an external request have different lifetimes. Identify which one actually owns capacity or truth before changing a finally block.

concepts.title: State the evidence limit
concepts.body: A representative test may verify an observable contract without forcing every defensive branch. Distinguish directly asserted behavior from a reasoned counterexample and proposed additional coverage.

concepts.title: Separate compatibility axes
concepts.body: Booking v4/v5 and work v1-v4 are different schema lines. Runtime validation and an owner upgrade have separate credentials, side effects and recovery obligations.

questions.title: Read the clock after waiting for authority
questions.question: Why does the lease guard call clock_timestamp after acquiring locks rather than use transaction_timestamp or the grant timestamp?
answer: The helper deliberately requests PostgreSQL wall time on the connection that owns the protected write. Its comment names the trap: transaction_timestamp is fixed when the transaction begins. A worker can start while its lease is live, block on admission, and acquire the lock only after expiry. Using transaction-start time would then authorize a late write. require_worker_lease locks the retained lease row before calling this helper and compares stored expiry against that newly sampled instant.

The returned datetime is also checked for exact type and a timezone before conversion to UTC. That verifies the observation's shape; it does not prove the database clock cannot jump or that a supplier honors the same lease. The representative test observes an actual SQL lock wait crossing server expiry, expects the old child to report lost authority, then acquires epoch two for useful progress.
questions.alternatives: The documented alternative being rejected is transaction-start time. Application monotonic time is useful for local occupancy budgets, but substituting it for database eligibility would require a new distributed-clock contract. A cached grant expiry remains context, not a fresh authority observation.
questions.counterfactual: Replace clock_timestamp with transaction_timestamp. An old transaction waiting on admission can retain an earlier valid instant and commit after the real lease expired, undermining the protected-write fence despite correct epoch values.

challenge.symptom: An old worker sometimes commits after a heavily contended transaction even though its logged cached expiry is in the past. The timing suggests stale eligibility evaluation rather than necessarily duplicate acquisition.
challenge.diagnosis: Compare transaction start, actual lock-wait observation and fresh database time after admission. A test that merely sleeps before opening the transaction cannot expose this particular ordering defect.
challenge.handling: Existing handling samples database time after locks and rejects expiry. A proposed operational improvement is to record bounded lock-wait timing separately; that would diagnose contention without making client clocks authoritative.

followups.question: Does clock_timestamp make all case reads atomic?
followups.answer: No. It supplies one time observation within a protected transaction. P2 history, public case reads and external supplier state may still be separately timed; their freshness must not be inferred from this helper.

followups.question: Why verify a timezone-aware datetime?
followups.answer: A naive datetime has no unambiguous absolute meaning. Rejecting it prevents accidental local-time interpretation at a permission boundary. The check validates the adapter output, while schema and role validation protect its expected source.

followups.question: Would a shorter lease solve the bug?
followups.answer: No. It can make the stale-time window easier to hit. The ordering must remain correct for every explicitly supported lease duration, and occupancy limits and supplier reconciliation remain separate mechanisms.

questions.watch_for: The helper is safe only in its documented post-lock calling context; copying it before admission changes the guarantee.

evidence.label: Real admission wait crosses server expiry

test.name: test_guard_samples_database_time_after_waiting_for_admission_lock
test.assertion: The child is observed actually waiting for the advisory admission lock before server expiry. Once expiry occurs, it reports lost authority; a successor acquires epoch two. This reads an existing test and does not rerun it.

diagram_hint.title: A transaction starts before the lease expires but obtains its lock afterward
steps: Conceptual timeline; labels such as blocked and rejected are explanatory observations, not new persisted enums.
Old transaction begins while the stored lease is still live, then waits on the admission lock.
The lock holder keeps admission until PostgreSQL time reaches lease expiry; the test observes the actual waiting lock graph.
After admission and lease-row lock, the old worker samples clock_timestamp and rejects the expired grant.
A dotted alternative arrow shows the bug: transaction_timestamp still points to the earlier start and would mis-authorize the old worker.
The successor acquires epoch two and releases it; annotate that this fences local writes and says nothing about stopping a prior supplier call.

questions.title: Check scope before revealing coordination state
questions.question: Why does require_worker_lease look up the scoped execution before reporting a missing or malformed lease?
answer: The first execution lookup is intentionally earlier than lease inspection. A caller outside the retained task's scope receives ExecutionNotFound before it can learn whether a lease is missing, busy or owned elsewhere. Only after that scoped existence check does the code inspect the schema version, require a typed grant, compare task and scope, and lock the lease row. Error precedence is therefore part of the disclosure contract, not just a cosmetic choice.

This helper receives trusted scope from application composition; it is not itself a credential verifier. The representative test exercises both levels: foreign-scope get and acquire fail as not found, and a missing grant for foreign scope also fails as not found. A real grant applied to a different accessible task produces LeaseLost. A reader can infer deliberate scoped observation order, but cannot infer a complete production IAM or side-channel guarantee.
questions.alternatives: Inferred tradeoff: validating the grant first would simplify some early argument errors, but it would expose coordination distinctions before scoped access is established. A separate authenticated facade can still reject invalid credentials before entering this store-level helper.
questions.counterfactual: Move the grant-is-None check above the scoped lookup. A foreign caller can now distinguish a task needing a lease from an unavailable scoped task through error behavior, violating the tested error precedence.

challenge.symptom: A support endpoint returns different lease errors for identifiers belonging to another account. Nothing was mutated, but the API exposes coordination detail that should remain unavailable to that account.
challenge.diagnosis: Trace the first database lookup and the first detailed error. Determine whether actor authentication and retained scoped existence checks run before grant inspection, rather than treating all validation as interchangeable.
challenge.handling: Existing handling performs the scoped read first and exposes a fixed not-found result. Production identity integration would be additional work; this source order should be preserved in that facade.

followups.question: Is an opaque UUID enough to prevent disclosure?
followups.answer: No. Unguessability reduces enumeration but does not define authorization, and identifiers can appear in links or logs. The operation must enforce retained scope even when the caller already knows the exact identifier.

followups.question: Why allow reads without a worker lease?
followups.answer: Authenticated inspection and controller cancellation belong to a different authority than worker execution. Requiring a worker grant for all reads would unnecessarily couple user visibility to an invocation owner and impede recovery.

followups.question: Can a request body choose scope_id?
followups.answer: The low-level store expects trusted application composition. Untrusted clients should receive the bound public facade, whose credential supplies scope. A body label cannot grant a different tenant or account identity.

questions.watch_for: Error ordering does not replace credential authentication; it preserves a narrower store disclosure boundary.

evidence.label: Foreign scope and wrong-task grant errors

test.name: test_scoped_lookup_precedes_coordination_observation
test.assertion: Foreign-scope lookup, acquisition and lease validation raise ExecutionNotFound. A grant bound to another accessible workflow raises LeaseLost. These assertions distinguish disclosure precedence from ordinary wrong-grant rejection.

questions.title: Reject hostile equality before comparing values
questions.question: Why does WorkPayload use exact type checks before equality, and reject True as a millisecond integer?
answer: Python equality and type relationships can hide surprising behavior at a public boundary. The operation test first requires type(operation) is str, so short-circuiting rejects an arbitrary object before evaluating its equality against the allowed operation. The test supplies HostileEquality, whose equality method raises if called. Body validation similarly requires immutable bytes instead of a mutable bytearray, and the timestamp helper requires exact int, excluding bool even though bool subclasses int.

After validation, the digest is derived from the retained bytes rather than accepted from the caller. These are defensive choices for a narrow value contract, not a claim that every subclass is malicious. The existing tests reject hostile objects, mutable or oversized bytes and boolean deadlines, then accept the exact maximum byte and timestamp bounds. P1 still treats the body as semantically opaque; P3 must validate its own payload schema.
questions.alternatives: Inferred tradeoff: isinstance would be friendlier to user-defined subclasses and coercion would accept more input formats, but both expand the callable behavior and representations a low-level value must tolerate. Exact primitives make a deliberately small wire-adjacent API easier to audit.
questions.counterfactual: Change the timestamp helper to isinstance(value, int). True becomes a valid one-millisecond deadline value, defeating the exact numeric contract and allowing booleans to cross an interface intended for absolute integer time.

challenge.symptom: An apparently simple invalid operation object executes user code during validation, or JSON true reaches an integer-only field. Static annotations did not prevent either value from arriving at runtime.
challenge.diagnosis: Inspect short-circuit order and Python bool/int semantics. Verify validation rejects unsupported objects before equality or conversion hooks execute, and distinguish immutable bytes from a mutable buffer carrying the same initial content.
challenge.handling: Existing handling uses exact primitives, immutable bytes and a computed digest. A more permissive convenience parser could be proposed above this boundary, with explicit conversion and independently tested ambiguity rules.

followups.question: Why not accept bytearray and freeze the dataclass?
followups.answer: Freezing prevents normal attribute reassignment, not mutation of a referenced buffer. Requiring bytes makes the retained body immutable under ordinary use; a separate parser could deliberately copy mutable input before constructing this value.

followups.question: Does the digest prove factual correctness?
followups.answer: No. It binds an exact byte sequence for identity and integrity comparisons. A factually false or adversarial result can have a perfectly valid digest, so semantic support and action permission remain separate checks.

followups.question: Can trusted code still tamper with a frozen value?
followups.answer: Python freezing is not a security sandbox against arbitrary privileged code. The public submit path reconstructs the payload and the store reconstructs it again, validating the boundary rather than trusting a cached caller-supplied digest.

questions.watch_for: Exact-type validation is an intentional narrow interface; do not present it as general Python style for every object model.

evidence.label: Rejected values and valid boundary progress

test.name: test_bad_values_reject_before_caller_hooks_and_valid_input_progresses
test.assertion: Hostile operation equality, bytearray, empty or oversized bodies, boolean and out-of-range deadlines are rejected. A payload at the exact allowed maximum remains accepted, proving rejection is paired with useful valid input.

questions.title: Bound the iteration rather than trusting len
questions.question: Why does WorkDirectory check the inventory size inside the items loop after it already checked len(registrations)?
answer: Mapping is a behavioral interface, not proof that len and items agree. A custom mapping can report one registration while yielding thousands, yield nothing, or repeat the same credential with different principals. WorkDirectory therefore bounds actual accumulated entries inside iteration, rejects duplicate token digests, and verifies that something was actually yielded. The outer length check remains a cheap ordinary-input filter, while the inner checks enforce what construction really consumed.

The resulting directory stores a finite snapshot of token digests and validated principals. Clearing the source mapping afterward does not remove registrations. The test's ReportedOne mapping records iteration count: overflow is rejected on the sixty-fifth yielded item, an empty iterator is rejected, and exactly sixty-four registrations remain usable. This establishes finite retained inventory and duplicate rejection for the tested iteration behavior, not a sandbox against a malicious iterator that blocks forever.
questions.alternatives: Inferred tradeoff: dict(registrations) would simplify later reads but could consume an unbounded custom iterator before any cap is checked. Requiring an exact built-in dict would narrow the contract further; the present implementation accepts Mapping while explicitly bounding consumed entries.
questions.counterfactual: Remove the in-loop size guard because len was checked already. A mapping that reports one item can grow the retained credential inventory beyond sixty-four, increasing memory and authentication work outside the documented bound.

challenge.symptom: A configuration object passes the inventory length check, yet startup consumes unexpectedly many credentials or silently replaces a principal. The failure appears during trusted configuration ingestion rather than an HTTP request.
challenge.diagnosis: Compare reported length with actual yielded items and repeated digests. A fixture that uses only a normal dict cannot exercise a lying Mapping, so the test deliberately supplies custom items behavior.
challenge.handling: Existing handling caps actual iteration and rejects repeated digests and empty output. If configuration can execute untrusted Python, process isolation or a data-only configuration format would be an additional proposed boundary.

followups.question: Why reject duplicate digest entries instead of last-wins?
followups.answer: Last-wins could silently change which account a credential authorizes depending on iteration order. Explicit rejection forces ambiguous configuration to be resolved rather than making a principal replacement look like an ordinary directory construction.

followups.question: Why store digests instead of the original mapping?
followups.answer: A snapshot prevents later mutation of the supplied mapping from changing authority unexpectedly, and digest storage reduces accidental token disclosure in the directory. The caller and facade may still hold the original credential and need safe handling.

followups.question: Does the loop cap bound construction time?
followups.answer: It bounds retained items and the number of successful iterations examined before overflow. An iterator or hash operation that never returns is a different execution risk; no line here can guarantee time bounds against arbitrary trusted Python code.

questions.watch_for: A finite collection interface does not guarantee finite or honest producer behavior.

evidence.label: Reported-one mapping and actual yield bound

test.name: test_mapping_items_cannot_exceed_the_credential_inventory_limit
test.assertion: A mapping reporting length one is rejected when it yields no entries or more than sixty-four; overflow stops at the sixty-fifth yield. Exactly sixty-four yielded registrations still authenticate successfully.

questions.title: Treat a conditional write as an assertion
questions.question: The case row was already locked and its revision checked. Why also require rowcount == 1 after the revision UPDATE?
answer: The conditional UPDATE encodes the expected revision in the write itself. The explicit rowcount assertion refuses to continue if that transition did not affect exactly one row. Without it, later wait expiration and returned state could make a command appear successful even though its intended revision change did not occur. The same pattern checks each pending wait update before advancing further inside the protected transaction.

Admission and row locking should prevent ordinary concurrent mutation from slipping between the preceding read and this write. The count check is therefore defensive evidence of the transition invariant, not proof that the current implementation is lock-free or relies only on optimistic concurrency. The representative race test checks the public expected-revision contract: revision-first invalidates old confirmation, then a fresh quote progresses. It does not directly force this rowcount branch or establish independent coverage for arbitrary catalog corruption.
questions.alternatives: Inferred tradeoff: trusting the lock and omitting the conditional predicate would reduce duplicate checks, but weaken the local assertion if surrounding code or storage behavior changes. A database function could centralize the transition, at the cost of a different public and migration surface.
questions.counterfactual: Ignore changed.rowcount and continue expiring waits. If the revision predicate affects zero rows after a future refactor, the operation can invalidate continuation context without performing its promised request revision, hiding a failed transition.

challenge.symptom: A command reports a later state but its requested revision never changed, or pending waits disappear after a no-op update. The symptom suggests control flow continued past a failed conditional transition.
challenge.diagnosis: Inspect the UPDATE predicate, expected revision and actual affected row count before examining subsequent wait updates. Distinguish an early StaleRevision error from the defensive post-write TransitionConflict branch; they are not the same test path.
challenge.handling: Existing handling raises TransitionConflict and rolls back the whole protected transaction on a wrong count. A proposed additional fault-injection test could force zero affected rows if direct coverage of that defensive branch is required.

followups.question: Does rowcount replace the lock?
followups.answer: No. The transaction still needs coherent revision, intent, cancellation and wait observations. Rowcount asserts that exactly one intended transition happened; it does not make a preceding multi-row decision atomic by itself.

followups.question: Why check each wait update too?
followups.answer: Wait expiry is part of the revision transition. Silently failing one expiry would leave incompatible pending context while returning a revised case. Raising before commit makes the whole operation fail consistently.

followups.question: What result should the UI infer from TransitionConflict?
followups.answer: It should refresh authorized current state and follow the operation contract. It must not assume its revision won or automatically rebase the same user instruction, particularly when the original acknowledgement is ambiguous.

questions.watch_for: The cited race test covers the observable revision contract, not every defensive rowcount error branch.

evidence.label: Conditional revision update and affected-row assertion
Revision-first race and useful fresh confirmation

test.name: test_revision_wins_race_and_stale_confirmation_cannot_commit
test.assertion: The winning revision becomes one, old confirmation fails with StaleRevision and no consent rows commit. A fresh quote then produces one confirmation, intent and dispatch. It does not directly inject a zero-row UPDATE.

questions.title: A committed read validates its original evidence
questions.question: Why reconstruct and compare consent and dispatch evidence when reading an already committed intent?
answer: The intent row is not trusted merely because its columns decode. The read path requires its original confirmation and dispatch records, reconstructs their expected canonical content from the immutable intent, and compares all bound fields. The excerpt shows the dispatch event rebuilt from original identity and timestamp, followed by exact comparisons for both evidence records. Missing evidence is rejected earlier; changed canonical content becomes InvalidStoredState here.

This prevents a readable commitment from drifting away from the exact consent and event that justified it. The representative test removes dispatch evidence, then inserts an empty payload under the right IDs; both reads fail. Restoring the original canonical event makes the existing intent readable again. These checks detect particular retained inconsistencies and fail closed; they are not cryptographic protection against a privileged owner rewriting every related record consistently, nor do they authorize runtime automatic repair.
questions.alternatives: Inferred tradeoff: foreign keys and immutable runtime grants could be considered sufficient for ordinary operation, reducing read cost. Reconstructing original evidence catches corruption or owner-side drift that referential existence alone misses, while adding queries and validation work to the read path.
questions.counterfactual: Replace exact evidence comparison with a check that the dispatch row exists. An empty or changed payload under the correct event and intent IDs would become a seemingly valid committed read, severing its original semantic evidence.

challenge.symptom: A retained intent is present, but inspection fails with invalid stored state after an administrative repair. The failure may protect against inconsistent evidence rather than indicate that consent should be recreated.
challenge.diagnosis: Read the original intent, confirmation and dispatch records under authorized tooling; compare canonical payloads and bindings. Checking only matching foreign keys misses the exact content and timestamps this read requires.
challenge.handling: Existing handling refuses the inconsistent read without repair. The test restores original evidence using owner credentials. Production recovery would need an explicit reviewed procedure and retained originals, not generated replacement consent.

followups.question: Why reconstruct from the intent instead of current quote state?
followups.answer: The intent binds an immutable original proposal. Later mutable state must not supply missing consent or silently reinterpret the committed operation. Current-state integrity is checked separately when the case snapshot is assembled.

followups.question: Can runtime recreate missing dispatch evidence?
followups.answer: No automatic repair is authorized by this read. Fabricating evidence could conceal data loss or an incomplete migration. An owner must investigate original receipts and use a declared recovery procedure before serving a trusted commitment again.

followups.question: Is canonical equality the same as a signature?
followups.answer: No. It is a deterministic integrity comparison within the trusted database boundary. It detects inconsistent representations and bindings; it does not prove who performed a privileged write or protect against an owner changing the whole evidence graph.

questions.watch_for: Readable committed state requires original evidence; reconstructing expected bytes does not grant permission to reconstruct lost consent.

evidence.label: Missing and altered dispatch rejected then original restored

test.name: test_committed_read_requires_mandatory_canonical_dispatch_evidence
test.assertion: Deleting dispatch evidence makes reads fail. Inserting the same IDs with an empty payload still fails. Restoring canonical original bytes returns the same intent and exact original dispatch event, with no invented replacement commitment.

questions.excerpt:
event = IntentDispatch(intent.dispatch_event_id, intent, intent.created_at)
            expected_dispatch = (
                event.event_id,
                intent.intent_id,
                canonical(event.payload()),
                event.created_at,
            )
            actual_dispatch = tuple(
                dispatch[name] for name in ("event_id", "intent_id", "payload_json", "created_at")
            )
            if expected_confirmation != actual_confirmation or expected_dispatch != actual_dispatch:
                raise ValueError("Intent evidence does not match its immutable snapshot")
        except (ValueError, TypeError, KeyError, OverflowError) as error:
            raise InvalidStoredState("Intent has invalid commitment evidence") from error

questions.title: Replay has precedence over new admission
questions.question: Why does WorkStore return an existing record before checking expiry and retained-record capacity?
answer: The nested acceptance function first finds the scoped key and compares the immutable payload. Identical existing work returns created=false; conflicting bytes or deadline return identity_conflict. Only a genuinely new identity reaches the deadline-window and capacity checks. That ordering preserves the ability to resolve an old acknowledgement even after time passes or the store fills. It does not extend the old deadline or authorize execution.

The store reconstructs WorkPayload before this function so the comparison uses validated operation, body and derived digest. The deadline is part of those original semantics. The representative one-record fixture fills capacity, rejects a new key and a second cancellation command, yet still replays the original submit and cancellation and reads retained cancellation state. A reader can infer exact recovery access at capacity, not permission to delete protected identities or treat an old accepted record as newly runnable.
questions.alternatives: Inferred tradeoff: checking capacity first is a common quick rejection optimization, but it makes replay depend on unrelated later load. A dedicated replay endpoint could preserve recovery separately, although all command retries would then need clear routing and equivalent conflict semantics.
questions.counterfactual: Move the capacity or expiry branch above existing-key lookup. A caller retrying an already committed command can receive capacity or expired instead of its original receipt, leaving acceptance unresolved and encouraging a dangerous replacement identity.

challenge.symptom: An outage fills retained capacity, and clients can no longer recover receipts for commands accepted earlier. Operators see rejection errors even though the original rows remain present and should be readable.
challenge.diagnosis: Trace whether new-work admission checks precede original-identity lookup. Confirm the retry retained the exact original payload and deadline; changed semantics should still conflict rather than be accepted as an old command.
challenge.handling: Existing handling replays before new admission and leaves reads available. Cleanup or capacity expansion would require an explicit owner and replay-horizon contract; dropping rows to clear the symptom is not a safe automatic remedy.

followups.question: Can an expired replay run again?
followups.answer: No. Replay returns retained acceptance truth. Issuance and action have separate current eligibility checks, so an old accepted record remaining inspectable does not renew its lease, deadline or business permission.

followups.question: Why is a changed deadline a conflict?
followups.answer: A new deadline changes accepted semantics and could extend authority after an ambiguous earlier submit. Recovery must preserve what was originally accepted; a new logical request needs its own explicit identity and eligibility decision.

followups.question: What if capacity counts are inconsistent?
followups.answer: The shared write wrapper validates persisted counters against actual retained rows under admission before running this function. A mismatch fails as schema_mismatch; the replay-first branch does not license ignoring corrupt authority metadata.

questions.watch_for: Replay-first applies within validated original authority; it is not a bypass for drifted counters or credentials.

evidence.label: Original record before new deadline and cap
One-record cap preserves replay and reads

test.name: test_retained_caps_preserve_replay_reads_and_original_cancel
test.assertion: With one retained record and cancellation command allowed, new identities hit capacity while the original submit and cancel replay and the retained record remains readable. This proves recovery remains useful when new admission is full.

questions.title: Mark possible commit before leaving the transaction
questions.question: What does the committing flag mean, and why is it set before the transaction context exits?
answer: The flag is a knowledge boundary, not a committed-state boolean. run has completed inside the transaction and the before_commit hook has passed. Setting committing=true before context exit acknowledges that the upcoming database commit may happen even if its acknowledgement, connection cleanup or after_commit hook fails. The outer error translation then returns acknowledgement_unknown rather than telling the caller the command definitely failed.

Before that point, a lock timeout can be capacity and an ordinary dependency failure can be storage_unavailable. After it, the wrapper conservatively maps even a domain-shaped exception to unknown because the caller cannot infer rollback from the error alone. The existing failpoint test proves before-commit failure leaves no row, whereas after-commit failure leaves one recoverable record and an identical replay. It does not simulate every network failure mode; it verifies the intended public distinction around the known commit hooks.
questions.alternatives: Inferred tradeoff: setting the flag only after commit returns seems more intuitive but misclassifies a lost commit acknowledgement. Returning the raw driver error could preserve diagnostics, but would leak details and still leave clients without a stable business uncertainty contract.
questions.counterfactual: Set committing=true after exiting the transaction. If PostgreSQL commits but the client loses the response during context exit, the catch block can label the call storage_unavailable instead of acknowledgement_unknown, obscuring possible accepted work.

challenge.symptom: A client receives a storage failure, creates a replacement request and later discovers two accepted identities. The original transaction may have committed despite the client never receiving a normal return.
challenge.diagnosis: Locate the possible commit point and inspect whether error translation preserves uncertainty after that point. Reconcile the original scoped key independently; the exception class alone cannot establish whether the row exists.
challenge.handling: Existing handling returns fixed acknowledgement_unknown and preserves exact original-key lookup. The caller must reconcile or replay that identity. Rich private driver diagnostics could be retained separately without altering the public result classification.

followups.question: Does unknown mean the commit definitely happened?
followups.answer: No. It means the caller lacks enough evidence to claim rollback or acceptance. The original identity must be looked up or replayed; both possible database outcomes remain compatible with that response.

followups.question: Why suppress the original exception text?
followups.answer: The wrapper exposes a finite safe code and avoids reflecting SQL, configuration or private sentinels. That translation is diagnostic hygiene, not proof that private traceback data no longer exists internally.

followups.question: Can the same wrapper decide whether to resend a supplier request?
followups.answer: No. This flag concerns a P1 database command. Supplier uncertainty requires its own separately documented immutable reservation, capability and lookup contract; a generic database error cannot authorize external effect retry.

questions.watch_for: committing means commit may have crossed the boundary; it must not be presented as durable proof of success.

evidence.label: Flag before context exit and fixed error translation

test.name: test_before_commit_rolls_back_after_commit_unknown_reconciles
test.assertion: The before-commit failpoint returns storage_unavailable and leaves no row. The after-commit failpoint returns acknowledgement_unknown; original-key lookup finds a row and replay returns it with created=false, without exposing the private sentinel.

            return result
        except psycopg.errors.LockNotAvailable:
            code = "acknowledgement_unknown" if committing else "capacity"
            self._emit(operation, code)
            raise WorkError(code) from None
        except WorkError as error:
            code = "acknowledgement_unknown" if committing else error.code
            self._emit(operation, code)
            raise WorkError(code) from None
        except Exception:  # noqa: BLE001 - Outer storage/failpoint/cleanup boundary.
            code = "acknowledgement_unknown" if committing else "storage_unavailable"
            self._emit(operation, code)
            raise WorkError(code) from None

questions.title: Release the slot when actual I O ends
questions.question: Why is semaphore release attached to the offload task completion callback instead of a finally around the caller await?
answer: The retained task owns the blocking operation and its slot. asyncio.shield allows the waiting caller to receive cancellation without propagating it into the owned offload task. The callback removes that actual task and releases capacity only after it finishes. It also retrieves a late exception without printing its private text, preventing an abandoned task failure from becoming an unobserved event-loop warning.

A finally around the caller's await would run as soon as the caller stopped waiting, even though the thread could still write. Repeated cancellations could then exceed the configured actual-I/O bound. The public-client test holds one operation, cancels its caller, confirms another call cannot start and close remains incomplete, then releases the underlying operation and observes successful closure. This preserves ownership; it cannot interrupt arbitrary blocking code or prove a remote supplier stopped.
questions.alternatives: Inferred tradeoff: a cancellable async database driver could offer a different cancellation contract, but remote commit uncertainty would still need reconciliation. The current bounded offload keeps synchronous adapters and makes actual lifetime ownership explicit at the cost of retained work after waiter cancellation.
questions.counterfactual: Release the semaphore in a caller-level finally. Every timeout can free a slot while its thread continues, allowing repeated abandoned requests to exceed the intended concurrency cap and race shutdown of shared resources.

challenge.symptom: The service advertises four active I/O slots but thread count and in-flight writes grow during client timeouts. The apparent semaphore accounting follows waiters instead of the operations actually consuming resources.
challenge.diagnosis: Hold an underlying operation, cancel its caller, then inspect pending_count and whether another operation enters. A timer-only mock that stops work on cancellation would hide the leak rather than reproduce this boundary.
challenge.handling: Existing handling retains actual tasks through completion and rejects excess admission. A proposed operational metric can expose abandoned-but-active work; it must not count a cancelled waiter as a freed resource.

followups.question: Why call completed.exception?
followups.answer: The original caller may have abandoned the await. Retrieving the late exception marks it observed and avoids an unhandled-task warning, while deliberately avoiding serialization of private error text into public diagnostics.

followups.question: What if the callback itself runs after close timed out?
followups.answer: The owner remains retained and releases capacity when it really finishes. A later close can observe drainage. The earlier timeout still means closure was incomplete; it is not retroactively a successful timely shutdown.

followups.question: Is shield a business cancellation mechanism?
followups.answer: No. It controls cancellation propagation between asynchronous tasks. Business cancellation is an explicit authenticated command with its own durable receipt and external-boundary semantics; a cancelled await cannot substitute for it.

questions.watch_for: Shield preserves task ownership; it does not make synchronous work remotely cancellable.

evidence.label: Actual offload task owns pending slot
Cancelled waiter retains slot and incomplete close

test.name: test_cancelled_waiter_keeps_slot_and_close_timeout_until_actual_work_finishes
test.assertion: Cancelling submit leaves pending_count at one, prevents a second underlying call and makes close time out. Releasing the held operation permits a later clean close; no business cancellation is invoked as a side effect.

questions.title: Preserve the primary failure during cleanup
questions.question: Why does __aexit__ attach a cleanup note when a body error already exists instead of raising the close timeout?
answer: The context manager makes error precedence explicit. If close times out with no existing body error, it raises that timeout. If the body already failed or was cancelled, it keeps that primary exception and adds a fixed note saying cleanup remains incomplete and work still owns capacity. This avoids replacing the useful business or control-flow failure with a secondary cleanup symptom.

The note does not declare cleanup successful, free the pending slot or swallow all close exceptions. The excerpt catches TimeoutError specifically; other close failures retain their ordinary semantics. The representative test checks object identity of the original RuntimeError, confirms the incomplete note and retained pending work, then releases the operation and closes successfully. Separate cancellation tests cover preserving CancelledError. A reader should not generalize this small handler into permission to ignore every shutdown failure.
questions.alternatives: Inferred tradeoff: always raising cleanup failure makes resource problems conspicuous but masks the initiating failure. An ExceptionGroup could expose multiple independent failures under a different API contract; this implementation preserves the original control flow and a safe fixed cleanup note.
questions.counterfactual: Unconditionally raise the close TimeoutError. A task cancelled for shutdown or a useful domain failure is replaced by a secondary timeout, obscuring the original cause and potentially changing how upstream cancellation handlers behave.

challenge.symptom: A meaningful failure disappears from reports and is replaced by a generic cleanup timeout. The original work is still active, so treating the new exception as the only event makes diagnosis and ownership tracking harder.
challenge.diagnosis: Compare the body exception object and cancellation state with what leaves the context manager. Verify whether cleanup mutated the error, masked it or silently claimed success; then inspect retained actual tasks.
challenge.handling: Existing handling preserves the primary exception and adds a safe incomplete-cleanup note. Operators still need to retain and reobserve resources. A proposed richer aggregate diagnostic must preserve cancellation semantics and private-data restrictions.

followups.question: Does adding a note finish resource cleanup?
followups.answer: No. It records unresolved ownership while preserving the original failure. The retained operation must still settle, and a later close must observe actual drainage before dependent shared resources are released.

followups.question: Why catch TimeoutError instead of Exception?
followups.answer: The code names one expected cleanup failure mode. Catching every exception could suppress unexpected bugs or corrupted closure behavior. Any broader policy would need explicit precedence and evidence rather than a blanket ignore clause.

followups.question: What if the body completed normally?
followups.answer: There is no earlier failure to preserve, so incomplete cleanup is the operation's failure and the timeout propagates. Normal body completion does not make a resource-owning context successful if it could not close.

questions.watch_for: A preserved primary exception and cleanup note are an honest failed-close result, not a clean-shutdown badge.

evidence.label: Specific timeout precedence in context exit
Original exception identity and pending owner preserved

test.name: test_context_preserves_body_error_when_close_is_incomplete
test.assertion: The exact original RuntimeError object escapes the context, carries a safe cleanup-incomplete note and leaves pending_count at one. After underlying work is released, another close observes zero pending work without replacing the original failure.

questions.title: Persist a deadline capped due time
questions.question: Why does the v5 retry branch persist min(now + backoff, original deadline), and why is NULL meaningful for upgraded rows?
answer: This branch is reached only for a known dependency_unavailable failure before any dispatch reservation, with attempts, time and cancellation conditions already checked. Version 5 computes an exponential delay from the retained attempt number, caps it at thirty seconds, then caps the due instant at the original business deadline. It persists that instant while returning the effect to pending and incrementing generation in the same protected transaction.

The selector can release execution resources and later honor the stored schedule after restart; it does not need a sleeping coroutine. The separate v4 branch omits the new column and preserves immediate eligibility. Existing rows upgraded to v5 retain NULL due time, meaning eligible at once rather than an invented historical wait. Tests show the first v5 retry waits exactly one second and then succeeds once. This branch does not pace post-reservation outages, which remain an explicit current limitation.
questions.alternatives: Inferred tradeoff: calculating delay only in the polling worker would avoid a stored column, but restart and competing workers could reset the schedule. Persisting jitter could help larger fleets; that would require a declared reproducible policy instead of silently changing this deterministic baseline.
questions.counterfactual: Store now + backoff without the deadline cap or recalculate due on every poll. The former schedules beyond the original boundary; the latter can postpone eligibility indefinitely and makes repeated observations change the intended schedule.

challenge.symptom: An unavailable dependency is called repeatedly after restart, or a pending effect never becomes due because every poll moves its due time forward. Both symptoms suggest schedule ownership is outside the persisted transition.
challenge.diagnosis: Inspect attempt_no, dispatch_count and stored next_attempt_at before and after polling and restart. First confirm the code reached the pre-dispatch retry branch; an ambiguous already-reserved call follows different recovery semantics.
challenge.handling: Existing v5 handling persists a finite capped due time; v4 and adopted NULL rows stay immediately due. Post-reservation outage pacing is proposed future work, not a behavior this excerpt establishes.

followups.question: Why cap by the original deadline?
followups.answer: The retry policy must not extend the accepted obligation. Reaching the original deadline makes it due for terminal handling rather than sleeping beyond it; the selector and transition still perform their own eligibility checks.

followups.question: Why retain a v4 branch?
followups.answer: A maintenance change must not issue SQL referencing a column absent from v4 or silently change its validated behavior. Only the explicit owner upgrade enables persisted retry metadata; serving does not migrate storage opportunistically.

followups.question: Can a paced retry delay cancellation?
followups.answer: It must not. The queue's due predicate separately admits cancellation, and cancellation tests prove a paced effect can be stopped with no supplier call. Backoff is pressure control, not permission to defer a safety command.

questions.watch_for: A stored due time paces one known pre-dispatch branch; it does not make every external retry safe or paced.

evidence.label: Wait until first due instant then useful success

test.name: test_paced_dependency_retry_waits_for_its_persisted_due_time
test.assertion: After a known pre-dispatch unavailability the effect is pending with dispatch_count zero and due at now plus one second. Selection returns none before due; at due the second attempt succeeds with one logical mutation.

questions.title: A lookup miss cannot erase a prior reservation
questions.question: Why does prepare_dispatch check dispatch_count before declaring cancellation or deadline prevention, even after absence_confirmed?
answer: The branch protects against an old request that was reserved but paused before external I/O. A newer worker can look up the operation and observe absence while that old request still has the ability to arrive. Therefore absence_confirmed cannot erase a positive dispatch_count. If cancellation or deadline now prevents a fresh call, the result must remain uncertain rather than claiming the old effect was prevented.

The guard records an immutable ambiguous outcome and keeps cancellation requested as a separate disposition. Only the following zero-prior-reservation paths can truthfully say cancelled before dispatch or definite expiry. The representative regression resumes a paused old call after takeover and cancellation and asserts UNCERTAIN, ambiguous_outcome and requested cancellation. This source decision was an actual audit repair. It does not promise that every uncertain supplier can later be reconciled or that killing the local worker stops an already external operation.
questions.alternatives: The tempting alternative is to trust the latest lookup as definitive absence. That is insufficient when an earlier call may still land. A supplier-supported fencing protocol could provide a stronger contract, but local database ownership alone cannot substitute for that participation.
questions.counterfactual: Remove dispatch_count from this condition because the takeover has a fresh lease. The new worker can label a paused old call cancelled_before_dispatch; the old call can then execute and make that stored prevention claim false.

challenge.symptom: A case displays prevented cancellation, yet the supplier later applies the old change. The problematic window is after a durable reservation and before an older paused request actually reaches the independent supplier.
challenge.diagnosis: Trace every retained reservation across epochs, then align the lookup miss and resumed old I/O. Current booking equality and the new worker lease cannot prove that this particular earlier call was never admitted.
challenge.handling: Existing handling records uncertainty whenever prior dispatch remains possible and cancellation or expiry blocks a new reservation. A stronger remedy would require a cooperating external fence; it is a distinct proposed supplier capability.

followups.question: Why retain the cancellation disposition?
followups.answer: It records the user request independently of effect truth. The system can truthfully say cancellation was requested while the effect remains uncertain; collapsing both into cancelled would invent prevention that the evidence cannot support.

followups.question: Would idempotent apply eliminate the need for this branch?
followups.answer: It can prevent duplicate logical effects, but cancellation after reservation still cannot prove no effect occurred. The UI and final outcome must preserve the possible original execution until reliable bound evidence establishes truth.

followups.question: Is absence_confirmed a permission token?
followups.answer: No. It is one separately supplied observation passed into the protected admission decision. Current cancellation, deadline and retained possible-dispatch history still constrain what the authority can truthfully reserve or finalize.

questions.watch_for: A newer owner and a reliable lookup miss do not retrospectively revoke an older admitted call.

test.name: test_cancel_during_paused_old_call_is_uncertain_not_prevented_after_takeover
test.assertion: The controlled paused-call takeover schedule returns UNCERTAIN with ambiguous_outcome and cancellation REQUESTED. It guards against falsely reporting pre-dispatch prevention when the original reserved external request can still land.

diagram_hint.title: A lookup miss cannot prevent a paused reserved supplier call
steps: A commits a dispatch reservation and pauses before supplier I/O; the durable dispatch_count is positive.
A loses its lease. B acquires the next epoch and looks up the original supplier key; lookup currently finds nothing.
The user cancellation is recorded before B attempts a fresh reservation.
B enters prepare_dispatch: positive prior dispatch_count plus cancellation means UNCERTAIN with ambiguous_outcome and cancellation REQUESTED.
A resumes its already-admitted external call, which may still apply. P1 rejects any stale local acknowledgement from A.
Show a crossed-out conceptual label prevented; show supplier outcome unknown or later known as a separate fact. Only the exact uppercase values above are enum-like code labels.

questions.excerpt:
# A prior reservation may still land after a lookup miss, so it cannot prove
            # prevention or a definite deadline failure.
            if not absence_confirmed or (
                row["dispatch_count"] > 0
                and (case.cancelled or now >= self._deadline(connection, case))
            ):
                self._finish_row(
                    connection,
                    case,
                    row,
                    EffectState.UNCERTAIN,
                    None,
                    EffectFailure.AMBIGUOUS_OUTCOME,
                    CancellationDisposition.REQUESTED
                    if case.cancelled
                    else CancellationDisposition.NOT_REQUESTED,
                    stamp,
                )

questions.title: Store late bytes and choose one disposition
questions.question: Why does complete classify superseded before cancellation, deadline and lease expiry instead of rejecting all late results?
answer: The ordered conditions choose one durable disposition for an exact issued attempt. An older attempt is superseded even if other later conditions are also true; otherwise cancellation, original deadline and lease expiry are considered in that order. Only the remaining case becomes eligible_at_commit. The result body is retained in all these branches, so rejecting current permission does not erase known historical bytes.

An earlier branch verifies exact stored grant equality and returns an identical existing result before reclassification. Consequently a later cancellation cannot rewrite the disposition of an already recorded eligible result. The representative attempt-cap test records an old result as superseded and the latest expired-lease result as lease_expired, retains both and reports exhausted execution. The branch ordering is visible behavior, but these tests do not exhaust every simultaneous-condition combination. Eligibility remains P1 timing and ownership evidence, not semantic validity or permission to mutate a case.
questions.alternatives: Inferred tradeoff: storing several independent reason flags would expose more detail when conditions overlap, but would change the result contract and consumers. Rejecting late bytes entirely would simplify current-state handling while losing evidence needed for reconciliation, audits and truthful historical display.
questions.counterfactual: Reject every result whose lease is expired before checking an existing result. A valid original result replay after expiry would stop returning its known truth, and late historical evidence would be lost instead of retained under its exact attempt.

challenge.symptom: A late specialist response disappears or an old result suddenly changes from eligible to cancelled after a later command. The problem may be mutable classification rather than inaccurate specialist output.
challenge.diagnosis: Compare original result identity, first recorded disposition and replay order. Separate the latest attempt relation from current cancellation and clocks; a single status string intentionally cannot express every overlapping reason.
challenge.handling: Existing handling retains immutable result bytes with one ordered disposition and replays originals first. A proposed multi-reason diagnostic could supplement history, but must not rewrite the original authoritative result or grant current action permission.

followups.question: Why give superseded first priority?
followups.answer: The code makes relation to the current issued attempt the first classification. That is an observable design choice; absent separate rationale, do not invent a product claim that it is the only valid ordering for every system.

followups.question: Can historical eligible bytes still be shown?
followups.answer: Yes, under authorized read and disclosure rules. Preserving an originally eligible result does not make it current for a revised case or permit a new delivery or action after cancellation and deadline.

followups.question: What if replay supplies a changed body?
followups.answer: The earlier immutable-result check rejects identity_conflict. A producer cannot replace historical bytes under the same attempt merely because the work is now expired or a new specialist answer seems better.

questions.watch_for: One disposition is a deterministic classification, not a complete causal explanation of every condition that was true.

evidence.label: Exact grant and original result replay first

test.name: test_attempt_cap_and_superseded_results_are_retained_without_current_promotion
test.assertion: After three issued attempts, new issuance hits capacity. Completing the first stores superseded history; completing the latest after expiry stores lease_expired. Both results remain readable and observation reports exhausted without promoting old output.

questions.title: Allocate cursor order inside the result transaction
questions.question: Why does the feed update a locked scope-local head instead of using a global PostgreSQL sequence?
answer: A sequence value can be allocated by a transaction that has not committed. If a consumer sees a later committed event and advances past it, the lower event could become visible too late and be skipped. Here the live result insertion already owns work admission; the feed locks the scope head, increments its sequence conditionally and inserts the event on that same connection and transaction. The head update therefore rolls back with result insertion.

The explicit rowcount check asserts the retained head advanced exactly once. Its thirty-thousand bound follows the finite profile capacity, not a throughput target. The representative test holds completion A before commit, observes B genuinely blocked on admission and an empty feed, then releases A and reads ordered events one and two. This serializes the qualified local ordering but introduces contention; it does not create cross-profile global order or solve restored-branch source identity.
questions.alternatives: Inferred tradeoff: a global sequence is simpler and scalable for unique IDs, but uniqueness alone is not safe committed-cursor ordering. A log or database change stream could supply another ordering contract, requiring explicit adoption, replay and source-incarnation semantics rather than a drop-in numeric replacement.
questions.counterfactual: Allocate event sequence numbers before acquiring admission using nextval. A stalled transaction can hold number one while number two commits and is consumed, allowing a later number-one commit to fall behind the consumer cursor.

challenge.symptom: A feed consumer occasionally misses a result during concurrent completions although every result row is present. The missing event may have committed after the consumer advanced beyond its earlier allocated number.
challenge.diagnosis: Reproduce two transactions with a held precommit boundary. Observe actual SQL blocking and the feed page while A remains uncommitted, rather than assuming numeric sequence allocation implies commit order.
challenge.handling: Existing handling shares result admission and transactional scope-head allocation. The test proves ordered visibility for that schedule. A proposed sharded design would need a revised cursor contract and independent proof of no skipped commits.

followups.question: Why keep the source UUID as well as sequence?
followups.answer: The sequence orders events only within one source and scope. A source UUID distinguishes the profile incarnation so a cursor cannot silently attach to a recreated profile with similar numbers; divergent restore semantics need additional qualification.

followups.question: Does this serialize every tenant?
followups.answer: The current wrapper holds a shared work admission guard before this per-scope head. The head is scope-local, but that does not mean all writes are independently sharded. Measure contention before claiming scalable tenant isolation.

followups.question: Can a feed read acknowledge execution?
followups.answer: No. The read returns bounded evidence and a cursor. P3 processing metadata has separate scan and terminal-ACK semantics, and neither source pagination nor derived ACK grants another specialist invocation or action.

questions.watch_for: Unique sequence allocation and safe committed pagination are different properties.

evidence.label: Existing admission and same-transaction append precondition
Append called in result insertion transaction

test.name: test_uncommitted_lower_event_cannot_be_skipped_by_later_completion
test.assertion: Completion A is held before commit; B is observed waiting on admission and cannot finish, while the feed is empty. After release, the page contains exactly sequences one and two for the corresponding original work IDs.

diagram_hint.title: Scope cursor order follows committed result visibility
steps: Safe lane: A owns admission, inserts its result and allocates scope sequence one, then is held before commit.
B waits on admission; the consumer sees an empty feed while A is uncommitted.
A commits; B obtains admission, inserts its result and allocates sequence two; the consumer reads one then two.
Failure alternative: an independent global sequence gives A one before commit, B commits two, and the consumer advances to two before A becomes visible.
Mark the alternative as a reasoned counterexample, not a separate implemented mode. Preserve source UUID and scope binding beside the safe cursor.

questions.title: Refuse the upgrade before creating leased tables
questions.question: Why does upgrade_v4 reject an unmanaged running v3 inquiry before performing its first DDL statement?
answer: The query distinguishes an execution marked running with no managed continuation row from a managed running inquiry. The old unmanaged worker has no v4 lease grant. Once serving requires leased writes, that old worker could no longer finish through its original boundary. The migration therefore refuses before DDL and leaves v3 available for reconciliation, instead of stranding accepted work behind a new authority requirement.

The surrounding transaction verifies owner credentials, shared admission, ACTIVE state and exact previous version before reaching this snippet. Managed running inquiries follow a separately tested upgrade path; the rule is not a blanket requirement that every running task disappear. The representative test proves no v4 tables appear after refusal, finishes the original inquiry through v3, then upgrades and compares retained records. It reads actual migration behavior; it does not establish that arbitrary external workers or production rolling upgrades are automatically safe.
questions.alternatives: Inferred tradeoff: automatically adopting every running inquiry would make upgrade smoother but would require inventing ownership for work already in flight. Explicit pre-upgrade reconciliation costs an operator step while keeping the original result and worker authority explainable.
questions.counterfactual: Create v4 tables and mark the version before checking unmanaged running inquiries. Refusal could leave the operator facing a partially changed authority surface, or allow leased serving to reject the only worker able to finish old accepted work.

challenge.symptom: After an upgrade, an old running inquiry cannot acknowledge its result and no valid lease identifies who should recover it. The new runtime boundary arrived before old unmanaged ownership was resolved.
challenge.diagnosis: Inspect the original schema version, ACTIVE marker and whether running executions have continuation controls. Distinguish unmanaged legacy work from managed work with a documented recovery path; process health alone does not settle that ownership.
challenge.handling: Existing handling refuses before DDL and directs v3 reconciliation first. Once original work is settled, the explicit owner upgrade proceeds. A proposed online adoption scheme would need new ownership and uncertainty evidence rather than a flag override.

followups.question: Why not simply mark the old inquiry failed?
followups.answer: The supplier may already have completed it or may still be processing. Changing a local status cannot erase that uncertainty. Reconciliation must preserve original identity and known results before storage authority changes.

followups.question: Does running always block the upgrade?
followups.answer: No. The query specifically looks for running execution without a managed control row. Managed running work has a separate tested recovery path through the new coordination model; the predicate preserves that distinction.

followups.question: Can application startup perform this procedure?
followups.answer: No. It requires explicit owner credentials and operational reconciliation. Serving code validates supported active storage and performs no DDL; silently upgrading during startup would collapse the migration and runtime role boundary.

questions.watch_for: The snippet is one migration guard within a larger owner-only transaction, not a complete deployment procedure.

evidence.label: Owner and active schema checks before upgrade
Refuse unmanaged running work before DDL
Refusal then original v3 reconciliation and upgrade

test.name: test_running_unmanaged_inquiry_refuses_upgrade_until_v3_reconciliation
test.assertion: Starting an unmanaged inquiry makes upgrade raise UnsupportedOperation, preserving v3 rows and creating no v4 tables. Finishing the same inquiry through v3 permits upgrade; the upgraded runtime returns the exact retained finished record.

questions.title: Validate metadata before selecting from it
questions.question: Why inspect pg_class before reading schema_metadata instead of querying the version row first?
answer: A relation named schema_metadata is not necessarily a passive table. It could be replaced with a view whose SELECT executes a function or advances a sequence. Reading the supposed version first would then run behavior before the validator had established what object it was trusting. The preflight queries PostgreSQL catalogs and requires the exact relation kind, persistence, owner and absence of extra triggers, rules and row-security settings.

Subsequent checks inspect column types and generated/default behavior before selecting metadata content; broader role and catalog validation still follows. The test replaces metadata with a view using nextval, then verifies both runtime construction and owner repeat-install reject it while the sequence remains uncalled. That is stronger evidence than rolling back a normal row write, because sequence advancement is not undone the same way. This protects a narrow declared catalog, not arbitrary hostile database administration.
questions.alternatives: Inferred tradeoff: selecting version first is concise and common for trusted migration systems, but it executes an unvalidated relation. A less strict catalog contract could allow approved views or functions; it would need an explicit trusted-behavior model and tests for their effects.
questions.counterfactual: Move SELECT version FROM schema_metadata ahead of _metadata_preflight. A malicious or drifted metadata view can execute nextval during validation, causing a nontransactional observable side effect even though the later schema check fails.

challenge.symptom: Opening a supposedly read-only client advances a sequence or invokes unexpected database behavior before schema_mismatch is reported. The version lookup itself, rather than later business code, can be the side-effecting action.
challenge.diagnosis: Inspect relation kind, rewrite rules, triggers, generated columns and custom types using catalogs before fetching metadata rows. A transaction rollback alone does not prove nothing observable happened during a version query.
challenge.handling: Existing handling performs catalog preflight and rejects the replacement view without evaluating it. An owner must explicitly restore the expected catalog; runtime repair or automatic adoption would reintroduce unreviewed behavior.

followups.question: Why reject a view if it returns identical columns?
followups.answer: Column shape does not constrain evaluation behavior. A view can run expressions or functions before producing familiar values. The contract requires a specific passive metadata table, not merely a row that looks compatible afterward.

followups.question: Why is the sequence fixture useful?
followups.answer: It exposes a side effect that a later rollback does not erase like an ordinary row update. Checking is_called remains false demonstrates the suspicious SELECT was avoided, rather than executed and then cosmetically rolled back.

followups.question: Does a matching version number prove compatibility?
followups.answer: No. Runtime validates catalog shape, owner and grants as well as version and definition metadata. The expected number is one signal; it cannot authorize changed triggers, defaults, object kinds or privileges.

questions.watch_for: Validation code can execute data-defined behavior unless it first validates the objects it reads.

test.name: test_metadata_view_is_rejected_before_nontransactional_side_effect
test.assertion: A replacement schema_metadata view would call nextval. Client construction and owner repeat-install both reject schema_mismatch, and the independent sequence reports is_called=false, proving the validator did not evaluate the dangerous metadata row.

questions.excerpt:
def _metadata_preflight(connection: Connection, schema: str) -> None:
    # Never select a row from an unvalidated view, generated column or custom type.
    relation = connection.execute(
        """SELECT c.relkind,c.relpersistence,c.relrowsecurity,c.relforcerowsecurity,pg_get_userbyid(c.relowner) AS owner,EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM pg_trigger t WHERE t.tgrelid=c.oid AND NOT t.tgisinternal) AS triggers,EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM pg_rewrite r WHERE r.ev_class=c.oid) AS rules FROM pg_class c JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid=c.relnamespace WHERE n.nspname=%s AND c.relname='schema_metadata'""",
        (schema,),
    ).fetchone()
    if relation != {
        "relkind": "r",
        "relpersistence": "p",
        "relrowsecurity": False,
        "relforcerowsecurity": False,
        "owner": "continuity_migrator",
        "triggers": False,
        "rules": False,
    }:
        raise WorkError("schema_mismatch")

limits: This pass makes no code changes, runs no application gates and invokes no providers. Existing named tests are reviewed evidence, not fresh passing results.
Inferred alternatives explain plausible tradeoffs; they do not invent the original author's private motivation or the reader's personal contribution.
The historical local P1 V1 provider_real v2 qualification remains distinct from the current open post-v5 P1-20 rerun and latest full PostgreSQL audit errors.
The zero-row revision card names a representative public-contract test and explicitly does not claim that test forces the defensive rowcount branch.
v5 pacing still excludes post-reservation outages. Exact runtime validation does not provide a sandbox against arbitrary privileged Python or a database owner rewriting all evidence consistently.

chapters.title: P2 One conversation across channels
chapters.subtitle: P2 interview questions about verified input durable dispatch and truthful communication
intro: P2 addresses a framework problem that is central to the Agents role: one user interaction may span a LiveKit room, browser text, a disconnected interval and an SMS follow-up. The durable unit is an accepted scoped input linked to one conversation and case, not the life of a model session. These questions focus on the actual TypeScript SDK, Python native adapter and selected local qualification in this checkout.

Use the source references to open the specific mechanism while practicing. Answer first with the contract, then the serialized or external boundary, then a failure and a test that could falsify the guarantee. The suggested answers describe repository behavior; replace first-person project stories with contributions and measurements you can personally defend.

Status boundary: selected P2 implementation slices are qualified, including original-result and origin-integration prerequisites. P2-I22 and all seventeen complete charter rows remain planned. The joined showcase and its selected successful journeys are useful implementation evidence, not a substitute for those broader acceptance gates.

concepts.title: Provider scope and account scope
concepts.body: A verified carrier principal authenticates an observation. A separately verified association binds the sender to retained account history. Neither a body label nor a current phone number silently rewrites the original association.

concepts.title: Input receipt and operation receipt
