concepts.body: The first proves durable intake at P2. The second proves acceptance by the cooperating investigation authority. Neither means carrier delivery or completion of a business effect.

concepts.title: Possible external call
concepts.body: The protected reservation precedes network I/O. A crash on either side of that call can leave uncertainty. A database claim cannot stop an already admitted remote operation.

concepts.title: Source qualified evidence
concepts.body: Generated text, actual SDK handle observations, browser playback reports and human acknowledgement have different producers and meanings. Preserve their original identities and avoid a single delivered flag.

concepts.title: As of context
concepts.body: P2 state, public case state and final disclosure permission are observed at different points. A fresh grant can authorize disclosure while the data remains explicitly non-atomic and historical.

questions.title: One case across several channels
questions.question: What does channel continuity add beyond putting an SMS gateway in front of a voice agent?
answer: Channel continuity makes an accepted input survive the transport and the agent that first saw it. P2 represents verified voice transcripts, browser text and synthetic SMS as scoped events, persists an inbox receipt and processing identity, and then hands bounded work to one selected case authority. Room, participant, sender, conversation, case, input and operation identities have different lifetimes. A room can disappear while the case and its accepted work remain.

The important abstraction is an explicit boundary between transport evidence and business authority. P2 owns retained channel input, routing and communication evidence. In integrated mode P1 owns current case state and action commitment; P2 does not maintain a second copy of the case. A newly joined room reads durable context rather than treating the previous model's chat history as the truth. The same library also supports a separate standalone reference authority, chosen explicitly. This separation makes replay, conflict, authorization and unknown outcomes part of the developer API instead of hidden assumptions about a persistent session.

followups.question: Why not use the LiveKit room name as the case ID?
followups.answer: A room identifies a transport session. Rejoin, SMS follow-up and a long-running investigation must survive that session. Mapping a room to a case belongs in trusted construction, and retaining the mapping does not make every participant authorized for the case.

followups.question: What would you demonstrate first?
followups.answer: Accept an input, observe its durable receipt, terminate its processing agent, then use a fresh process to recover the same original input and operation. Show one business acceptance and separately show the later reply. This exposes the useful guarantee more clearly than an uninterrupted chat.

questions.watch_for: Do not describe a room transcript, a model summary or a P2 projection as the case authority.

evidence.label: P2 observation followed by public case read

questions.title: Authenticate the bytes before interpreting them
questions.question: Walk through the fake SMS authentication boundary and explain its security properties.
answer: The integration is constructed from a trusted provider scope and copied HMAC key. authenticateFakeSms rejects missing or oversized bytes and malformed timestamp/signature fields, enforces the sixty-second transport window, snapshots the caller-owned byte buffer, and computes a domain-separated HMAC over the configured scope, timestamp and exact raw body. It uses timingSafeEqual before accepting UTF-8 or parsing the message. Provider scope comes from the integration, not from a tenant field inside the webhook.

Only after authentication does the strict parser interpret the fixed message shape. It rejects duplicate keys and unexpected authority fields before projection can erase that evidence. Authentication proves that this configured synthetic provider made an observation; it does not prove which customer account owns the sender. The durable intake transaction separately resolves the current verified sender association. Errors collapse to a safe WebhookRejected value, avoiding leaked parsing, key or account detail. A production carrier adapter would need that carrier's actual signing and replay contract; this fake scheme is deliberate test infrastructure, not carrier certification.

followups.question: Why snapshot the Uint8Array?
followups.answer: The caller retains a mutable transport buffer. Copying it before MAC and parsing ensures both operations concern the same bytes, and later mutation cannot change the accepted observation. Object freezing alone would not protect the buffer's underlying storage.

followups.question: Why sign the provider scope as well as the body?
followups.answer: A valid signature should not be reusable under another integration or provider account. Domain separation and trusted scope bind the meaning of the bytes to this protocol and principal. A signed body label cannot select a more privileged principal.

questions.watch_for: A valid HMAC is provider authentication, not customer authorization, consent or delivery proof.

questions.title: Sender association has a lifecycle
questions.question: How does P2 bind an SMS sender to an account, and what happens after revocation or reassignment?
answer: A sender is not an account credential. P2 has an explicit challenge and completion flow authenticated by a seeded account capability and verified carrier observation. The challenge records the expected sender epoch. Completion locks the sender head, checks the epoch, expires any previous active association and installs a new association version. Revocation advances the epoch and removes the active binding. A delayed challenge cannot recreate an association whose epoch has moved.

New SMS acceptance resolves the current active association and stores its account, conversation, case and epoch with the original event. Historical inbox reads establish access to that retained account history; they do not silently reinterpret the event using today's sender owner. Different operations intentionally have different permission checks. Revision routing consumes authenticated retained input, while linked exact confirmation performs an additional original-current-association preflight. Outbound sends also require a currently authorized route. I would explain each boundary precisely rather than claim one global revocation fence: separate P2 and P1 transactions cannot atomically revoke a P1 commitment already admitted elsewhere.

followups.question: Can a message accepted before revocation still appear in history?
followups.answer: Yes, to a caller with the retained account capability. Historical truth must not be reassigned to a new owner of the same phone number. Reading retained history is different from admitting a new send, confirmation or native input.

followups.question: Why not compare message timestamps to the revocation time?
followups.answer: Provider timestamps do not establish database serialization or trusted causality. Epochs and protected current association checks decide admission. A timestamp can be retained as an observation without becoming an authorization rule.

questions.watch_for: Do not claim that every read rechecks the sender or that an association preflight atomically fences a different database authority.

questions.title: A language-neutral event contract
questions.question: Why did you implement strict codecs in both TypeScript and Python instead of passing JSON through?
answer: The JSON transport is not itself the contract. P2 defines a versioned event shape, trusted provider and account scopes, byte bounds, semantic canonicalization and a stable identity. Both languages must agree on what constitutes an equal replay and what constitutes changed content under the same identity. The implementation rejects duplicate object keys before ordinary JSON parsing can discard them, validates Unicode and numeric forms, and separates canonical semantic payload from wire representation.

The TypeScript codec caps wire bytes at 32,768 and text bytes at 4,096; those are UTF-8 limits rather than character counts. The canonical representation orders object fields deterministically and preserves meaningful text. TrustedPrincipal constrains scope during decoding, so a well-formed event that claims another account is still denied. Cross-language positive and negative fixtures make this an interoperability contract rather than two independently plausible parsers. In an interview I would use a reordered JSON object as an equal case, a duplicate-key object as a rejection, and the same event identity with changed body as a conflict at intake.

followups.question: Why have both an event ID and canonical payload?
followups.answer: The ID selects the logical replay slot; the canonical payload proves what was originally accepted into it. Equal content replays the receipt. Changed content under that ID must conflict instead of updating the original event or creating another operation.

followups.question: Can you truncate oversized text?
followups.answer: Silent truncation would change the request and potentially its identity semantics. Reject the complete input at the declared byte boundary. If a future API supports attachments or chunking, give that behavior an explicit versioned contract and independent bounds.

questions.watch_for: TypeScript types do not validate network data, and JSON.parse alone loses duplicate-key evidence.

questions.title: Commit before acknowledging input
questions.question: What happens if the gateway dies after PostgreSQL commits an input but before the sender receives HTTP 200?
answer: The acceptance transaction stores the inbox row, scoped receipt, conversation acceptance sequence and one processing intent with its stable operation key. The response follows commit. If the process dies in the gap, the sender has an unknown acknowledgement, but the input is durable. Replaying the original provider identity and unchanged canonical content returns the retained receipt rather than creating another processing intent. The caller should preserve that original request while reconciling the ambiguity.

The negative case matters just as much: if the transaction never committed, a retry can create the first acceptance; if content changes under the same identity, it conflicts. The implementation distinguishes failures before commitment from acknowledgement uncertainty after a possible commit. The real PostgreSQL fixture has an actual child-process exit after commit and a fresh-process read, which is stronger than throwing an exception in a mocked handler. None of this proves the investigation completed, that a reply was sent, or that a user heard anything. It proves durable intake under a specific identity and the ability to recover it after process loss.

followups.question: Does HTTP 200 mean the business request succeeded?
followups.answer: It means the input was durably accepted by this boundary. Processing, external operation acceptance, case mutation, carrier acceptance and user acknowledgement are later facts. Expose them separately so an API client cannot accidentally interpret a queued receipt as completed work.

followups.question: What must the browser retain after an ambiguous response?
followups.answer: The exact original input ID and body. The latest audit also froze the composer identity across retries and duplicate clicks. Generating a replacement ID would turn an acknowledgement retry into a new logical request and defeat deduplication.

questions.watch_for: Do not retry an ambiguous acceptance with a new logical identity.

evidence.label: Original identity and payload replay check
Inbox and processing intent committed together

questions.title: Capacity cannot erase replay protection
questions.question: How does intake behave when the retained inbox is full?
answer: The inbox limit measures all retained input identities, not just currently pending work. Acceptance checks an existing scoped event and its canonical content before admitting growth. An exact replay remains available at capacity; changed bytes still conflict; only a genuinely new identity receives Overloaded. The same principle applies to reads and other receipt-bearing APIs: capacity should stop additional retained state, not prevent recovery of facts the system already accepted.

This deliberately sacrifices unlimited lifetime admission in the bounded local profile. Marking work complete or evicting it from a display window does not remove the identity, operation key or effect protection. Otherwise a delayed webhook could become new work after the record disappeared. A production cleanup design would need an explicit replay horizon, retained tombstones and a provider/client contract that makes expiration safe. It would also need measured storage growth, archival ownership and migration behavior. The current workload study makes the retained-capacity meaning explicit and verifies useful replay and scoped reads after the sixty-four-row active study fills.

followups.question: Why not count only pending rows?
followups.answer: That is a backlog limit, which can be useful separately, but it does not bound retained replay identities. Conflating the two either permits unbounded storage or silently frees duplicate protection when processing finishes. Name and enforce both dimensions if both are required.

followups.question: Would you delete old successful rows to recover?
followups.answer: Not without a defined replay contract. Preserve protected identities and receipts first. Operational recovery from overload can reject new work or require an explicit profile change; it must not make an old accepted request executable again by accident.

questions.watch_for: A display-history cap is not an idempotency retention policy.

questions.title: Freeze the preparation before external acceptance
questions.question: Describe the dispatch protocol and explain what is replayed after a crash.
answer: Dispatch begins from a committed inbox receipt and claims bounded ownership. If there is no retained preparation, it reads the selected case authority, asks the agent for a bounded investigation decision, validates the result against the original accepted message and freezes a PreparedDispatch. The frozen request binds scope, case revision, source input and stable operation key. The next step first looks up that exact operation at a cooperating acceptance port.

A known durable receipt is validated and recorded. Only after an absence observation and a protected possible-external reservation does normal dispatch call accept. A restarted attempt reuses the preparation instead of reading a changed case and regenerating a different request under the old key. Explicit reconcile is lookup-only; absence there remains uncertain and cannot become another acceptance call. This protocol relies on the declared stable-idempotency-and-lookup capability of the cooperating operation port. It does not turn an arbitrary HTTP endpoint into an exactly-once service. It also keeps SQL transactions short: case, agent and operation I/O happen outside the protected storage transactions.

followups.question: Why perform lookup before accept?
followups.answer: A previous process might have committed remotely and lost its response. Lookup can recover that original durable receipt. The response must match the retained operation identity and payload; merely finding a similar case or status is insufficient evidence.

followups.question: Why not regenerate a plan on retry?
followups.answer: The case or model output may have changed. Reusing an operation key with new semantics is a conflict; choosing a new key can duplicate accepted work. Persist the original preparation, then use an explicitly new user request for changed business intent.

questions.watch_for: Reliable absence and authority to perform a new accept are different protocol facts.

evidence.label: Read or reuse frozen prepared request

questions.title: Claims fence writes without fencing remote calls
questions.question: How do P2 dispatch claims prevent two workers from corrupting one input?
answer: A claim records a random owner, monotonically increasing epoch, kind and database-time expiry under the protected row. A competing live claim returns busy. After expiry, takeover closes the old attempt and preserves whether an external call may already have happened. Protected prepare, reserve and finish operations validate the current owner, epoch, kind and expiry. An old worker cannot commit through a grant that a newer worker superseded.

The database clock is read after the relevant locks, so time spent waiting for a lock cannot authorize an already expired grant. Claim expiry is still a local write fence, not proof that the old process, thread or remote operation stopped. The possible_external marker survives and makes takeover state uncertain where necessary. Recovery uses the original stable operation and cooperating lookup. The system also enforces persisted active and attempt limits. For the joined profile, the latest audit increased newly created claim leases beyond the dispatch step budget and aligned nested request timeouts; otherwise a slower but valid accept could expire ownership while its caller was still working.

followups.question: Can the epoch be sent to a supplier as a universal fence?
followups.answer: Only if that supplier explicitly implements and enforces the same fencing protocol. A database epoch by itself cannot revoke a network request that was already admitted. Preserve uncertainty and use cooperating idempotency or reconciliation at that boundary.

followups.question: What race would you test?
followups.answer: Pause a worker after reservation, let its claim expire, allow takeover, then release the first worker. Assert stale protected writes fail, the original external identity remains fixed, and independent external evidence shows whether an operation occurred. Also show unrelated current work progresses.

questions.watch_for: Lease expiry does not prove cancellation of a paused external request.

evidence.label: Owner epoch kind and fresh expiry guard

questions.title: A gateway polls durable eligibility
questions.question: Why does the gateway poll PostgreSQL instead of owning an in-memory accepted-message queue?
answer: The durable inbox and processing intents own acceptance. A process-memory queue cannot be the only place that remembers an HTTP-acknowledged request, because a restart would lose it. The gateway's bounded loop asks existing persisted eligibility, steps selected receipts and uses an optional nudge only to reduce latency. If the nudge is lost, polling still discovers the input. HTTP acceptance and background processing have separate outcomes and lifetimes.

The polling policy must also preserve useful progress. A recent audit found that uncertain inputs parked for a missing sender association were reclaimed every poll, preventing idle backoff and potentially starving newer inputs. Current eligibility excludes that specific parked state from automatic polling while preserving explicit step and lookup-only reconcile. The idle delay resets after a dispatched step or a nudge rather than after any inspected row. These details matter more than simply saying the gateway has exponential backoff: backoff must reflect progress, and persisted eligibility must describe work that can usefully advance. The loop is bounded and remains subordinate to the durable authority.

followups.question: Could an event bus replace the poll?
followups.answer: It could provide a wake-up hint, but a durable discovery or replay path is still needed. A dropped notification must not lose an accepted input. If the bus becomes authoritative, define durable subscription, replay, acknowledgement and ownership semantics rather than assuming them.

followups.question: Does excluding parked work hide it?
followups.answer: It removes it from automatic eligibility, not retained state or explicit inspection. Operators can see the uncertain condition and use the supported explicit path. It should not be silently labelled not_executed, because the earlier possible external call remains a fact.

questions.watch_for: A wake-up signal is not a durable acceptance record, and scanning a row is not useful progress.

evidence.label: Bounded durable polling and idle backoff

questions.title: Timeout means the waiter stopped waiting
questions.question: How do you avoid leaking an agent subprocess when its caller times out or shuts down?
answer: The scripted process adapter owns the actual child process group, its private files and the occupied slot. Caller timeout may reject the wait and request cancellation, but it does not release ownership. Cleanup signals the registered process group, escalates if necessary and observes actual group disappearance before declaring the worker reaped. A completed top-level child is insufficient if descendants still exist.

The same distinction appears in asynchronous HTTP adapters: AbortSignal is a request to stop, and a rejected Promise.race does not prove underlying I/O settled. P2 retains real tasks until settlement and reports CleanupIncomplete when ownership cannot be resolved within the close budget. This prevents another generation from borrowing a supposedly free slot while the previous one still consumes resources or performs an external effect. In tests I would use a child with a descendant and a deliberately uncooperative cancellation path, then verify actual group state and later useful admission. Timer-only mocks establish waiter behavior but cannot qualify process closure. The latest audit also records remaining rare timing flakes honestly instead of treating timeout increases as evidence of guaranteed performance.

followups.question: Why retain private files after failed cleanup?
followups.answer: The process may still hold them or need them, and they are evidence for the unresolved owner. Deleting them can hide the primary failure or cause another race. Cleanup must follow verified ownership closure rather than make the filesystem look tidy.

followups.question: Can close simply call abort on every task?
followups.answer: It should request cancellation, then observe actual settlement and close in dependency order. If a task ignores abort, keep it owned and return an honest incomplete-close result. A retryable close may finish later after the dependency really settles.

questions.watch_for: Do not equate a cancelled waiter, elapsed timer or parent PID exit with reaped descendants.

evidence.label: Observe the entire process group before release
Close retains and drains real tasks

questions.title: Native grants bind the original participant
questions.question: What authority does the native LiveKit adapter receive, and what must stay out of the browser token?
answer: Trusted construction fixes tenant, account, case, conversation, room and participant. An explicit native publisher creates a bounded, expiring grant; durable native acceptance uses the associated private bearer and checks the original room and participant. The browser RTC token authorizes transport participation and does not contain the native ingress, preparation or operation credential. Model text cannot choose a tenant or upgrade that authority.

Native acceptance locks the stored binding, obtains fresh PostgreSQL time, and rejects revoked or expired grants before admitting a new event. The resulting event uses a native provider identity and binding sender; it does not pretend to be SMS. Later preparation and reservation use the retained original binding and recheck their own permission boundary. A previous possible external call is not retrospectively cancelled by grant revocation, while retained historical facts remain readable through the appropriate authenticated APIs. This narrow capability design lets transport reconnect independently of durable case ownership and limits the damage of a browser or prompt that supplies forged scope labels.

followups.question: Why check expiry after acquiring the binding lock?
followups.answer: A request may wait behind another transaction until its grant expires. Checking application time before the wait could admit an expired capability. Fresh database time under the protected binding makes the admission decision correspond to the actual serialized point.

followups.question: Can a new participant reuse the old native input ID?
followups.answer: The original binding and exact payload still determine the event. A new room or participant does not acquire the old ingress authority by knowing an ID. Rejoin uses a new trusted grant and a read-only context path for historical facts.

questions.watch_for: RTC transport membership is not durable intake or business-action authority.

evidence.label: Locked grant and fresh database-time acceptance

questions.title: Final recognition belongs to one source turn
questions.question: How do you prevent a late speech-to-text result from being attached to the next voice turn?
answer: The runtime creates an explicit caller-bound input ID at start_turn and opens recognizer capture for that source. Commit disables audio and asks the SDK to complete that same turn. The completion hook requires a genuine CommittedTranscript whose input ID and body match the captured turn; it freezes the original transcript before awaiting durable acceptance. Interim promotion and ordinary SDK user text are insufficient proof of a genuine final result.

The turn state records capturing, committing and settled behavior, with bounded history and repeat-commit results. A duplicate commit returns the original turn outcome instead of creating another input. Closing the source turn never relabels a later recognizer callback as belonging to a newer caller input. The current timeout path can report no_audio while durable acceptance remains unresolved; the latest audit records that UX ambiguity as an open finding. Therefore that status must not be treated as proof that nothing was accepted. This is a source-ownership problem as much as a transcription problem: mutable current-speech state cannot be the identity authority across awaits, interruption and recognizer stream replacement.

followups.question: Why not accept the text passed into the SDK hook directly?
followups.answer: The hook text alone does not prove which explicit caller source produced it or whether it came from genuine final recognition. Matching the immutable recognizer snapshot and input ID prevents a delayed callback or interim promotion from acquiring new durable identity.

followups.question: What is the retry behavior after commit times out?
followups.answer: Keep the original input identity and inspect or replay the supported original operation. Do not synthesize a final transcript or create a replacement logical request merely because the waiter stopped waiting. The durable receipt and recognition outcome remain separate observations.

questions.watch_for: Never bind late recognition using whichever turn happens to be current after an await.

evidence.label: Repeatable commit for the matching turn
Freeze genuine original final transcript before acceptance

questions.title: Durable intake must precede generation
questions.question: How do you stop the SDK and the application from independently consuming the same text or voice input?
answer: The native runtime takes explicit ownership of intake. AgentSession uses manual turn handling with preemptive generation disabled, and room I/O has SDK text consumption disabled. The custom text reader validates the original participant and accepts the bounded input durably. The voice completion hook hands the genuine final transcript to the same acceptance path and raises StopResponse so the SDK does not start a competing automatic reply.

Generation happens later through prepare for a retained accepted context. That context binds the original message, operation and case revision, and the runtime waits for the source handoff before invoking generate_reply. Tools are disabled for this bounded preparation. This prevents a reply from becoming evidence that intake succeeded, and it avoids two conversational contexts for one caller event. The implementation also compares retained original input bodies to reject a changed body under the same ID. The tradeoff is more lifecycle code and a version-sensitive SDK seam, which is why actual pinned-SDK tests, browser media and isolated package consumers are separately useful evidence.

followups.question: Why disable preemptive generation?
followups.answer: The selected contract requires one durable acceptance before this reply is generated. Speculative generation would need a separate explicit contract for ownership, discarded output and side effects. Disabling it makes the boundary straightforward and testable for this local implementation.

followups.question: Is StopResponse a business cancellation?
followups.answer: No. It prevents an SDK response path from continuing after the custom hook took ownership. It neither cancels durable case work nor revokes a supplier request. Those operations have separate authenticated APIs and separate dispositions.

questions.watch_for: An SDK transcript or generated answer is not a durable acceptance receipt.

evidence.label: Custom turn hook ends the competing SDK path
Manual turns and no preemptive generation

questions.title: Generation scheduling and completion are different
questions.question: What does a successful native preparation mean, and how do the timing profiles change it?
answer: The default native path owns a bounded generation, records its original generation identity, invokes generate_reply with tools disabled and waits for SDK playout. It records completed, interrupted or unknown observations against the already accepted input and operation. The runtime caps retained generation identities at sixty-four and rejects another preparation while owned preparation or context work still occupies the relevant slot.

The joined showcase also supports an explicit scheduled-reply timing mode that can return a preparation after scheduling speech while a bounded observer retains the actual handle. That improves responsiveness, but scheduling is not completed generation, completed playback or consent. Response capture rejects that scheduled mode because its contract needs stronger source-qualified settlement. The selected inference mode remains explicit in metrics and readiness. When discussing latency, I would separate input acceptance, preparation return, first audible audio, final generated text and eventual SDK completion. A short preparation duration alone is not proof of low conversational latency, and a configured provider badge is not proof that actual recognition and synthesis occurred.

followups.question: What if a scheduled reply never finishes?
followups.answer: The observer keeps the actual handle owned until settlement or honest incomplete cleanup. Its cap prevents an unbounded set of abandoned replies. A timeout changes the caller's observation; it must not manufacture a completed generation or free an active resource prematurely.

followups.question: How would you compare scripted and provider modes?
followups.answer: Use the same identity and authority invariants, but record actual mode, provider calls, numeric usage and media observations separately. Scripted checks establish deterministic behavior. They cannot establish model quality, real recognition or the latency of a hosted provider pipeline.

questions.watch_for: Preparation return, speech scheduling, generated completion and browser playback are distinct milestones.

evidence.label: Preparation can return before scheduled playout
Scheduled mode refused with response capture

questions.title: Prove what was generated and what was played
questions.question: How does the response evidence model avoid claiming that the caller heard an answer?
answer: P2 keeps source-qualified facts: a durable response anchor bound to the accepted input and operation, exact generated text captured from the actual model stream, SDK observations attached to the actual SpeechHandle, and browser reports attached to the original response. These records are evidence from different producers. They do not collapse into a single delivered boolean, and none grants quote confirmation or business mutation authority.

The capture implementation waits for the handle and durable anchor before reading model output. It streams through a two-item queue, bounds bytes and chunks, and records generated completion only after the source ends normally with validated complete text. TTS can start before model EOF, preserving streaming latency; a prefix followed by an error must not become generated_complete. A browser report remains a report from that browser, while SDK completion describes SDK work. Neither proves physical hearing or human understanding. The actual SDK tests cover durable-anchor ordering, early audio, interrupted handles, prefix failures and cancel-ignoring producers; actual browser/media gates qualify the selected additional observation layer.

followups.question: Why store the generated text rather than reconstruct it from chat history?
followups.answer: Chat history can be compacted, interrupted or updated by SDK behavior. Capturing the actual bounded stream under a response ticket preserves exactly what this generation produced and prevents another speech handle from being borrowed as its evidence.

followups.question: What happens if TTS fails after the model finished?
followups.answer: The completed generated-text fact can remain true while SDK preparation or playback is unknown or failed. Do not erase known generation truth and do not promote it into successful communication. Keep the two observations independently inspectable.

questions.watch_for: Generated text, SDK playout and browser playback reports are not human acknowledgement.

evidence.label: Two-item streaming queue and owned producer
Anchor precedes source reading and bounded capture
TTS failure preserves separate generation truth

questions.title: Interrupt the intended response
questions.question: How do you keep an old interruption request from stopping a newer answer?
answer: Interruption is response-scoped when communication evidence is enabled. The capture manager resolves the original response ticket, verifies it still owns a valid handle and interrupts that handle. It does not look up whichever SDK speech happens to be active at the time the request finishes. The legacy unscoped interruption endpoint is refused in this profile because it cannot express that ownership contract.

This distinction matters during barge-in, late browser RPC and reconnect. A delayed interrupt for response A must not stop response B. The original A observations remain attached to A even if B has already started. Producer cancellation also retains actual ownership: an LLM or TTS source that ignores cancellation remains in the capture manager until its real task settles, so a watchdog cannot silently free its capacity. I would test an old response ID after the new handle exists, an unbound queued SDK call, retired captured context, and a source that keeps running after cancellation. Those tests explore incorrect retargeting and resource leaks, not merely whether one interrupt method was invoked.

followups.question: Should interruption cancel the underlying investigation?
followups.answer: Usually it stops or requests stopping speech. Durable work cancellation needs a separate explicit user action and authenticated business API. The caller interrupting a sentence is not necessarily withdrawing an investigation or a previously confirmed supplier action.

followups.question: Can you mark the answer not executed after interruption?
followups.answer: Only if the relevant boundary proves that. Some text or audio may already have been produced, and external work may already have been reserved. Preserve the actual partial and unknown facts; avoid a single label that erases them.

questions.watch_for: Never implement response-scoped interruption by looking up mutable current speech.

evidence.label: Unscoped interrupt refused in capture profile
Old interruption does not retarget new handle

questions.title: Rehydration is an explicitly timed read
questions.question: A user leaves voice, sends SMS and rejoins. How do you reconstruct context safely?
answer: The current-case reader derives scope from the authenticated current source, takes a coherent P2 snapshot of retained history and related facts, releases SQL, reads the selected public case authority, and then performs a fresh final permission check against the original grant before disclosure. It returns separate p2ObservedAt, caseObservedAt and disclosureAdmittedAt fields with atomic set to false. No transaction or connection is held across the external case read.

A new session therefore receives durable case facts and original source-qualified history without inventing a fresh input, generation or effect. Equal request revision does not prove that workflow or supplier state remained unchanged between observations. The context remains as of its separate reads. Pagination is bounded and preserves original receipt identities rather than truncating protected facts. A current grant can disclose old account history while the old sender or room binding remains historical. Pure P1 revision-zero context is read-only until an explicit versioned command contract supports execution from that state. This makes the UI honest about freshness and prevents a loaded summary from becoming action permission.

followups.question: Why recheck after reading P1?
followups.answer: The native grant might expire or be revoked while the public case call is in flight. The final protected check prevents disclosure under that stale grant. It does not make the P2 and P1 observations atomic or guarantee they remain current after the response.

followups.question: Can the model act immediately on a rehydrated result?
followups.answer: It can explain the bounded observation within its permitted tools. Any new mutation or delivery must cross its own current guard and exact confirmation rules. A cached applicability badge or loaded quote cannot grant consent.

questions.watch_for: Matching revisions do not establish a current workflow snapshot or renewed action authority.

evidence.label: Snapshot public case read and final disclosure admission
Retained history does not rebind original identities
Complete bounded records instead of silent truncation

questions.title: Revision routing needs one authority
questions.question: How does the revision router handle two conflicting requests and a lost acknowledgement?
answer: RevisionRouter begins with an authenticated retained inbox receipt and a finite trusted case mapping. It accepts a strict structured investigation-revision command and calls one selected authority: either the standalone PostgreSQL reference implementation or the explicit public-P1 bridge. It does not extract action authority from natural language, copy P1 case state into P2, or use arrival timestamps to decide which request wins.

The public P1 revise command is expected-revision compare-and-set. One concurrent revision can win; another sees a conflict. Unlike exact confirmation, that revise API has no command receipt that identifies which caller caused the transition. If the acknowledgement is lost after the possible write, the router returns outcome_unknown. Reading a matching later state cannot prove this command won, because another request might have produced the same state. Therefore automatic retry, rebase or a new operation identity is not authorized. The API exposes the ambiguity and lets a later explicit user decision proceed against current facts. Quote confirmation and supplier effects remain outside this router.

followups.question: Why not say success when the current state equals the requested state?
followups.answer: State equality is not command identity. Another actor could have won the same revision with equal content. Without a durable command receipt, that read cannot establish causation. It may inform the user, but it cannot retroactively turn an unknown acknowledgement into a proved winner.

followups.question: Does the router recheck the sender association?
followups.answer: Its retained inbox read establishes access to the accepted account input. The selected revision contract does not add a current association-revocation fence. Linked confirmation has a different, explicit current-association preflight. Explain the API-specific boundary rather than generalizing one rule.

questions.watch_for: Do not silently retry or rebase a possibly committed public-P1 revision.

evidence.label: Writing state changes timeout to outcome unknown

questions.title: An exact quote needs linked confirmation
questions.question: Why is confirmation a separate router, and how is a text yes bound to the intended quote?
answer: ConfirmationRouter links an original accepted input to a retained immutable response and quote prompt. The prompt preserves opaque canonical P1 quote bytes, revision, quote identity and digest. A structured answer identifies that response, and optional expected revision or digest must agree. The command sent to P1 uses the original operation key as command identity and includes the exact frozen quote material rather than rebuilding it from current supplier state.

Before the new controller call, the router rereads the original message through inspectForConfirmation and checks the same original association and fingerprint. It then performs one public exact confirmation call; P1 atomically validates revision, quote and intent, avoiding a read-then-commit gap inside the case authority. That API's retained command receipt supports explicit original replay after acknowledgement loss. The P2 association preflight is still a separate observation and cannot atomically fence a later P1 commit across stores. The model never receives quote-confirmation authority. An unlinked yes, an altered quote or a stale response requires clarification instead of guessing which business action was intended.

followups.question: Why preserve quoteJson if you also have a digest?
followups.answer: The digest commits to exact bytes but does not reconstruct them or explain the quote. P1 validates its canonical quote contract. Preserving the original opaque payload avoids filling missing supplier bindings from today's mutable state or changing serialization during replay.

followups.question: What makes confirmation replay safer than revision replay?
followups.answer: The public confirmation API has a durable command receipt for the original command identity and semantics. The selected revise API does not. Recovery behavior follows the actual authority's contract; two operations should not share a retry policy simply because both use HTTP.

questions.watch_for: A model yes, a playback report or a response correlation ID cannot authorize mutation.

evidence.label: Current association preflight before public authority call

questions.title: Reserve the send before carrier I O
questions.question: What is the outbound commitment point, and how does it interact with route revocation?
answer: A reply is first an immutable logical outbound intent bound to the account, conversation, case and recipient. Before sending, the protected reservation transaction reads retained attempts, checks earlier evidence, callback vetoes, suppression and the current authorized original-recipient route, then records an immutable possible-send attempt with its exact route, body and provider operation identity. Carrier I/O happens only after that transaction commits and outside SQL.

This is a precise admission boundary, not a promise that later revocation can stop an already admitted call. If the process pauses after reservation, revocation can prevent another new reservation but cannot independently fence the paused carrier request. A later route cannot retarget that possible send. If the result is lost, the attempt stays unknown under its original route and recipient. Result recording has its own bounded admission slots after the latest audit, so ordinary read or send saturation cannot discard a known carrier fact. API state should distinguish held, possible, accepted_by_provider and unknown; provider acceptance is still not physical delivery or human acknowledgement.

followups.question: Why is the possible-send marker persisted before I/O?
followups.answer: A crash after the call but before result storage otherwise looks indistinguishable from never trying. Persisting possible first conservatively preserves uncertainty. The cost is that a crash before actual I/O may leave unknown, which is safer than an unjustified resend.

followups.question: Can route revocation guarantee no SMS arrives afterward?
followups.answer: It fences new guarded reservations, not a call already admitted or accepted by a carrier. State that operational limitation and preserve original attempt facts. A stronger guarantee requires an external provider protocol that actually supports it.

questions.watch_for: A current route authorizes a new reservation; it cannot rewrite an existing attempt.

evidence.label: Callback veto and current route permission

questions.title: Retry the provider operation under its real contract
questions.question: How does recovery differ for ordinary and explicitly idempotent carriers?
answer: Ordinary fake-SMS sends have no safe automatic resend after an ambiguous outcome. The policy is hold_no_resend. A timeout or absent local response does not prove nonacceptance, and even a lookup can report historical truth without authorizing another call. For an explicitly cooperating idempotent provider, the original provider operation freezes capability, namespace, recipient, address, body and operation digest independently of each local attempt UUID and request digest.

Recovery is an explicit controller command, not a background resend loop. A supported retry reuses that provider operation key and validates the original operation semantics, current permission and accumulated evidence. Command replay returns its original receipt without I/O. Old attempts adopted by the v5 owner upgrade remain ordinary permanently; changing configuration cannot retroactively grant idempotency to a call that was made under another contract. This design is intentionally conservative because an ordinary ambiguous resend can create duplicate messages. The interview answer should distinguish a new local attempt, a new provider operation and an original command replay; those are three different identities with different permissions.

followups.question: Can you turn idempotency on after a timeout?
followups.answer: Not for the old operation. The first call's actual provider contract determines whether reusing its key has meaning. The migration explicitly adopts history as ordinary, preserving uncertainty instead of claiming a later configuration change alters past behavior.

followups.question: What if the user moved to a new number?
followups.answer: An old possible operation remains bound to its original recipient and address. A new route may be used only by a separately admitted new operation when all earlier evidence and current permissions permit it. It cannot silently retarget an ambiguous retry.

questions.watch_for: A fresh attempt UUID is not a fresh business operation, and a new provider key can duplicate an old ambiguous send.

evidence.label: v5 adopts historical sends as ordinary

questions.title: Later evidence cannot rewrite admitted history
questions.question: Why do you check all bounded earlier send operations and retain an admission witness?
answer: A logical reply can accumulate several provider operations only under strict policy. It is unsafe to inspect just the latest attempt: an older operation may later reveal acceptance or conflict, and that evidence must veto a new reservation. Current reservation logic evaluates bounded earlier operations under the same admission protection used for callback and route checks. It does not assume that a latest definitive nonacceptance proves every prior operation was absent.

When terminal nonacceptance permits a new operation, the system stores an immutable admission witness identifying the predecessor evidence that justified that decision. If later observations contradict the old operation, they add truth and conflict; they do not mutate the already admitted history or pretend the new reservation never had a valid basis at its commit point. This separates current eligibility from historical correctness. It also makes the race reviewable: tests can pause callbacks and reservations, inspect which transaction serialized first, verify frozen identities and show useful progress afterward. A single mutable status field would lose the evidence needed to explain these outcomes.

followups.question: Why not revoke every later attempt when an old callback arrives?
followups.answer: The callback can veto future reservations but cannot fence an external call already admitted. Preserve both the new attempt's original admission witness and the late evidence. Report uncertainty or conflict rather than rewriting either observation.

followups.question: How many earlier operations should you inspect?
followups.answer: The implementation's persisted caps bound the set, so evaluate every relevant earlier operation within that set. Sampling or checking only the most recent one could miss accepted evidence. If growth becomes too large, redesign retention and indexing without weakening the invariant.

questions.watch_for: Current evidence may block future work without invalidating the original serialized reason for past admission.

questions.title: Callbacks add evidence without granting permission
questions.question: How are provider callbacks correlated, and what do you do with contradictory reports?
answer: Callback authentication uses a distinct raw-byte HMAC capability before replay lookup. A verified callback is then matched to its original provider scope, attempt ID, provider operation key and exact request digest. Claimed account labels or a newly associated sender do not grant access to an old recipient's data. Equal original callback identity replays; changed bytes conflict, and persisted global and per-attempt caps bound retained observations.

The reduction rule preserves contradictory facts instead of overwriting one status with the last timestamp. It exposes strongestReported, reported failure and unknown flags, provider message identities and explicit conflicts such as terminal_reports, provider_identity or send_result. A delivered report remains provider evidence, not proof that a human understood the message. Any retained callback vetoes a new reservation under shared admission; a callback does not itself grant resend authority, even if it reports failure. A reservation serialized before the callback still represents an already admitted possible external call. This gives operators a truthful audit trail while avoiding causal claims based on untrusted event time.

followups.question: Why authenticate before checking duplicate event ID?
followups.answer: Otherwise an unauthenticated request could probe the existence or contents of retained events, or exploit a shortcut that returns a receipt without proving the provider principal. Replay is an authenticated operation, not an exemption from authentication.

followups.question: What if delivered arrives before accepted?
followups.answer: Keep the observations and apply the deterministic provider-specific evidence rule. Network arrival order and provider timestamps do not define business authority. A stronger reported state may be useful evidence while contradictions remain visible rather than being erased.

questions.watch_for: A callback report cannot authorize resend, change the recipient or prove human acknowledgement.

evidence.label: Original exact-attempt correlation and bounded retention

questions.title: A stable receiver accepts the original result
questions.question: How does a P3 result become a P2 notice without confusing the result digest with the message body?
answer: ChannelResultReceiver is constructed with a retained receiver UUID and finite trusted publisher bindings. Accept and find require a distinct publisher capability scoped to the account, case, conversation and logical recipient. The original canonical P1 delivery intent fixes delivery, work, attempt and result digest. Exact replay returns the same receipt; changed intent conflicts. The receiver ID cannot rotate on serving startup or be borrowed from an unrelated ordinary outbox row.

Under the existing outbox admission lock and maxReplies cap, result metadata and a fixed ordinary notice commit together. The notice's bodyDigest describes the notice text; it is not the P1 result_sha256. This preserves the original result as opaque authoritative bytes while exposing a bounded notification. Receiver acceptance is an application receipt that the result was retained at this explicit receiver. It grants no carrier send, physical hearing, human acknowledgement or business action. The real storage fixture tests atomic acceptance, concurrent replay, changed and foreign data denial, ordinary UUID collision, full opaque result separation and populated restore. These are separate from later current-native disclosure.

followups.question: Why retain a receiver UUID rather than generate one per process?
followups.answer: P1 binds delivery to its original receiver before the first send. A restart must reconcile the same receiver identity. Rotating it would either make original receipts unreachable or silently redirect an ambiguous delivery to a new receiver.

followups.question: Can a result receipt be returned when maxReplies is full?
followups.answer: Exact replay and read remain available because they do not add protected identity. New acceptance still obeys the cap. Checking replay before growth prevents overload from blocking reconciliation of a result already accepted.

questions.watch_for: An ordinary notice digest is not the result digest, and receiver acceptance is not carrier delivery.

evidence.label: Stable receiver and trusted publisher bindings
Atomic original result and notice acceptance
Original atomic acceptance and retained receipt
Opaque result versus ordinary notice separation

questions.title: Disclose an old result through a current grant
questions.question: How can a new room read an old result while still enforcing the current participant permission?
answer: ChannelResultReader derives the route from the current native grant and verifies that its inbox and outbox refer to the same configured database identity. It takes a bounded P2 observation of the original result under the stable receiver, releases SQL, calls the exact public P1 case adapter, then rechecks the original native grant under locks with fresh database time. The final check compares binding, room, participant and full logical reference before disclosing the result.

One shared outbox call slot stays owned across the entire sequence, even though no connection or transaction spans the external read. The returned intent and receipt retain original identities; the accompanying case and observation times are separate as-of facts with atomic false. If permission is lost while P1 is being read, disclosure is denied rather than returning the earlier snapshot. A first genuine denial must still release the slot so a later authorized read can progress. This is a read boundary only: an old result becoming visible through a fresh room does not create a new generation, resend, consent or action permission.

followups.question: Why retain the call slot while releasing the SQL connection?
followups.answer: The slot bounds the whole application operation, including its external read. Releasing the connection avoids holding database resources across I/O; retaining the slot prevents a caller from creating unbounded in-flight case reads while each appears locally idle.

followups.question: Does the final check make the result current?
followups.answer: It makes disclosure admitted under the original current grant at that final point. P1 and P2 remain separate timed observations, and the result's applicability must still be interpreted against them. It does not make a cross-store atomic snapshot.

questions.watch_for: A fresh room grant can permit a historical read without reauthorizing the historical result for action.

evidence.label: Current-native result read with one owned slot
Useful read after a permission denial

questions.title: Schema changes belong to the owner
questions.question: Why are inbox upgrades explicit, and what do versions five through nine actually change?
answer: Serving code uses a restricted runtime role and performs no DDL. The trusted owner upgrades a quiescent selected schema through explicit versioned functions, preserving original identities and old API behavior. v5 adds immutable provider operations and recovery metadata, adopting all old attempts as ordinary. v6 adds native grants, v7 adds communication evidence, and v8 adds original P1 result receipts linked to ordinary notices. These are distinct storage capabilities rather than one automatic startup migration.

v9 adds three operating indexes for due dispatch, provider-operation attempts and outbound recovery commands; it changes no row. The latest audit added explicit locks around that maintenance upgrade. Compatibility means older upgrade functions do not downgrade newer schemas, source and installed consumers keep original receipt semantics, and populated backup/restore/reopen procedures are exercised. I would discuss the operational price honestly: quiescent owner upgrades require a maintenance procedure, but make privilege and data transitions reviewable. Installing schema in a library constructor would hide irreversible work in ordinary serving startup and weaken the separation between trusted administration and request handling.

followups.question: Why not infer idempotent capability while migrating old attempts?
followups.answer: The old external call was made under its original contract. A migration cannot manufacture a provider guarantee after the fact. Preserve it as ordinary and require explicit semantics for future new operations.

followups.question: How do you validate an index-only migration?
followups.answer: Verify the expected source version and owner role, protected maintenance locks, exact new index definitions, unchanged logical row snapshots, idempotent original reopen behavior and compatibility reads. Faster queries alone do not prove the upgrade preserved history.

questions.watch_for: A schema version bump or successful startup is not proof of safe populated migration.

questions.title: Original input provenance survives the bridge
questions.question: Why did the joined application need an operation-only client instead of pretending native text was SMS?
answer: The operation-only ExternalOperationClient overload takes a trusted profile, loopback endpoint, finite account/case/conversation/sender binding and operation bearer. It does not require synthetic carrier configuration for a native publisher. The original canonical channel input stays in P2; the application bridge returns the actual P1 work UUID as its external receipt. A kind label or receipt shape alone cannot prove whether an operation originated from native text or signed SMS.

The qualified source join follows the retained accepted event through its exact prepared operation to the original P1 work and result. Mapped P3 identifiers are restricted at the bridge without narrowing unrelated P2-only event and sender bounds. Closed descriptors and independent encoded-frame and canonical-input limits are checked before I/O. The old two-argument client remains compatible. An accept error stays OutcomeUnknown while a failed lookup stays Unavailable; neither authorizes choosing another operation key. The latest audit aligned the joined client call budget with the five-second step while preserving the default two-second budget for existing consumers. This is an example of improving composition without broadening authority.

followups.question: Why is a returned work UUID not enough to prove origin?
followups.answer: It identifies a work record, but provenance requires comparing the original retained channel input and operation binding that produced it. A service can otherwise return a valid work UUID unrelated to this caller's accepted event.

followups.question: Where should unsupported IDs be rejected?
followups.answer: At the explicit integration seam that maps into the narrower P3 contract. Reject without truncation or rewriting. A bridge limitation should not silently shrink the standalone channel SDK's existing valid input space.

questions.watch_for: Never fabricate carrier identity for native input or treat an operation label as provenance proof.

questions.title: Operations pages are bounded readers
questions.question: What makes the operations view safe to expose, and how do its cursors work?
answer: The operations API is a scoped read model, with independent operator diagnostics and no mutation or resend control. Context reads still use the native permission and final disclosure checks. Signed cursors bind application source, full logical scope, section and retained anchor; they are pagination state, not authentication. HMAC verification and anchor validation prevent one section or profile's cursor from being replayed against another, and an incompatible case-source revision returns cursor_stale.

Telemetry uses finite producer maps, metric names and error vocabularies. Bodies, tokens and arbitrary labels are excluded; failed getters are unavailable rather than substituted with zero. Exporters and observers are bounded and owned before invoking callbacks or thenable access, including reentrant close and ignored asynchronous work. This matters because diagnostics themselves can leak resources or block ordinary useful work. The tests retain actual returned promises through incomplete close, verify later settlement, and separate caller-span completion from real reader ownership. An accepted-row page is also not a complete status-event feed: explicit refresh and separately timed observations remain part of the UI contract.

followups.question: Why is a signed cursor not authorization?
followups.answer: It protects pagination integrity but can be copied or outlive the original read permission. Each request must still authenticate its proper principal and pass current disclosure checks. Do not embed a privileged bearer into the cursor or treat possession as case access.

followups.question: Why report a failed metric as unavailable rather than zero?
followups.answer: Zero is a real measurement and can falsely imply healthy inactivity. Unavailable preserves the observation failure. Bounded enums and source ownership also keep exporter errors from introducing untrusted labels or leaking private exception text.

questions.watch_for: A read-only UI can still leak data or resources unless permission, telemetry and closure are explicit.

evidence.label: Source revision makes incompatible cursor stale
Ignored exporters stay owned through close

questions.title: A workload is evidence within a declared envelope
questions.question: What did the P2 workload study measure, and what would be an overclaim?
answer: The selected workload freezes its manifest, digest, schedules, seeds, child roles, cleanup and numeric ceilings before measurement. It exercises fake-SMS intake, persisted processing, duplicate and changed-payload behavior, overload, restart, populated restore and dormant conversations through public ports. The active schedule fills a sixty-four-input retained-capacity profile; the dormant profile retains 1,024 inputs through bounded public credential windows. These are local synthetic workload shapes, not production customer counts.

The study records sampled process RSS, CPU, event-loop delay and latency observations with explicit denominators. Its ceilings include 512 MiB RSS, 1,000 ms maximum observed event-loop delay, 5,000 ms accepted admission and 15,000 ms useful fake-operation completion. Crossing a ceiling fails that profile; passing does not establish a production SLO or fair scheduling. Two gateways share one Node process, so RSS includes both and the runtime baseline. Restarts and restore must preserve original receipts, body conflicts and operation keys. The latest audit records an initial workload timeout under host load and its isolated rerun, which should be described as observed evidence rather than erased.

followups.question: Can you divide total RSS by conversations to estimate production capacity?
followups.answer: Not reliably from this experiment. Runtime baseline, shared pools, active versus dormant work and sampling all affect memory. Build a separate controlled study with the production workload, resource limits, steady state, tail behavior and failure recovery before making capacity claims.

followups.question: Why prove cleanup as part of a benchmark?
followups.answer: Leaked children, held SQL sessions or unresolved observer work can contaminate the measurements and the next run. A pass requires reconciling actual results and owned resources, not merely producing an attractive latency percentile.

questions.watch_for: Local synthetic ceilings are neither production throughput nor a fairness or availability guarantee.

evidence.label: Seed and predeclared numeric study ceilings

questions.title: A clean SDK includes honest release boundaries
questions.question: How would you defend the package design, test strategy and remaining P2 work to a framework team?
answer: The package exposes typed subpaths for codec, security, storage, dispatch, routing, confirmation, outbox, native composition, rehydration, operations and result reception. Construction keeps trusted capabilities explicit, public errors use finite safe codes, runtime data is validated, and resources have owned close methods. The installed starter composes these APIs while staying inert on import; owner bootstrap and serving are distinct. Isolated npm-pack and Python consumers are important because checkout imports can hide missing files, undeclared sibling dependencies or broken exports.

I would then separate evidence layers. Pure codec tests prove parsing and contracts; real PostgreSQL races prove selected lock and replay behavior; actual process and socket tests prove ownership; browser media tests prove selected playback observations; provider runs prove selected real inference. None automatically closes the other layer. Current documentation marks selected I01-I21 capabilities and later receiver/origin prerequisites qualified, while I22 and all seventeen complete P2 charter rows remain planned. The latest audit records remaining lifecycle findings and rare timing flakes. A strong interview answer explains those gaps and proposes the next measurable gate instead of relabelling the whole project production-ready.

followups.question: What would you simplify for a first-time SDK user?
followups.answer: Offer a small opinionated composition example with explicit authority selection, one accepted-input path and one recovery walkthrough, while retaining narrow public ports underneath. The starter already demonstrates that direction. Do not hide scope, unknown outcomes or cleanup behind magical defaults merely to shorten the example.

followups.question: What would you improve next?
followups.answer: Choose a remaining charter scenario and its full supported-platform, fresh-consumer and integrated-media evidence, then address verified lifecycle gaps that block that proof. Preserve the closed selected checkpoints and document the actual boundary. Avoid adding a second orchestration platform just to make the architecture appear more complete.

questions.watch_for: Selected local qualification is not full P2 acceptance, and a public type signature is not a runtime contract.

evidence.label: Installed composition through existing public boundaries
Selected qualification and all full charter rows still planned

questions.title: Defend the unresolved lifecycle findings
questions.question: If an interviewer points to the latest audit, which P2 or joined lifecycle limitations would you discuss first?
answer: I would start with the two high-priority joined findings rather than claim the local demo has complete shutdown safety. GW-A1 records that a normal stop can exhaust pending input attempts while the Parent endpoints are already closing and the gateway still claims work. GW-A2, with medium confidence, records that End can strand a room's final input because the worker stops before the binding is closed and revoked. These are composition and lifecycle-order problems, even though the individual SDK has explicit ownership and recovery mechanisms.

The repair direction is to stop new dispatch admission while dependencies still exist, drain or truthfully retain accepted in-flight work, observe dependent closure, then close the shared sources. Validate this with actual barriers and processes: accept the last input, pause at preparation or possible-call boundaries, trigger End or normal stop, then restart and reconcile the original identity without spending attempts on a closed dependency. Also inspect the inverted shutdown budgets, interrupted scripted playout that may repeat speech, and no_audio reported while acceptance is unresolved. Explain which are verified defects and which need further lifecycle proof. Do not describe these proposed fixes as already implemented.

followups.question: Does acknowledging these findings weaken the project?
followups.answer: It makes the guarantee reviewable. The useful evidence is that the design exposes stable identities and uncertainty, the audit found concrete counterexamples, and the next gate can target them. Hiding a known failure behind passing unrelated unit tests would be a much weaker engineering answer.

followups.question: How would you prevent retry exhaustion during shutdown?
followups.answer: First define the closing transition and which component owns it. Stop eligibility or classify shutdown before charging a fresh attempt, retain original preparation and possible-call state, and keep required endpoints alive until dependent dispatch is closed. Test actual interleavings before selecting the final mechanism.

followups.question: Would increasing every timeout fix it?
followups.answer: No. Larger budgets can reduce incidental flakes but do not establish correct dependency ordering or retained ownership. Use a coherent budget hierarchy plus observed resource closure, and preserve the primary failure when cleanup remains unresolved.

questions.watch_for: A component-level close contract does not establish safe closure of the entire composed application.

evidence.label: Gateway closure and owned dependency shutdown
Current unresolved lifecycle findings and confidence

walkthrough.detail: Authenticate original raw SMS bytes or the private native grant. Resolve trusted scope, validate the bounded event and atomically retain the inbox receipt plus processing key before acknowledging.
Claim persisted eligible work, inspect the selected case authority and freeze the original bounded investigation preparation. Never regenerate changed semantics under an old operation identity.
Lookup the original operation, record possible external work before a new call, and retain a matched durable receipt. Explicit reconcile remains lookup-only.
Bind generation and response evidence to the accepted original input. Keep SDK output, browser reports, carrier results and acknowledgement separate.
Load retained P2 facts, read the public case outside SQL and perform a final current-grant disclosure check. Explain the separate observation times.
Use the documented local gate evidence for a commit-before-ACK kill or an ambiguous send. Show the unchanged original identity and later useful progress, while naming the exact qualification scope.

limits: Real carrier certification, production traffic capacity and multi-region availability are not established by the synthetic fake-SMS and local workload lanes.
A callback, carrier acceptance, SDK playout or browser report is not physical hearing, exact quote consent or human acknowledgement.
A current sender preflight or native grant check is not an atomic cross-store revocation fence over P1 commitment or a previously admitted external call.
The checkout records selected qualified implementation slices; complete P2-I22 release evidence and all seventeen complete P2 charter rows remain planned.
This review did not execute the gates again. Existing recorded outcomes and their limitations are described from the repository, including the latest audit reruns and remaining findings.

chapters.title: P2 Code decisions across channels and awaits
chapters.subtitle: Read the order of operations and defend the alternative
intro: These sixteen cards are a second source-first review of the actual channel implementation and specific tests. Each includes a short unmodified source range to read aloud, the mechanism its ordering protects, a plausible alternative, one dangerous edit and an interview challenge.

Alternatives marked inferred tradeoff are engineering reasoning from the code, not claims about the author original intent. Existing behavior and recorded audit fixes are distinguished from proposed improvements. Test references identify assertions already present; this review did not rerun gates, invoke providers or change implementation.

Use the earlier question links for conceptual context, then explain this exact code. A strong answer names the value retained before an await, the permission checked under a lock, the point a result becomes known and the resource still owned after the caller leaves.

concepts.title: Order is part of the public contract
concepts.body: Moving a check across an await or lock can change who is authorized, what is replayed and whether a failure is definite. Treat the sequence as behavior, not a cosmetic refactor.

concepts.title: Negative and useful progress
concepts.body: A rejection test should also show later valid progress where relevant. Universal denial, leaked slots or a paused cleanup owner can make a superficially safe implementation unusable.

concepts.title: Different proof layers
concepts.body: Synthetic driver tests inspect fine statement order. Actual SDK, socket, PostgreSQL and process fixtures establish other boundaries. Do not relabel one layer as another or treat an existing test name as a fresh passing run.

questions.title: A cheap authentication pass before SQL
questions.question: Why does rejectForged authenticate using the signed timestamp before opening a database connection, then authenticate again inside the transaction?
answer: The first pass rejects forged bytes and malformed payloads before acquiring a PostgreSQL connection or durable admission lock. It reads the timestamp through a property descriptor, avoiding a caller getter, and passes that signed timestamp as the comparison clock. Consequently this pass checks MAC and payload integrity but deliberately cannot establish present freshness. The four-call in-memory admission check still happens before this precheck; the guarantee is specifically about avoiding SQL resource consumption.

The transaction later authenticates the original input against database time after the shared admission lock. A correctly signed but stale request can pass the cheap pass and still fail there. This two-stage ordering limits forged traffic impact without letting a caller-selected timestamp authorize new durable input. The tests distinguish zero connections for forged input from one cleanly rolled-back connection for stale signed input.
questions.alternatives: Inferred tradeoff: authenticate once against host time before SQL to reduce repeated hashing. That is simpler, but host time and lock waiting would become part of the freshness authority. A second protected database-time check preserves the selected storage admission contract at modest bounded CPU cost.
questions.counterfactual: Tempting edit: delete the second authentication because the signature was already checked. A signed request held behind a lock could then be admitted after its freshness window expired, using the sender-controlled precheck timestamp.

challenge.symptom: Hypothetical symptom: a burst of forged SMS requests consumes the same finite database connections needed for already accepted work, even though none of those requests should reach durable state.
challenge.diagnosis: Existing diagnosis: inspect connection counts and the rejection boundary separately. Invalid signatures should fail before pool.connect, while stale but authentic requests deliberately require the protected database-time check inside the transaction.
challenge.handling: Existing handling: retain the precheck and the later freshness check. For a future public endpoint, add measured transport admission controls separately; this local four-slot mechanism does not claim internet denial-of-service protection.

followups.question: Why not trust Date.now for the second check?
followups.answer: The selected durable admission contract uses PostgreSQL time after locks. A host clock check before a long lock wait can become stale. It can be a transport filter, but it should not replace the protected authority clock.

followups.question: Does the first pass bypass overload?
followups.answer: No. The in-memory four-call check occurs before precheck. The code promises forged requests take no SQL connection or durable lock; it does not promise authentication has priority over every local resource limit.

followups.question: Does a valid signature identify the customer?
followups.answer: It identifies the configured synthetic provider observation. The current verified sender association supplies account and conversation scope inside the durable intake path. A signed sender string alone cannot select an arbitrary customer account.

questions.watch_for: Name both checks and their different clocks; do not call the signed-timestamp pass a freshness check.

evidence.label: Local call admission precedes the optional precheck

test.name: rejects forged SMS and association bytes before taking a connection
test.assertion: Submit altered bytes and a wrong signature, then assert WebhookError and zero pool connections. Separately send an authentic stale request and assert it reaches one transaction but fails freshness with a reusable clean connection.

diagram_hint.title: Two authentication checks with different authority
steps: Local call capacity is checked first; precheck obtains no SQL connection.
Read the signed timestamp without invoking a caller getter; verify scoped MAC and bounded payload using that signed time only.
Forged bytes stop before pool.connect; authentic stale bytes may proceed to SQL.
Acquire shared admission lock, read PostgreSQL time, authenticate again for actual freshness.
Only valid current association and bounded new-identity admission can commit the durable input.

questions.title: Reject complete byte overflow before parsing
questions.question: Why does parseEventJson call text on the complete wire string before strictJson?
