answer: text checks the complete string and its UTF-8 byte count before recursive parsing. This separates the wire ceiling of 32,768 bytes from the smaller semantic text ceiling. A short-looking JavaScript string can encode to more bytes, and a valid message padded with whitespace can exceed the wire limit without changing its eventual JSON value. Rejecting before parse prevents that transport envelope from bypassing the declared budget.

strictJson then retains duplicate-key evidence and bounds recursive structure before projection. Only afterward does the event-specific closed schema apply. The order matters because ordinary parsing and schema projection could discard duplicate fields or spend work on a frame that should have failed immediately. Exact-boundary tests accept a valid padded frame at the ceiling, reject one extra byte, and separately reject deep nesting. They test visible contract behavior rather than merely spying on the parser.
questions.alternatives: Inferred tradeoff: parse first and validate only the extracted body. That keeps the API implementation short but permits large whitespace or envelope overhead and loses duplicate-key evidence with ordinary JSON.parse. A streaming parser could enforce equivalent limits, at a substantially more complex incremental validation boundary.
questions.counterfactual: Tempting edit: replace the UTF-8 limit with raw.length. A non-ASCII request can then fit the character count while exceeding the promised wire bytes, making memory and cross-language acceptance differ at the boundary.

challenge.symptom: Hypothetical symptom: TypeScript accepts a message rejected by the Python consumer, or a mostly-whitespace envelope uses far more transport memory than the body-length limit suggests under repeated inputs.
challenge.diagnosis: Existing diagnosis: compare encoded wire bytes, body bytes and canonical semantic bytes independently. The parser guard addresses the complete wire frame; the body limit and canonicalization solve different problems after parsing.
challenge.handling: Existing handling: reject the complete oversized request without truncation. Preserve the exact boundary fixtures in both languages; any future chunking or attachments need their own explicit versioned protocol and resource accounting.

followups.question: Why does whitespace count if it is semantically irrelevant?
followups.answer: The transport still receives and buffers those bytes. Semantic equivalence does not make parsing, memory or network costs disappear. The wire ceiling protects the whole envelope, while canonicalization decides whether accepted meanings are equal.

followups.question: Why not truncate to the allowed body size?
followups.answer: Truncation silently changes the accepted user request and its replay semantics. A later original replay can then appear changed or two distinct requests can collapse. Reject the whole input and let the caller submit an explicit new bounded request.

followups.question: Does a byte cap stop every parser attack?
followups.answer: No. Depth, duplicate keys, invalid Unicode, field count and schema constraints remain separate. The useful property is layered bounded validation, with each guard stating the resource or ambiguity it prevents rather than claiming one universal parser defense.

questions.watch_for: UTF-8 wire bytes, character count and canonical payload size are three different measurements.

evidence.label: Semantic validation remains separate from wire size

test.name: accepts the exact raw UTF-8 byte limit and rejects one extra byte
test.assertion: Construct a semantically valid JSON message padded to exactly 32,768 encoded bytes and verify canonical identity is unchanged. Add one byte and require InvalidEvent.

questions.title: Validate time as one canonical representation
questions.question: Why does the timestamp validator combine a fixed-format regex with a Date toISOString round trip?
answer: The regex restricts the accepted spelling to millisecond UTC timestamps with a literal Z, and the text bound prevents a valid-looking prefix with extra data. The Date round trip then rejects calendar values that match the shape but normalize to a different instant, such as an impossible day. Rejecting year zero also preserves the selected cross-language date domain.

This is representation validation, not causality or authority. Equal instants written with offsets are intentionally outside this event contract rather than normalized after acceptance. That keeps canonical byte comparisons and Python/TypeScript fixtures consistent. receivedAt and occurredAt are validated before storage, but neither determines the winner of a case revision or replaces database time for grant freshness. The shared negative fixture explicitly includes both an invalid calendar date and an offset spelling, so removing either layer would change observable acceptance.
questions.alternatives: Inferred tradeoff: accept any Date.parse-compatible input and normalize to UTC. That can be useful in a user-facing import API, but it broadens ambiguous platform-specific input behavior and changes bytes before replay comparison. This protocol chooses a narrow canonical wire form instead of a forgiving date entry interface.
questions.counterfactual: Tempting edit: retain only the regex. The string 2030-02-30T10:00:00.000Z has the right shape yet an impossible calendar date, and a normalizing runtime can silently reinterpret it as another day.

challenge.symptom: Hypothetical symptom: two languages disagree on an event timestamp or a malformed date is accepted and displayed as another day, despite the event digest appearing internally consistent after normalization.
challenge.diagnosis: Existing diagnosis: separate syntax acceptance from calendar validity. Check the exact raw timestamp against the shared invalid-calendar-date and timestamp-offset fixtures rather than comparing only parsed epoch values or display output.
challenge.handling: Existing handling: require the canonical form and exact round trip. If future integrations need offset conversion, perform that in an explicit producer adapter before the immutable event is created, not during replay comparison.

followups.question: Why reject a correct instant with plus zero offset?
followups.answer: The protocol chooses one spelling. Allowing equivalent textual forms would require an explicit normalization contract shared by every producer and consumer. Rejecting unsupported spelling makes identity and diagnostics predictable without claiming the instant itself is invalid.

followups.question: Can occurredAt order concurrent case changes?
followups.answer: No. It is a producer observation, with clock and delivery limitations. The expected-revision case authority serializes changes. A valid canonical timestamp does not become a stronger permission or prove that one concurrent request caused current state.

followups.question: Why test this through the shared fixture?
followups.answer: A local helper test could pass while another language accepts a different date domain. The same frozen negative wire cases exercise the public decoders and require stable payload-free errors, preserving the interoperability boundary rather than only one implementation detail.

questions.watch_for: A canonical timestamp is validated data, not proof of ordering, freshness or business permission.

test.name: rejects $name with a payload-free code
test.assertion: Run the shared invalid-calendar-date and timestamp-offset entries through the public decoder. Require the fixture error code and a message containing only that code, while valid canonical fixture values preserve the agreed cross-language bytes.

questions.title: A rolled back connection is not necessarily broken
questions.question: Why does the transaction wrapper track committed, commitStarted and broken separately?
answer: A routine domain rejection can leave the SQL connection reusable after a clean rollback. A rollback failure means its state is unsafe, while a failed COMMIT response can be ambiguous even if a later rollback command appears to succeed. The wrapper therefore starts broken from commit uncertainty and upgrades it on rollback failure. finally releases the client with that explicit flag rather than discarding every connection on every application error.

The public error also depends on the boundary crossed. A known commit followed by a hook failure, or a write whose commit started without a known outcome, becomes AcknowledgementUnknown. AssociationRequired before commitment can remain a definite domain rejection. The final nested finally decrements active admission even if releasing the pool client raises. This combination preserves business uncertainty, pool hygiene and actual call accounting; optimizing only one of those concerns would leave the other two vulnerable.
questions.alternatives: Inferred tradeoff: always destroy a client after any error. That is conservative about session state but increases connection churn for normal conflicts and rejections. Always reuse is cheaper yet unsafe after failed rollback or ambiguous commit. Explicit boundary flags distinguish recoverable rejection from uncertain transport state.
questions.counterfactual: Tempting edit: set broken only when ROLLBACK fails. A COMMIT whose response was lost could then return a client with unresolved transactional history to the pool and be reported as a definite rejected write.

challenge.symptom: Hypothetical symptom: harmless association errors churn the entire connection pool, or a network failure during commit is reported as a clean rejection and the caller submits replacement work under a new identity.
challenge.diagnosis: Existing diagnosis: record which boundary failed and inspect pool release disposition independently of the public error. A rollback completing does not retroactively prove that a previously attempted COMMIT failed to commit.
challenge.handling: Existing handling: reuse after clean precommit rollback, discard on rollback or commit uncertainty, and expose AcknowledgementUnknown for possible writes. Reconcile the original identity before any application-level decision to submit new work.

followups.question: Why attempt rollback after an uncertain commit?
followups.answer: It is cleanup, not evidence that the earlier commit did not happen. The broken flag remains true for an uncertain commit, and the application still receives an unknown acknowledgment. Cleanup commands cannot replace original-operation reconciliation.

followups.question: Should a test inspect release true or false?
followups.answer: Yes, at this pool boundary the release disposition is the observable resource contract. Pair it with public error assertions, so a correct business code cannot hide unsafe reuse and correct disposal cannot hide a falsely definite outcome.

followups.question: What does an after-commit hook failure mean?
followups.answer: The business transaction may already be committed. Treating the hook exception as rollback would lie to the caller. Preserve the committed state and report acknowledgment uncertainty while retaining the original request and receipt path for reconciliation.

questions.watch_for: Successful cleanup after a possible commit does not prove the write was rolled back.

evidence.label: Pool release and active accounting remain independent

test.name: keeps a connection after a clean rollback and discards it otherwise
test.assertion: Force AssociationRequired with clean rollback, rollback failure, then write-commit failure. Assert the first releases false, the latter two release true, and the uncertain write reports AcknowledgementUnknown rather than a definite rejection.

questions.title: Carry quote JSON without reparsing it
questions.question: Why are P1 quote bytes kept as an opaque ASCII string instead of JSON.parse and JSON.stringify in P2?
answer: P1 canonical quote JSON can contain integer literals outside JavaScript safe integer precision. Parsing and serializing through JavaScript numbers could change those literals even when no code intended to edit the quote. quoteBytes therefore checks a bounded ASCII object-shaped envelope while preserving every byte, and quoteDigest hashes that original string. P2 transports and binds the quote; P1 retains authority for its exact semantic validation.

The stored prompt carries that same opaque payload, revision, quote ID and digest into one exact confirmation command. No current supplier state is used to fill missing bindings. The HTTP test uses two adjacent int64 values near the signed limit and asserts the actual outgoing quoteJson remains identical. This is a case where stricter local semantic parsing would weaken the protocol unless it implemented exactly the same arbitrary-precision canonical contract as the owner.
questions.alternatives: Documented mechanism, inferred tradeoff: a shared arbitrary-precision quote parser could validate semantics in both languages. That adds version coupling and duplicate authority-sensitive parsing. Preserving opaque bytes keeps the bridge narrow while leaving exact quote structure and consent validation with the existing P1 public authority.
questions.counterfactual: Tempting edit: replace quoteJson with JSON.stringify(JSON.parse(quoteJson)) before hashing. The int64 revisions in the existing HTTP fixture lose precision, changing the approved quote or causing a valid exact confirmation to conflict.

challenge.symptom: Hypothetical symptom: exact confirmation works for small revisions but fails or changes meaning at large supplier revisions, even though the JSON looks equivalent in a debugger and the user saw one unchanged quote.
challenge.diagnosis: Existing diagnosis: compare the outgoing byte string and digest to the original canonical P1 quote, using adjacent large integers. Comparing parsed objects alone can hide the same precision loss in expected and actual values.
challenge.handling: Existing handling: preserve the bounded opaque bytes and verify their digest at the bridge. A future quote contract upgrade belongs to the owner and explicit compatibility tests, rather than a convenient local reserialization helper.

followups.question: Does the object-shaped check prove the quote is valid?
followups.answer: No. It bounds the transport envelope and preserves bytes. P1 must validate the exact quote contract and revision atomically with commitment. A digest proves matching bytes relative to the trusted binding, not semantic correctness or consent.

followups.question: Why not store only the digest?
followups.answer: The digest identifies the approved bytes but cannot reconstruct them for exact replay. Retain the original payload and identity so the same command can be validated after an ambiguous acknowledgment without reading a new mutable quote.

followups.question: Would converting every number to a string fix it?
followups.answer: That would change the P1 canonical quote schema and approved bytes. It might be a valid future owner-defined contract, but a bridge cannot silently transform existing quotes and still claim exact original confirmation compatibility.

questions.watch_for: Do not let helpful JSON normalization alter the exact quote the human approved.

evidence.label: Original quote and command replay after lost acknowledgment

test.name: preserves opaque int64 quote bytes and validates the complete stable receipt
test.assertion: Send a quote containing 9223372036854775806 and 9223372036854775807 through the actual loopback client. Assert the server receives the exact original quoteJson and the client accepts only the fully matching stable receipt.

questions.title: Reuse the stored preparation before consulting a new world
questions.question: Why does dispatch skip case inspection and agent preparation when the claim already has a PreparedDispatch?
answer: A retained preparation fixes the accepted message, case revision, operation key and complete canonical request. Re-reading the case or regenerating an agent decision during retry could produce new semantics under the same idempotency key. The dispatcher therefore initializes prepared from claim.prepared and enters case inspection and agent preparation only when it is absent. It later looks up the original operation before deciding whether a normal dispatch may accept.

Storage independently validates owner, epoch, current source binding and equality if a preparation already exists. Thus reuse is not permission to ignore current admission; it is preservation of original command meaning. Explicit reconcile is narrower still: it requires retained preparation and performs lookup only, with absence remaining uncertain. The test observes case and agent ports are not invoked on a stored-plan retry, while a separate test proves reconcile never reserves or accepts.
questions.alternatives: Inferred tradeoff: regenerate a plan on every retry to use fresh context. That can improve relevance only for an explicitly new request. Reusing the old operation key would conflict; generating a new key could duplicate a previously accepted original operation. Freshness and replay need separate APIs.
questions.counterfactual: Tempting edit: clear claim.prepared before every step so the agent always sees current state. A retry after lost acknowledgment then submits a changed revision or body under the original key, breaking deterministic reconciliation.

challenge.symptom: Hypothetical symptom: a resumed request conflicts after an unrelated case edit, or repeated model runs produce different investigation payloads for what the UI still presents as a retry of one accepted input.
challenge.diagnosis: Existing diagnosis: inspect the persisted preparation and its canonical digest before invoking the agent. Verify the same scoped operation key is being replayed; current matching case state cannot identify which earlier submission won.
challenge.handling: Existing handling: reuse the frozen preparation and reconcile its original identity. If the user wants current revised intent, require a separately accepted input or explicit revision path rather than silently rebasing the old operation.

followups.question: Does replay still check permission?
followups.answer: Yes. Retaining old semantics does not authorize new calls. The store checks current binding and the dispatch grant at protected preparation and reservation boundaries. Original factual reads and eligibility for another external call are distinct.

followups.question: Why can normal dispatch accept after absence but reconcile cannot?
followups.answer: They are different explicit contracts. A normal step can cross a new guarded reservation under the cooperating stable-idempotency port. Reconcile is observational; its purpose is to recover an original receipt without converting absence into new invocation permission.

followups.question: What if a known receipt arrives after the caller deadline?
followups.answer: The dispatcher retains and validates that useful durable fact before reporting the caller deadline. The late response must match the frozen operation and payload. Losing the waiter does not justify throwing away original acceptance truth.

questions.watch_for: Replay freezes meaning; it does not renew case freshness or external-call permission.

evidence.label: Stored plan bypasses case and agent recomputation
Lookup-only reconcile has no new acceptance

test.name: freezes a prepared plan and skips changed case/agent computation on retry
test.assertion: Return a claim with retained preparation and assert the observed port sequence contains lookup and accept but no case or agent call. For reconcile, assert only lookup runs and absence retains uncertain status without reservation.

questions.title: Freeze final recognition before the first asynchronous boundary
questions.question: Why does _voice_completed construct a new CommittedTranscript before awaiting durable acceptance?
answer: The SDK completion hook is asynchronous, while recognizer and current-turn state can advance. The function first selects the committing turn, rejects duplicate processing, and verifies an exact genuine CommittedTranscript snapshot whose input ID and body match the callback. It copies that original identity, body and recognizer request ID into frozen local data before awaiting _accept. The resulting NativeInput cannot be relabelled using a later mutable turn.

Genuine final recognition is distinct from SDK interim promotion. A delayed final keeps its original caller-bound source, and repeat commit retains one durable input and conversational context. The pinned-SDK test holds final recognition, refuses a new turn, verifies no input or generation yet, then releases it and checks the original ID. The current no_audio timeout UX can still mask unresolved acceptance; this source binding does not solve that separately recorded limitation.
questions.alternatives: Inferred tradeoff: read self._turn or recognizer current text after the acceptance await. That shortens local snapshot code but makes identity depend on callback timing. An alternative immutable event queue could work, provided it retains genuine-final provenance and one explicit source owner across SDK lifecycle changes.
questions.counterfactual: Tempting edit: construct NativeInput from self._turn after awaiting another callback or network operation. A late final from turn A can then be stored under turn B, merging unrelated caller intent despite matching transcript text.

challenge.symptom: Hypothetical symptom: a delayed recognizer final appears in the next turn history or a repeated commit creates two user messages, while the UI shows only one push-to-talk interaction and one spoken request.
challenge.diagnosis: Existing diagnosis: correlate recognizer request ID, explicit input ID, committed snapshot and stored acceptance. A callback body alone is insufficient; determine whether it was genuine final recognition or SDK-promoted interim text.
challenge.handling: Existing handling: freeze the original final before awaits, reject mismatches and keep repeat commit stable. Proposed UX follow-up: distinguish unresolved durable acceptance from no_audio without weakening the original-source predicate or generating a replacement input.

followups.question: Why use an exact type check for CommittedTranscript?
followups.answer: The selected recognizer contract supplies that immutable final value. Accepting an arbitrary object with matching fields could let a different observation masquerade as genuine source finality. The type gate complements the input and body comparisons, rather than proving business consent.

followups.question: Does final recognition start generation?
followups.answer: No. The runtime durably accepts first, and the SDK hook stops automatic response continuation. Later explicit dispatch preparation owns generation from the accepted context. Recognizer finality, durable acceptance and model invocation are separately observable facts.

followups.question: What if the recognizer answers after its source closes?
followups.answer: It must not borrow a later source identity. The original turn state and snapshot checks reject or retain the observation under its original contract. A timeout must not fabricate a transcript or authorize a new business key.

questions.watch_for: Never fetch mutable current-turn identity after an await to label earlier recognition.

evidence.label: Closed source cannot be relabelled into the next turn
Recorded unresolved no_audio and acceptance UX boundary

test.name: test_delayed_genuine_final_keeps_original_turn_and_never_generates_automatically
test.assertion: Hold the genuine final, attempt another turn and require rejection, then release the final. Assert acceptance retains the original input ID and no automatic model invocation occurred; the interim-only control must accept nothing.

questions.title: Stop the default SDK path after custom intake
questions.question: Why do manual turns, text_input false, session_host false and StopResponse all appear in the native adapter?
answer: The settings address different competing consumers. Manual turn handling and disabled preemptive generation control timing; text_input false prevents room I/O from independently consuming the custom text stream; session_host false avoids a second host owning this session. After the custom voice hook performs durable intake, StopResponse prevents SDK default reply continuation. Manual mode alone is insufficient: the positive-control SDK test shows a normal hook still generates after commit.

The hook also retains a source handoff and schedules its release with call_soon so it unwinds through the SDK boundary before explicit preparation proceeds. That prevents custom dispatch from racing the still-active SDK turn callback and creating duplicate conversational context. The selected implementation therefore has one durable intake path and one later generation owner. These are pinned-SDK composition choices, with actual session tests; they are not a claim that LiveKit default behavior is defective.
questions.alternatives: Inferred tradeoff: let the SDK own normal intake and observe transcript events afterward. That is simpler for a transient agent, but it cannot satisfy this selected persist-before-generation contract without a different interception seam. The explicit adapter accepts more lifecycle code to make that boundary testable.
questions.counterfactual: Tempting edit: remove raise StopResponse because manual turn detection is already enabled. The SDK positive control demonstrates automatic generation after commit, allowing a reply before the application selected durable dispatch owns that generation.

challenge.symptom: Hypothetical symptom: one text or committed voice input creates two replies or two user context entries, and generation counters advance while durable intake is still blocked behind a test barrier.
challenge.diagnosis: Existing diagnosis: identify the actual consumer and callback owner instead of deduplicating the final transcript afterward. Compare the native runtime with the plain-SDK positive control to prove the competing generation path exists.
challenge.handling: Existing handling: disable competing room consumers, stop default hook continuation, and release the retained handoff only after hook unwinding. Verify one accepted input, one model invocation and one user context in the real SDK fixture.

followups.question: Why not suppress the duplicate generated answer later?
followups.answer: That is too late for a contract requiring durable intake before generation. The model may already consume resources or produce observable output. Prevent the competing invocation at the ownership seam, rather than hiding only the final text.

followups.question: Why call_soon instead of releasing immediately?
followups.answer: The retained handoff must outlive the hook body until StopResponse unwinds through the SDK callback. Immediate release could allow explicit preparation to race the SDK own turn completion. The scheduled callback preserves that sequencing contract.

followups.question: Does StopResponse cancel durable work?
followups.answer: No. It ends the SDK response continuation for this hook. Durable case cancellation has a separate authenticated command and external-effect boundary. A conversational exception cannot revoke an already accepted investigation or prove a supplier call stopped.

questions.watch_for: Manual turn timing alone does not disable default SDK generation after commit.

evidence.label: Competing room text and session host disabled
Actual native intake and sole-generation assertion

test.name: test_positive_control_plain_sdk_hook_would_automatically_generate_without_intake
test.assertion: Run a real AgentSession with manual turns but a plain Agent hook and observe one automatic model call. Compare the native adapter holding intake: it must invoke no model until accepted dispatch, then produce one user context.

async def on_user_turn_completed(
        self, turn_ctx: sdk_llm.ChatContext, new_message: sdk_llm.ChatMessage
    ) -> None:
        current = self.owner._turn
        turn = current if current is not None and current.state == "committing" else None
        if turn is not None:
            self.owner._enter_handoff(turn.input_id)
            self.owner._finish_voice_handoff(turn)
            turn.hook_started = True
        try:
            await self.owner._voice_completed(new_message.text_content or "")
        finally:

        raise StopResponse()

questions.title: Read the authority clock after waiting for the binding
questions.question: Why does NativeStore.binding acquire FOR UPDATE before its fresh clock and expiry check?
answer: A native event retains the binding ID in its original sender identity. Before new dispatch preparation or reservation, binding locks that exact native row and validates its stored shape and retained-capacity metadata. Only after those awaits does it fetch clock_timestamp and compare expiry, revocation, tenant, account, case, conversation, provider and original epoch. Time spent waiting for the row therefore consumes grant lifetime rather than extending it.

The order prevents a request from checking time while eligible, waiting behind another transaction, and then using an expired grant. It returns null for an ineligible original source so dispatch can preserve blocked versus uncertain state appropriately. The unit barrier test advances the supplied clock while the binding lock is held and asserts denial after release, then proves an independent valid binding progresses. This is a lock-ordering proof with a synthetic driver, distinct from the real PostgreSQL gate.
questions.alternatives: Inferred tradeoff: fetch one timestamp at transaction start and reuse it everywhere. That is convenient and coherent for some observations, but it makes late protected admission use stale eligibility after lock waits. This implementation deliberately refreshes the authoritative clock at the point relevant to granting another action.
questions.counterfactual: Tempting edit: move clock_timestamp before the binding query to save a round trip later. A request paused until expiry can then pass with the earlier timestamp and reserve another external call from an expired original grant.

challenge.symptom: Hypothetical symptom: expired native grants occasionally dispatch under contention but fail in an unloaded test, suggesting a timing-dependent permission leak rather than a permanently incorrect binding or clock configuration.
challenge.diagnosis: Existing diagnosis: place a barrier at actual binding-lock acquisition and advance beyond expiry before release. A wall-clock sleep alone cannot prove that the tested call was waiting at the intended protected boundary.
challenge.handling: Existing handling: use fresh database time after the lock and validate all original binding fields. Keep later possible external calls explicitly uncertain; revocation or expiry cannot retrospectively prove an already admitted call was cancelled.

followups.question: Why compare account and provider fields if the binding ID matches?
followups.answer: An identifier lookup alone does not validate the retained event relationship. Corrupted or forged message fields must not borrow another binding authority. The full comparison checks the original scope and source semantics before another protected call.

followups.question: Does the lock freeze a remote carrier call?
followups.answer: No. It orders database decisions about new admission. A call already reserved outside SQL may still execute after the lock is released or the grant later expires. Preserve its original identity and uncertainty at that external boundary.

followups.question: What constitutes useful progress in the test?
followups.answer: After the expired blocked request settles, an independently valid binding must still succeed. A test that only proves every call is denied could hide a broken clock, leaked slot or universal authorization failure rather than a correct temporal fence.

questions.watch_for: Fresh permission time belongs after the relevant wait, not merely at transaction entry.

evidence.label: Lock original native binding before fresh time
Expired or revoked binding invokes zero useful external ports

test.name: fresh clock after binding lock expiry then independent eligible progress
test.assertion: Hold the binding query, advance the test clock to expiry, release it and require null. Confirm the locked query precedes clock_timestamp and then verify a separate valid fixture returns the original association epoch.

questions.title: Recheck disclosure after the public case read
questions.question: Why does readNativeResult run a second protected native-grant check instead of returning its first snapshot?
answer: The first transaction derives the trusted route from the current native bearer and reads the original result. The code then releases SQL and calls the public P1 case adapter. Because the grant may expire or be revoked during that external await, a second protected transaction rereads it and compares the original binding, room, participant and complete logical reference. Only that final admission permits disclosure.

This keeps external I/O outside database transactions while preventing stale authorization from authorizing a returned result. One shared outbox call slot remains owned across the sequence, so releasing a connection does not make the whole operation unbounded. The result explicitly reports separate observation times and atomic false. A denied final check is not an unknown business write: it is a failed disclosure with no mutation. The transaction test verifies the public case read happened, the final permission failed and rollback produced no insert or update.
questions.alternatives: Inferred tradeoff: hold the first database transaction and lock across the P1 read. That might avoid a local reread but makes remote delay occupy SQL resources and permission locks. Returning immediately after P1 is faster, yet omits the required post-await disclosure permission check.
questions.counterfactual: Tempting edit: remove the second transaction because the bearer was checked at entry. Revocation during the public P1 read then fails to block disclosure, so a formerly permitted room receives data after losing the grant.

challenge.symptom: Hypothetical symptom: a result still appears after the operator revokes a room while its current-case HTTP read is paused, even though new reads with the same bearer are correctly denied afterward.
challenge.diagnosis: Existing diagnosis: pause the public case adapter between the first snapshot and response, revoke the original grant, then release the read. Inspect the final protected check and ensure its failure is preserved as AccessDenied.
challenge.handling: Existing handling: retain the operation slot, release SQL for external I/O and recheck the original grant before disclosure. Independently test later authorized progress so a failed permission check cannot leak reader or outbox capacity.

followups.question: Does the second check create an atomic P1 and P2 snapshot?
followups.answer: No. It validates disclosure permission at the final P2 point. The case and result remain separately timed observations. The returned atomic false flag prevents consumers from treating equal revisions or a late permission check as cross-store freshness.

followups.question: Why compare the same room and participant again?
followups.answer: A bearer-derived read must remain bound to the original principal context throughout the operation. Finding some eligible binding afterward would silently retarget the disclosure. Exact original binding and route comparisons prevent that substitution.

followups.question: Why must a denied read release its slot?
followups.answer: Otherwise one correct authorization denial could permanently consume finite capacity and block unrelated later reads. The negative case should preserve privacy, while a subsequent valid read proves that actual ownership and rollback cleanup completed.

questions.watch_for: A current permission preflight before external I/O is insufficient for this disclosure contract.

evidence.label: Public case call occurs between separate transactions
Later useful read after permission denial

test.name: preserves genuine ChannelError AccessDenied at protected=%s through actual rollback
test.assertion: Make the final currentBearer check deny after one successful public case read. Require AccessDenied, one rollback, no insert or update, then verify an independently permitted later read leaves reader and outbox active counts at zero.

diagram_hint.title: Permission can change during the external case read
steps: Reserve one application slot for the complete read.
First transaction derives original grant and route, reads retained result, then releases SQL.
Public P1 case read runs outside SQL; revocation may occur during this await.
Second transaction locks and rechecks the original binding, room, participant and route using fresh database time.
If revoked or expired: deny disclosure. If current: return separately timed observations with atomic false.
Release the application slot only after the real operation settles.

questions.title: Retain the evidence that admitted a new provider operation
questions.question: Why store predecessor and evidence digests instead of recomputing the admission reason from the latest operation status?
answer: A new provider operation after definitive nonacceptance needs a durable reason explaining why it was allowed. admissionFor validates a retained send result or lookup observation, then records its exact predecessor operation, attempt and evidence digest. createOperation stores that immutable witness with the new operation. Later observations can change current eligibility without rewriting the serialized evidence that justified the earlier admission.

New reservations also inspect every bounded earlier operation, not only the latest one. An old operation may later disclose acceptance or conflict and veto another reservation. The temporal-history fixture deliberately creates contradictory late provider evidence after a newer operation exists: original attempt history remains identical, but another send becomes unknown and explicit retry is held for prior_operation_evidence. This distinction is essential for auditability; current truth must block unsafe future work without pretending a previously admitted operation never had a valid witness.
questions.alternatives: Inferred tradeoff: keep only one mutable latest send status. It is simpler to query and display but destroys the original basis for admitting a later operation. An append-only event log could represent the same history, provided admission validates and retains exact correlated evidence atomically.
questions.counterfactual: Tempting edit: check only the most recent provider operation and drop predecessor evidence. A late accepted report for an older operation can then be ignored while another new send is admitted, duplicating one logical outbound reply.

challenge.symptom: Recorded test challenge: a provider first reports nonacceptance, enabling a later operation, then a previously delayed lookup reports acceptance for the earlier operation and creates a deliberate contradiction in the historical evidence.
challenge.diagnosis: Existing diagnosis: inspect original attempt bytes, the immutable admission witness and current reduction separately. The temporal fixture must preserve the admitted history while exposing conflict; overwriting history would conceal the actual race rather than resolve it.
challenge.handling: Existing handling: retain the witness and veto future reservations from any unsafe earlier operation. Contradictory late facts do not revoke an external call already admitted; further remediation requires a separately designed explicit business operation.

followups.question: Why hash the specific evidence instead of just recording its status?
followups.answer: The status alone cannot identify the observation that was actually validated at admission. A digest and exact identity bind the witness to immutable bytes, so later contradictory reports remain distinguishable rather than replacing the historical reason.

followups.question: Can late evidence invalidate the old admission receipt?
followups.answer: It can change what new work is safe now, but it must not rewrite the already committed witness or original receipt. Preserve both facts and show the conflict. A past serialized decision and present eligibility are different questions.

followups.question: Does the fixture prove a real carrier obeys the contract?
followups.answer: No. It deliberately violates provider expectations to test conservative local behavior. The assertions establish retained history and future veto under that synthetic scenario, not a guarantee that any production carrier provides reliable absence or physical deduplication.

questions.watch_for: Preserve past admission evidence while allowing later truth to block future work.

evidence.label: All earlier distinct provider operations are rechecked
Witness and digest persisted with provider operation
Late contradiction preserves history and vetoes future work

test.name: main mode exercise stage temporal_history
test.assertion: Create a newer operation after recorded nonacceptance, then release contradictory acceptance for its predecessor. Assert original inspect history is byte-for-byte unchanged, another send is unknown, and explicit retry returns prior_operation_evidence.

questions.title: A callback must win admission to veto a new reservation
questions.question: Why are callback authentication, exact attempt correlation and the shared admission lock all required?
answer: CallbackStore authenticates and snapshots the raw callback before scheduling I/O, then rechecks transport freshness with database time. Replay lookup is scoped to the authenticated provider event. For a new observation, the exact original attempt, provider operation key and request digest must match before capacity or insertion. A later association or body label cannot supply another recipient relationship.

The callback write and outbound reservation share the durable admission lock. That gives a precise race result: a retained callback vetoes a new reservation, but one arriving after a call was already reserved cannot revoke that possible I/O. The callback-race fixture exercises both schedules with barriers, including a paused admitted send followed by revocation and callback. This code therefore combines authentication, immutable correlation and serialization; dropping any one allows a different class of forged, misattributed or racy evidence.
questions.alternatives: Inferred tradeoff: verify callbacks asynchronously after inserting them, or check callback veto outside reservation SQL. Those approaches reduce time in one transaction but either admit unauthenticated evidence or introduce a check-then-reserve race. The current design keeps bounded evidence writes and send admission under one serialized guard.
questions.counterfactual: Tempting edit: move the callback veto check before acquiring the admission lock. A callback can commit between that read and the new reservation, so both appear individually valid while another carrier call is admitted after the veto existed.

challenge.symptom: Hypothetical symptom: a correctly authenticated callback for an earlier attempt is retained, yet an explicit retry still reaches the carrier because a separate preflight read happened before the callback committed under contention.
challenge.diagnosis: Existing diagnosis: inspect the actual SQL serialization boundary and original attempt tuple. Test callback-first and retry-first schedules with explicit barriers; delayed provider timestamps cannot determine which protected admission happened first.
challenge.handling: Existing handling: authenticate every callback, preserve exact tuple correlation and serialize the veto with reservation. In the inverse schedule, retain the already admitted send result honestly rather than claiming the late callback or revocation stopped it.

followups.question: Why authenticate a callback that appears to be a replay?
followups.answer: Replay can reveal a receipt or history. The event ID must not become an unauthenticated lookup oracle. Authentication establishes the provider principal before any shortcut, and the exact retained payload still detects changed bytes under the same ID.

followups.question: Can a failed callback permit resend?
followups.answer: No. The selected callback contract is evidence with a conservative new-reservation veto. A provider failure report does not automatically establish reliable nonacceptance, and it cannot grant current recipient permission or choose a replacement operation key.

followups.question: What does the retry-first schedule prove?
followups.answer: It proves the limit of the database fence. Once reservation admitted the call, later callback or route revocation cannot undo external I/O. The test must retain the original attempt and known response, rather than falsely classify cancellation before dispatch.

questions.watch_for: A callback veto orders new admission; it cannot fence a carrier call already admitted.

evidence.label: Raw authentication precedes scheduling and replay
Callback writes acquire the shared admission lock
New reservations inspect retained callback veto

test.name: main mode callback-race
test.assertion: Serialize callback before explicit retry and require callback_veto. Invert the order by pausing a reserved carrier call, then revoke and store a callback; release it and retain the original known acceptance under its exact attempt.

diagram_hint.title: Callback first and reservation first have different outcomes
steps: Callback first: authenticate and correlate exact old attempt, acquire shared admission, retain callback, commit.
New reservation later sees retained callback and returns callback_veto without another carrier invocation.
Inverse schedule: reservation acquires admission first, checks current route and callback absence, records possible call, commits.
Carrier call pauses outside SQL; route revocation and callback can now commit.
Release paused carrier call: late veto cannot undo earlier admission; retain its original attempt and known result.

questions.title: Idle polling should respond to progress rather than activity
questions.question: Why exclude parked uncertain rows from automatic eligibility and reset idle backoff only after dispatch?
answer: The audit found an uncertain input with a missing sender association could be reclaimed every poll. Because it remained a possible external operation, the state could not truthfully become not_executed. Current eligibility excludes the precise parked combination uncertain plus association_required, while explicit step and lookup-only reconcile remain available. That prevents one unadvanceable row from repeatedly consuming automatic attempts and scan attention.

The gateway separately treats only dispatched status or a local nudge as a reason to reset its idle delay. Merely inspecting or reselecting a row is activity, not useful progress. A mocked dispatcher repeatedly returning uncertain now causes exponential idle backoff instead of a hot loop; a fresh local accepted input still nudges immediate work. These are two complementary choices: storage describes useful automatic candidates, and the loop avoids treating every candidate observation as success. They do not establish global fairness or fix all joined shutdown findings.
questions.alternatives: Documented audit fix, inferred tradeoff: retry every retained uncertain row aggressively to minimize recovery latency. That wastes bounded attempts and competes with useful work when permission is absent. Excluding all uncertainty would be too broad; the implementation parks only the documented association-required condition from automatic discovery.
questions.counterfactual: Tempting edit: set dispatched true whenever an eligible row is returned. A permanently uncertain row then resets delay every cycle, defeats idlePollMs and recreates the audit hot-loop and starvation risk without completing any work.

challenge.symptom: Recorded audit symptom: uncertain input parked for missing sender association was repeatedly claimed, defeating idle backoff and potentially starving newer inputs even though the loop was technically busy and its timers were firing.
challenge.diagnosis: Existing diagnosis: compare eligible scans and step calls against actual dispatched outcomes and retained last_code. High polling activity with no useful completion is not evidence of healthy processing; identify the exact parked state.
challenge.handling: Existing handling: exclude that parked combination from automatic discovery and back off on no progress. Keep explicit observation available, preserve possible-call uncertainty, and test a later nudge or independent valid input for useful responsiveness.

followups.question: Why not delete the parked row?
followups.answer: It may represent a possible external acceptance and retains replay protection. Removing it would trade CPU pressure for lost business truth. Parking changes automatic discovery only; retained history and explicit reconciliation remain available under their own permissions.

followups.question: Is less than eight polls a production performance guarantee?
followups.answer: No. That unit test distinguishes backoff from the previous constant interval under a small controlled window. Production capacity needs a frozen workload, actual resource measurements and useful-completion evidence. The test proves the selected policy, not throughput.

followups.question: Could a remote input wait longer than a local one?
followups.answer: A local input can nudge the loop immediately, while externally visible eligible work may wait up to the configured idle delay. That latency tradeoff is explicit. A future notification transport could reduce it without replacing durable discovery.

questions.watch_for: A busy polling loop may be making no useful progress.

evidence.label: Only the precise parked uncertain state is excluded
Parked uncertainty is retained outside automatic eligibility

test.name: backs off while re-selected eligible work makes no dispatch progress
test.assertion: Return the same eligible ID repeatedly with uncertain step results and verify the loop makes fewer than eight steps in the controlled window. Separately verify local intake interrupts idle delay and the parked eligibility predicate preserves uncertainty.

questions.title: Reserve capacity to record facts already learned
questions.question: Why give carrier-result recording its own four slots instead of using the four ordinary outbox calls?
answer: A carrier response is useful truth that may arrive after the ordinary read or reservation slots are saturated. The previous shared cap could reject recordResult, leaving a known accepted_by_provider outcome permanently unknown locally. The store now tracks recording work separately: ordinary capacity is calls.size minus recordings, while recording has its own four-slot cap. Both kinds remain in the owned call set until actual settlement.

The recording helper also uses its own non-aborted signal, so caller abandonment does not discard a validated late fact. Identity and canonical-result checks still run in SQL before insertion. The change is a bounded reserved lane, not an unlimited bypass or promise to survive storage failure. The regression test holds all four normal calls, verifies another ordinary read is overloaded, then confirms an exact carrier result is inserted and unknown count remains zero.
questions.alternatives: Documented audit fix, inferred tradeoff: increase one shared pool limit. That postpones saturation without reserving room for facts from already admitted sends. A durable independent result journal is another design, but it would add new persistence and reconciliation ownership beyond this contained bounded-lane repair.
questions.counterfactual: Tempting edit: simplify admission to calls.size greater than or equal to four for every operation. Four held pending reads then block recordResult after the carrier already accepted, converting a known external outcome back into unknown local state.

challenge.symptom: Recorded audit symptom: the carrier returned a known result, but ordinary outbox call saturation prevented storage recording. The application subsequently displayed unknown and could not establish that result from its retained local state.
challenge.diagnosis: Existing diagnosis: distinguish send invocation capacity, ordinary storage calls and late result recording. Hold the four ordinary calls deliberately, then inspect whether the actual result insert occurs rather than merely whether send returned promptly.
challenge.handling: Existing handling: preserve a separate bounded recording lane and retain both classes through settlement. A real database outage can still leave uncertainty; the repair prevents ordinary local saturation from manufacturing it when storage is available.

followups.question: Why exactly four recording slots?
followups.answer: The implementation matches the outbox maximum active task count, so every admitted carrier task has bounded capacity to record. This is a structural reservation, not a benchmark-derived production setting. Changing active task limits requires reviewing the relationship.

followups.question: Does this give recordings a separate database pool?
followups.answer: No. It separates application call admission while sharing the configured pool and transaction machinery. It prevents rejection at the local four-call guard; database availability, locking and connection limits remain independent constraints that can still delay or fail recording.

followups.question: Can a late response overwrite a conflicting retained result?
followups.answer: No. Recording validates the original request tuple and canonical result. Equal data replays; changed data conflicts. Reserving a lane preserves capacity for truth, not authority to replace immutable facts or accept an unrelated carrier response.

questions.watch_for: Capacity for new requests and capacity to retain results of already admitted work need different treatment.

evidence.label: Recording helper explicitly owns a separate bounded lane
Exact request and result validation precede insertion

test.name: records a %s send result instead of reporting unknown
test.assertion: Hold four ordinary pending reads, require a fifth ordinary read to overload, then return a known carrier acceptance or nonacceptance. Assert exact send_results insertion and unknown remains zero before releasing the held reads.

questions.title: An index migration still needs protected ownership
questions.question: Why does the v9 owner upgrade explicitly lock indexed tables and revalidate before its index-only DDL?
answer: v9 adds three operating indexes and changes no business row, but it still changes the validated catalog and schema metadata. The owner first acquires the schema advisory transaction lock, checks the supported source version, then takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE locks on metadata, admission and affected tables. It revalidates the catalog after acquiring those locks before any index DDL. Quiescence remains the required operational procedure; locks protect the actual maintenance boundary.

The explicit ordering closes a race in assuming that an earlier validation remains current while waiting for DDL locks. A repeated complete v9 invocation revalidates under protection without recreating indexes or downgrading state. The synthetic ordering test asserts lock then validate then DDL, and the real populated fixture interrupts after index creation to prove rollback, compares original rows and receiver identity, then verifies the exact three indexes and unchanged legacy reads.
questions.alternatives: Documented owner-upgrade contract, inferred tradeoff: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY could reduce blocking for a production online migration. It requires a different transaction and partial-failure procedure. This local explicit quiescent upgrade chooses one atomic owner transaction with populated rollback and replay evidence instead of claiming zero-downtime DDL.
questions.counterfactual: Tempting edit: remove the explicit table locks because CREATE INDEX locks something anyway. Validation and metadata operations then lack the declared shared maintenance boundary, and tests can no longer establish revalidation after acquiring all protected tables.

challenge.symptom: Recorded audit issue: the v9 upgrade lacked explicit locks despite its maintenance-only contract. Index creation appearing harmless obscured that validated catalog and version metadata still need a coherent protected transition and rollback.
challenge.diagnosis: Existing diagnosis: inspect owner statement order, not just final index names. Also compare full populated logical snapshots around injected interruption; an apparently complete catalog can hide changed receiver identities or partially committed metadata.
challenge.handling: Existing handling: take explicit maintenance locks, revalidate, create indexes and update metadata in one owner transaction. Keep runtime DDL forbidden; any future online migration needs a separately designed compatibility and recovery procedure.

followups.question: Why validate again after locking?
followups.answer: An earlier check can become stale while waiting for locks. The protected revalidation ties the assumptions to the state actually being changed. Advisory locking coordinates cooperating owners; explicit table locks additionally protect the relevant maintenance state during the transition.

followups.question: Does index only mean the entire database is byte identical?
followups.answer: No. Catalog objects and schema metadata intentionally change. The stronger relevant assertion is that business rows, original receiver identity, receipts and public legacy reads remain unchanged, while exactly the declared indexes appear and interrupted upgrade rolls back.

followups.question: Can serving code automatically repair a missing index?
followups.answer: Not under this contract. Runtime performs validation using its restricted role and reports mismatch. Schema creation, upgrade and repair remain explicit owner operations so an ordinary request or startup does not acquire hidden DDL authority.

questions.watch_for: Index-only business semantics do not make catalog transitions or migration ownership optional.

evidence.label: The index specification changes no business rows
Actual populated index upgrade and rollback fixture

test.name: locks the indexed tables and revalidates before any v9 DDL from version %i
test.assertion: For source versions eight and nine, assert explicit locks follow the version read and immediate revalidation precedes DDL. Pair this ordering proof with populated PostgreSQL rollback, unchanged logical rows and exact index-name assertions.

questions.title: Do not derive the external receipt from source UUIDs
questions.question: Why does the operation client validate operation key scope and digest, yet accept an independently returned receipt UUID?
answer: The original P2 operation UUID identifies the accepted input processing intention. The input receipt UUID identifies durable intake, and the external receipt identifies acceptance by the cooperating authority. They are separate identities. The client checks that the returned operation key, full account scope and payload digest match the original request, then validates the independent receipt UUID instead of deriving it from the P2 source IDs.

At the origin-bound application bridge the external receipt is the actual P1 work UUID; a caller correlation ID is not proof of that join. checkedPrepared retains original receipt, event, message and sender fields in canonical request bytes. A malformed or mismatched response to accept remains OutcomeUnknown, while the corresponding failed lookup is Unavailable. Neither outcome permits replacing the operation key. The loopback test returns a wrong digest first, proves those distinct errors, then returns an exact binding and demonstrates later useful acceptance.
questions.alternatives: Inferred tradeoff: derive the P1 receipt deterministically from the P2 operation UUID. That makes demos easy to correlate but conflates source and authority identity unless the public acceptance contract explicitly defines it. Returning the actual retained receipt preserves a verifiable boundary and supports independent authoritative record allocation.
questions.counterfactual: Tempting edit: overwrite the response operationKey with the expected key without comparing it first. A well-formed receipt for another operation or payload can then be adopted as this input acceptance, hiding a provenance or routing defect.

challenge.symptom: Hypothetical symptom: the UI shows a valid-looking work UUID and policy result that belong to another source input, or a response-matching bug is hidden because every receipt ID was fabricated from local correlation fields.
challenge.diagnosis: Existing diagnosis: join original accepted receipt and operation, canonical preparation, returned digest and actual P1 work independently. A kind label or UUID shape proves no provenance; compare the complete retained binding and independent authority record.
challenge.handling: Existing handling: retain original source IDs, validate exact response correlation and return the actual receipt. Preserve accept uncertainty and read unavailability distinctly; a future narrower identifier mapping belongs at the explicit bridge without truncating standalone SDK identities.

followups.question: Why not require receiptId equals operationKey?
followups.answer: They identify different commitments. Requiring equality would impose an unstated allocation policy on the external authority and could hide fabricated receipts in tests. Validate each domain and prove the relationship using retained request correlation and the actual authority receipt.

followups.question: Why is the wrong accept response unknown rather than rejected?
followups.answer: The remote service may already have committed before returning malformed or miscorrelated bytes. The client cannot conclude nonacceptance. A read failure is unavailable because that read creates no new obligation; operation-specific reconciliation must preserve the original request.

followups.question: Can the input digest alone establish provenance?
followups.answer: It binds bytes relative to a trusted source record, but identical text can be two legitimate inputs. Origin identity needs the original operation and receipt relationship as well. A matching body digest without the retained scoped source join is insufficient.

questions.watch_for: Original intake, processing operation and external acceptance receipts are related identities, not interchangeable UUIDs.

evidence.label: Canonical preparation retains distinct original source IDs
Source operation and input UUIDs remain independent

test.name: keeps malformed/wrong receipt acceptance unknown and lookup unavailable, then accepts the exact receipt
test.assertion: Use an actual loopback peer returning the correct operation and scope but wrong digest. Require OutcomeUnknown for accept and Unavailable for lookup; then return exact correlation, require useful success and retain the independently allocated receipt UUID.

limits: All source snippets refer to this checkout and are unmodified continuous ranges. The PDF builder should preserve whitespace and wrap long source lines without changing code.
This is source and test review, not a new execution report. Historical selected qualification remains bounded by the repository recorded gate scope; complete P2 charter rows remain planned.
Current joined shutdown and no_audio ambiguity findings remain open. The cards do not imply a global cancellation fence, full carrier certification or production capacity.
The first webhook precheck occurs after local call admission but before a database connection and durable admission lock; its signed timestamp is not present freshness authority.

chapters.title: P3 Delegation with explicit result authority
chapters.subtitle: P3 Delegation Reliability Kit
intro: P3 is the strongest place to demonstrate reasoning about distributed agent boundaries: a conversational tool may stop waiting, a specialist may finish late, and the case may change while all of that happens. The implementation keeps those facts separate instead of promising that one timeout or one receipt settles every question.

Read these answers as code-grounded rehearsal material. The local POC retains one durable execution authority in P1, channel identity and routing in P2, and narrowly scoped P3 coordination and derived metadata. Selected gates and historical reports are evidence for their declared schedules; this review did not rerun infrastructure or provider tests.

Start with P3-01, P3-05, P3-06, P3-08, P3-10, P3-13, P3-15, P3-17 and P3-22. Then practise a late-A/current-B scenario and a crash after a possible result delivery. Each answer should name the authority, the commitment point, what remains unknown and how useful later work progresses.

concepts.title: One owner per durable decision
concepts.body: P1 owns acceptance, issuance, result disposition, delivery intent and guarded action. The specialist registry is ephemeral live capacity. P3 projection and refresh state are derived references rather than a second work queue.

concepts.title: Four independent result questions
concepts.body: Are the bytes structurally valid and matched? Are the facts supported by the exact immutable sources? Was the result eligible at P1 commit? Is it applicable and permitted for the proposed next operation now? A positive answer to one never substitutes for the others.

concepts.title: Cancellation has several meanings
concepts.body: Stopping SDK speech or a tool waiter, recording a P1 business cancellation request, asking an HTTP peer to abort and observing actual remote settlement are different events. Retain ownership and capacity until the underlying work is known settled.

concepts.title: Replay preserves the original world
concepts.body: A command replay returns original accepted semantics or original receipt truth. It does not choose new evidence, renew a deadline, change the receiver or produce a new external accept. Unknown writes reconcile the same identity.

concepts.title: Selected qualification is bounded evidence
concepts.body: P3 has three registered complete lab acceptance rows and fourteen planned full rows. Many later slices passed selected local gates, including installed artifacts and process fault schedules. They do not imply full release, general real-model quality or production scale.

questions.title: Choose a delegation boundary
questions.question: Why did this project build a remote specialist after implementing native LiveKit tools and tasks?
answer: The native baseline compares an ordinary function tool with AgentTask and TaskGroup inside a real AgentSession. It deliberately holds the same read-only policy evaluation while another question exercises conversational progress. AgentTask temporarily controls that session; it is not an independent durable process. The baseline therefore answers a specific orchestration question before adding a service boundary.

The remote specialist introduces Python-to-TypeScript contracts, independent resource limits and a separately authenticated deployment boundary. P1 supplies durable acceptance, issued attempts and result recording; the HTTP service performs one bounded read-only calculation. Remote execution is justified by isolation and a real consumer boundary, rather than by assuming another process improves latency. It also costs serialization, authentication, network uncertainty, resource ownership and more complicated cleanup.

In an interview, defend both choices. A small local conversational subtask should usually remain a native tool or task. Work that must survive the conversational process needs durable authority, irrespective of whether the computation is local or remote. The final fair three-way performance and quality comparison remains separate release work; the baseline alone does not establish that remote delegation wins.

followups.question: Would TaskGroup recover after a worker process dies?
followups.answer: The baseline does not provide that guarantee. Its tasks belong to one SDK session and process. Recovery must inspect persisted accepted work and issued attempts through P1, retain the original logical identity, and request a genuinely new eligible issuance when required.

followups.question: What would make you remove the specialist service?
followups.answer: If all consumers are Python, isolation brings little operational value, and measurements show transport overhead dominates useful work, I would keep the same typed execution and evidence contracts behind a local adapter. Durable acceptance and exact action authorization would remain separate.

questions.watch_for: Do not describe a native task as a durable workflow engine or claim an unmeasured remote latency advantage.

evidence.label: Native task and same-session TaskGroup baseline

questions.title: Keep one execution authority
questions.question: Which state does P3 own, and why is the specialist HTTP registry not another accepted-work queue?
answer: P1 owns immutable accepted work, execution issuance, result disposition, delivery intent and guarded action receipts. The P3 coordinator composes public ports and stores no competing accepted-work ledger. Its durable input is the canonical request body submitted through P1's work API. P3 projection, processing and refresh stores contain derived references and observations over that authority.

The specialist's AttemptBoundary is a finite live permit map. It authenticates a principal, validates scope and evidence, rejects a conflicting active attempt, and reserves global and per-principal capacity. Release requires the actual minted permit object. It has no timer that deletes active work, no retry scheduler and no recovery ownership. A server restart loses those ephemeral observations without changing whether P1 accepted or issued the work.

This division prevents two components from independently deciding that a timed-out task should run again. A production expansion should preserve one recovery decision point and make any notification transport advisory. P3 can report that an HTTP attempt is running, cancelled or unavailable, but those observations cannot create execution permission or replace P1 result truth. The caller must distinguish a live service status response from a durable business receipt.

followups.question: Could Redis or NATS own the retry queue instead?
followups.answer: That would require an explicit authority redesign, including atomic acceptance, identity retention and reconciliation with P1. Adding a broker notification is easier: P1 remains authoritative and workers reconcile by original work identity when a notification is duplicated or lost.

followups.question: Why retain permits until explicit release?
followups.answer: A deadline can stop the caller while computation still uses CPU, memory or a provider request. Releasing the slot at waiter timeout would admit replacement work before the original settled and make the configured concurrency bound fictional.

questions.watch_for: An ephemeral attempt observation is not acceptance, recovery ownership or proof that remote work stopped.

evidence.label: Exact permit identity required for release

questions.title: Design a cross-language contract
questions.question: What must Python and TypeScript agree on beyond a JSON schema?
answer: They must agree on exact supported fields, primitive types, bounds, version handling, canonical encoding and semantic identity. P3 bounds requests to 16 KiB and results to 8 KiB, with finite node count, nesting depth and a maximum 60-second request window. Its Python integer validator explicitly rejects booleans even though bool subclasses int. Equivalent TypeScript checks must reject unsafe or nonintegral numbers.

A request binds tenant/account scope, delegation identity, case, request revision, context/evidence references, result route and deadline. Attempt correlation is separate from the immutable logical fingerprint, so a new authorized attempt does not silently change accepted business input. Receiving code reparses even caller-created frozen dataclasses; a typed value is not evidence that it passed the boundary correctly.

Shared valid and invalid fixtures exercise the actual producer/consumer boundary, including unsupported versions, changed identities and schema-valid but unsupported facts. The current facades explicitly separate original v1 policy, fixed-policy v2 and origin-bound v3 envelopes. That costs more API surface, but prevents a new schema from silently changing the meaning of an old consumer. A schema library alone cannot establish factual support or permission to act.

followups.question: Why reject unknown fields rather than ignore them?
followups.answer: For these closed authority-related envelopes, an ignored field can make two producers believe they requested different behavior while a consumer sees the same command. Explicit versioning and exact field sets make unsupported semantics fail visibly and keep replay comparison defensible.

followups.question: Does a matching SHA-256 prove the result is correct?
followups.answer: It proves byte identity relative to the digest, assuming the digest came from a trusted binding. It does not establish that the input was authorized, the computation was correct or the result applies to the current case. Those checks remain separate.

questions.watch_for: Do not confuse structural parsing, request/result matching, source verification and action authority.

evidence.label: Wire byte, structure and deadline bounds
Typed nested values revalidated on encoding

questions.title: Authenticate service scope
questions.question: How do you stop a specialist caller from choosing another tenant in the request body?
answer: The request body carries scope for correlation, but authority comes from trusted construction of LocalTrust and its configured PrincipalGrant records. Authentication hashes the bearer token and compares equal-sized digests with constant-time comparison across a bounded grant inventory. Authorization then checks the authenticated principal's allowed scope and the specific invoke, result, cancel or evidence capability.

Evidence access is separate: the caller must have permission for the selected source ID, and the registry resolves only configured immutable records. The HTTP invoke path requires result permission as well as invocation and evidence permission. The coordinator and runner also verify that their injected P1 clients expose the expected configured WorkScope before durable operations. A model-generated tenant label or a matching correlation ID cannot bypass those construction-time bindings.

The current local trust mechanism is intentionally finite and synthetic; it is not enterprise identity infrastructure. The latest audit also records a narrower remaining issue: status and cancel permissions are scope/capability checked but are not bound to the principal that originally started the attempt. State that limitation clearly and propose an explicit starting-principal binding if independent same-scope principals require stronger isolation.

followups.question: Why separate result and invoke grants?
followups.answer: A caller allowed to start computation should not automatically read another attempt's output, and an observer may need result access without invocation access. Separate grants make that distinction expressible and allow the service to verify all permissions required by the chosen endpoint.

followups.question: How would you fix the same-scope principal gap?
followups.answer: Retain the authenticated starting principal with the exact active attempt and require the same identity for status/cancel unless an explicit administrative delegation grant permits otherwise. Add two-principal same-scope tests, preserving independent operation permissions and safe unknown-attempt diagnostics.

questions.watch_for: Claim the authorization actually implemented; do not turn finite local bearer grants into a production identity claim.

questions.title: Persist before acknowledging delegation
questions.question: Walk through a coordinator submission and its lost-acknowledgement behavior.
answer: The coordinator snapshots and runtime-validates the request before its first await. It first looks up the original idempotency key. If work already exists, it validates the persisted canonical bytes and compares the appropriate logical semantics before returning the retained record. For new work it reads the trusted case adapter, checks exact scope/case/revision and cancellation, checks the finite deadline window, and submits the entire canonical envelope through the public P1 work API.

The important failure cut is a possible commit followed by acknowledgement loss. The coordinator performs one lookup by the original delegation key; it does not submit a second proposal, replace the deadline, or guess that the write failed. If the original record is found, it returns that validated winner with created=false. If the read is absent or unavailable, acknowledgement_unknown remains the honest result.

The case read is an admission preflight rather than an atomic action guarantee. A later case revision can make accepted read-only work outdated; exact action commitment still rechecks case authority. This design preserves useful historical computation while preventing acceptance from being mistaken for permission to mutate the booking.

followups.question: Why look up replay before checking the current case?
followups.answer: An already accepted command must remain readable and replayable after the case changes, cancellation or deadline expiry. Revalidating new-admission conditions first would hide original truth or accidentally encourage a caller to create a replacement command.

followups.question: What if two callers both miss the initial lookup?
followups.answer: The durable P1 admission guard chooses the original winner. The losing caller reconciles that same key and compares the retained semantics. A process-local lock would not solve independent-process races or survive a crash.

questions.watch_for: A failed response is not proof of rollback; preserve the original envelope and reconcile the original identity.

evidence.label: One submit followed by original-key reconciliation

questions.title: Separate acceptance from invocation
questions.question: Why does only Issuance.created=true permit a specialist call?
answer: Acceptance means P1 durably retained a bounded request. Invocation needs a distinct P1-issued attempt with an owner, command identity, epoch and lease. The runner observes current work, returns an already eligible result without reinvocation, and asks the public execution port to issue the caller's explicit command. Only a newly created issuance can proceed toward HTTP.

An existing issuance may already have reached the specialist, so a replayed command is observation only. An ambiguous issue acknowledgement is reconciled by find_issue; even if it finds the grant, this runner does not invoke.
