challenge.diagnosis: Inspect the created flag and compare the post-issue observation with the exact grant. An existing command can be real without being fresh permission, and stale running status may predate a cancellation.
challenge.handling: Existing replay and after-issue cancellation tests assert zero replacement invocation. Recovery after a conservatively unused grant remains explicit: a caller supplies a new command only when P1 creates a new eligible issuance.

followups.question: Why not invoke after find_issue succeeds?
followups.answer: The lookup proves issuance, not whether the original caller reached HTTP. It is deliberately observation-only. Otherwise an unknown acknowledgement followed by successful lookup would become a duplicate invocation path disguised as reconciliation.

followups.question: Is the second observation an atomic cancellation fence?
followups.answer: No. Cancellation can still race after that read. It prevents calls when a known change is observed before transport; P1 result disposition and operation-specific guards handle later races. The HTTP peer is outside the protected transaction.

followups.question: What is lost after a pre-HTTP crash?
followups.answer: One grant may have been issued without computation. The system preserves that uncertainty rather than guessing. Its accepted bytes and attempt history remain readable; a later explicit eligible issuance can recover useful progress without replaying the original authority.

questions.watch_for: A returned grant is not necessarily newly created permission to invoke.

test.name: test_fresh_current_observation_blocks_known_cancelled_issue
test.assertion: The fake execution port marks the work cancelled immediately after issue. The runner must reject and leave both specialist requests and completion count empty, demonstrating the value of the second observation rather than just checking a predicate.

evidence.label: Original issue replay preserves one invocation
Lease check immediately follows the excerpt

diagram_hint.title: Permission to invoke has two gates
steps: Runner asks issue(original command)
Existing or ambiguous issuance returns lookup only; no HTTP
New issuance is followed by exact fresh running-grant observation
Known cancellation or supersession prevents invocation
Only the surviving new grant crosses into specialist HTTP
After HTTP begins, retain actual I/O and let P1 classify the returned result

questions.title: Release only the permit that was minted
questions.question: Why compare permit object identity instead of accepting a newly constructed equal permit?
answer: AttemptBoundary is a process-local live capacity owner, not a durable credential service. acquire stores one minted AttemptPermit object together with its validated request. release checks both the lookup key and object identity with is before deleting the active entry. A dataclass copy with equal fields is therefore not a release capability.

This prevents a caller that merely knows correlation fields from retiring someone else's occupied slot. Premature release would permit replacement work while the original invocation still runs, invalidating the resource bound. The permit is intentionally nonportable: restart recovery belongs to P1's durable grants, not reconstruction of this ephemeral object. Scope and operation authorization still occur separately; object identity is a narrow ownership token inside one process, not general authentication.
questions.alternatives: Inferred trade-off: accepting structural equality would make serialization and testing easier, but it would let any holder of visible fields forge release authority. A signed portable token could be designed if required; this finite local boundary instead uses opaque minted object possession.
questions.counterfactual: Change observed[0] is not permit into observed[0] != permit. dataclasses.replace(permit) would then free the slot despite never being the object issued to the actual invocation owner, enabling a fifth live computation behind a four-slot claim.

challenge.symptom: Active count drops while the original work still executes, and replacement work is admitted too early. Correlation fields look correct, so equality-only logs may not reveal the unauthorized release.
challenge.diagnosis: Check whether release validates an actual minted capability or merely reconstructible public fields. An ephemeral map must not treat knowledge of attempt identity as proof that its current owner finished using resources.
challenge.handling: Existing handling rejects a copied equal permit, keeps the slot occupied, accepts the real object once and rejects its second release. A separate capacity test proves valid work progresses after the genuine release.

followups.question: Can this permit survive a process restart?
followups.answer: No, intentionally. Its purpose is live in-process capacity ownership. Persisted acceptance and execution recovery use P1 identities and grants. Reconstructing a local permit after restart would confuse observation state with durable authority.

followups.question: Does object identity protect against malicious code in the process?
followups.answer: It is not a security sandbox for arbitrary same-process code. It prevents accidental or unsupported API composition from substituting equal values. The threat and failure contract still assumes trusted application code owns the boundary object.

followups.question: Why reject a second genuine release?
followups.answer: Double release can hide lifecycle bugs and corrupt accounting. The original entry is gone after successful release, so a second call returns unknown_attempt instead of claiming another resource was freed or silently masking mismatched ownership.

questions.watch_for: Knowing the attempt fields is not the same as owning its live resource permit.

test.name: test_deadline_unknown_attempt_and_forged_permit_fail_without_admission
test.assertion: The test acquires a permit, rejects replace(permit), asserts active remains one, releases the original, rejects another release and asserts zero. It proves occupied capacity survives the forged equal value rather than merely testing an error string.

evidence.label: TypeScript uses the same permit reference identity

questions.title: Observe worker exit before trusting its message
questions.question: Why is a PNG worker message retained until exit instead of resolving the caller immediately?
answer: The worker may send a plausible message and then fail, send another message, emit unexpected output or remain alive. The parent therefore records the first message without resolving. A second message or output establishes a fixed failure and requests termination. The exit callback clears the timer and validates the actual exit outcome before exposing normal pixel evidence.

Abort similarly requests worker termination while retaining the owned worker entry until exit is observed. close waits for those settlement promises and bounded observer notices, reporting cleanup_incomplete if either remains. This is the concrete process analogue of retaining a shielded Python task after its waiter cancels. A returned timeout is an observer result; it is not proof that the underlying resource stopped or that a slot can be reused.
questions.alternatives: Inferred trade-off: resolving on message yields an earlier result and simpler code. It gives up proof of normal exit and can leak a worker that already produced output. The implementation pays a small settlement delay to align reported capacity with actual owned workers.
questions.counterfactual: Resolve directly in worker.on(message) and remove the worker from active there. A worker can then keep running after its slot is reused, or a late nonzero exit can no longer invalidate the prematurely reported normal pixel result.

challenge.symptom: A caller receives valid-looking pixels while worker metrics or thread state remain live, or repeated aborts admit extra decoders. Promise completion and actual worker exit have diverged.
challenge.diagnosis: Follow the owner through message, error, abort, terminate and exit callbacks. Identify the one event that releases active ownership, and check whether observer promises are also retained through close rather than discarded.
challenge.handling: Existing tests require normal results only after exit zero, retain an aborted started worker until exit and retry incomplete observer cleanup after release. They establish this fixed worker contract, not termination of arbitrary external providers.

followups.question: Why does abort not reject and release immediately?
followups.answer: Abort requests termination promptly; release and result settlement wait for observed worker exit in this decoder. Otherwise repeated cancellation could bypass the concurrency limit while old threads still decode or retain memory. The exit observer preserves that actual bound.

followups.question: What if the cleanup observer never settles?
followups.answer: It remains part of owned cleanup and close reports incomplete within its budget. The reference is retained for a later observation. It must not silently disappear because pixel computation finished or a race timer rejected.

followups.question: How is Python runner ownership similar?
followups.answer: The runner retains the actual task in its call set, shields it from caller cancellation and releases the slot in the settled callback. That supports late result recording without claiming the caller is still waiting or that cancellation stopped remote work.

questions.watch_for: A message, a timed-out waiter and a confirmed worker exit are different observations.

test.name: retains a started worker after abort until actual exit is observed
test.assertion: Immediately after abort the assertion requires one active worker. Only after the real decode promise rejects may active become zero, and the retained worker observation must report no normal result. This tests actual worker lifetime, not timer behavior alone.

evidence.label: Close waits on worker settlement and observer notices
Incomplete observer close retries actual settlement
Python owned task releases only on settlement
Worker ownership released only inside exit callback

questions.title: Record validated results even after cancellation
questions.question: Why does the runner complete the exact result after I/O instead of checking cancellation and dropping the bytes?
answer: After HTTP returns, the runner reparses the result, checks exact correlation and factual evidence, and passes the validated body to P1.complete. It does not replace the result with a caller timeout or discard it because cancellation arrived during the read-only computation. P1 decides commit disposition under its own protected time, attempt and cancellation state.

The historical result and current applicability are then reported separately. A valid supported answer can remain eligible=true for its immutable request while its P1 disposition is cancelled and its current view is execution_ineligible. Retaining those bytes improves reconciliation and audit without granting delivery or mutation permission. Unknown completion acknowledgement is looked up by the original attempt, with no second completion write; semantic validity remains mandatory even for late history.
questions.alternatives: Inferred trade-off: discard everything after cancellation reduces retained data and feels responsive. It also loses known remote output and obscures the difference between no result and an ineligible result. The implementation retains bounded validated history while keeping new authority guarded separately.
questions.counterfactual: Insert a current-cancelled return before complete and discard the already validated body. Inspection would incorrectly show missing output after the specialist actually finished, and recovery could no longer explain or reconcile the known late result under its original attempt.

challenge.symptom: The agent says no result exists after interruption even though the specialist returned a valid answer, or a late answer is displayed as currently actionable. Both collapse historical truth and permission.
challenge.diagnosis: Join the immutable attempt result with its P1 disposition and the separately derived applicability. Check whether cancellation changed the stored fact, prevented a fresh operation, or only stopped the caller from waiting.
challenge.handling: Existing handling stores the validated result with cancelled or expired disposition when applicable, then exposes it as ineligible. It preserves known original receipts after later changes and never derives human confirmation from the retained answer.

followups.question: Why not call complete only when eligible?
followups.answer: P1 must observe and classify valid historical results even if time or cancellation makes them ineligible. Otherwise missing and ineligible become indistinguishable. Completion stores evidence; fresh execution, delivery and action have separate eligibility guards.

followups.question: Can a wrong late answer be retained the same way?
followups.answer: No. Structural, correlation and factual checks run before completion. Expiry does not waive that contract. The retained history path accepts supported bytes with an ineligible disposition, not arbitrary output accompanied by a timing excuse.

followups.question: Does later cancellation rewrite eligible_at_commit?
followups.answer: No. That immutable field records the authority conditions at original result commit. Current cancellation can prevent new use and change the derived applicability view without rewriting what was eligible when recorded or erasing the exact original result.

questions.watch_for: Preserving a result is not granting permission to act on it.

test.name: test_cancel_during_http_retains_known_historical_result
test.assertion: The specialist is held while the work cancellation flag changes, then released. The test independently requires a cancelled recorded disposition, execution_ineligible applicability and the original true policy conclusion, proving three distinct facts survive together.

evidence.label: Known result survives later cancellation and old lease

questions.title: Make close respect the write boundary
questions.question: Why does coordinator.close abandon only calls that have not started writing?
answer: A call still waiting for a case preflight has not accepted new business responsibility. close marks it abandoned so that, when the read eventually returns, the next check prevents a late submit. A call already inside P1 submission may have committed; close keeps that actual task observed rather than cancelling it and pretending no acceptance happened.

The distinction is encoded by call.writing and checked at each admission boundary. Close stops new API admission, waits for retained operations, then closes the owned execution client. Its observer wait is bounded and shielded; unresolved cleanup remains explicit and can be observed later. This repairs a documented liveness/safety issue without adding a new scheduler. It does not by itself prove the joined application's dependency shutdown order is correct.
questions.alternatives: Documented policy with inferred trade-off: cancelling every task is superficially simple but confuses no-write preflight with possibly committed I/O. Waiting for every preflight without abandonment allows new accepted work during shutdown. The phase marker makes both outcomes explicit at a narrow boundary.
questions.counterfactual: Remove the not-writing abandonment loop. A case read paused before close can later return and submit new accepted work after shutdown began, even though no external or durable obligation existed when closing started.

challenge.symptom: Shutdown appears to finish its admission phase, then a previously paused read creates new work. The opposite bug reports cancelled even though an already-started submission later commits.
challenge.diagnosis: Locate the last preflight check and the exact transition to call.writing. Determine whether close merely cancelled its waiter or retained the actual operation and prevented new writes from calls that had not crossed that point.
challenge.handling: Existing tests hold the preflight through close and require zero submit calls, then separately hold a live write and require truthful incomplete close until it settles. Application-wide dependency ordering remains a separate open integration concern.

followups.question: Can close undo a submit already in flight?
followups.answer: No. It can bound how long it waits and retain the observer, but it cannot infer rollback from cancellation. The original key and request remain the reconciliation path if the caller no longer receives an acknowledgement.

followups.question: Why does the abandoned read keep its slot?
followups.answer: The read still consumes an actual operation until settlement. Abandonment prevents a later write; it does not certify that the underlying I/O stopped. Keeping its slot prevents replacement calls from exceeding the real concurrency bound.

followups.question: Would increasing cleanup time fix wrong ordering?
followups.answer: It can reduce incidental deadline failures but cannot establish the missing phase rule. First stop admission and retain dependencies until their users close, then allocate coherent budgets. A longer timeout cannot turn a late unauthorized submit into correct lifecycle behavior.

questions.watch_for: Stopping new admission and observing already admitted writes are separate shutdown duties.

test.name: test_close_during_case_read_never_starts_acceptance
test.assertion: The test pauses the case read, begins close, releases the read and requires request_aborted with both zero submit calls and zero pending calls. A separate held-write test verifies existing writes remain owned through incomplete close.

questions.title: Leave transiently unavailable rows unacknowledged
questions.question: Why does the completion processor translate selected dependency failures into per-row unavailable instead of failing or ACKing the whole batch?
answer: The processor distinguishes uncertainty, transient availability and definite invalidity. acknowledgement_unknown remains unknown. Selected dependency failures and changing applicability preconditions produce an unavailable row with no terminal acknowledgement. Definite unauthorized or invalid source relationships still raise, because they are not evidence that a temporary retry will become safe.

Returning a per-row outcome lets the bounded scan inspect later useful events without asserting that the first event finished. The processing store advances discovery separately from the contiguous terminal watermark. This fixes an actual audit defect: a transient dependency capacity failure previously became invalid_source_state and aborted the entire step. The current mapping is shared with refresh code, so temporary inability to observe a fact does not masquerade as proof that immutable source bytes are corrupt.
questions.alternatives: Documented correction with inferred trade-off: fail-fast batches are easier to reason about locally, while ACKing failures makes dashboards drain quickly. The former blocks useful later work; the latter loses unresolved obligations. Per-row unACKed outcomes preserve progress and require a separate truthful terminal watermark.
questions.counterfactual: Map capacity to invalid_source_state or write a terminal failed ACK for it. A saturated result reader would either stop every later result or permanently retire a result that was never actually reconciled.

challenge.symptom: One temporary busy reader stalls all completion processing, or an event vanishes from retries after a transient outage. Overall batch error counts cannot reveal whether useful later rows progressed.
challenge.diagnosis: Inspect the dependency code mapping and the returned ack/state pair. Distinguish a failed observation from a definite identity violation, then check the scan cursor and terminal watermark independently after the same step.
challenge.handling: Existing tests inject capacity into feed, delivery and result reads. Each first row stays unACKed while the second completes; a later step closes the gap. Definite unauthorized and invalid-source failures still stop before unsafe writes.

followups.question: Why is unknown separate from unavailable?
followups.answer: Unknown indicates a possible commit or external acceptance that cannot be resolved. Unavailable can mean no reliable observation was obtained now. Both may stay unACKed, but their recovery and operator explanations differ and must not imply an authorized resend.

followups.question: Should a corrupt event block every later event?
followups.answer: Definitely invalid P3 content can have a supported quarantine disposition after source identity is established. Corrupt or missing authority relationships cannot be guessed away. Follow the exact source/content distinction rather than catching every exception as an ordinary row failure.

followups.question: What happens if close arrives between rows?
followups.answer: The next proceed check prevents a new row from starting. A row already committing remains retained. This preserves the completed first-row fact while stopping later delivery or acknowledgement work after closing begins.

questions.watch_for: Unavailability is an observation failure, not a terminal business disposition.

test.name: test_result_read_capacity_is_unacked_unavailable_while_later_work_progresses
test.assertion: The shared helper injects one result-reader capacity error and asserts unavailable followed by acknowledged, only event two ACKed and scan_after=2. A later step ACKs the first and advances the terminal watermark to two.

evidence.label: Shared independent row outcomes and later gap closure

questions.title: Spend one shared budget across cursor wrap
questions.question: Why does the wrapped processing query use limit minus len(rows), and why is scan_after not the terminal watermark?
answer: The first query discovers unACKed rows after scan_after up to the projected head. If fewer than the requested number were found and an older gap remains, a second query wraps once, requesting only the unused portion of the same budget. The explicit public call caps the total at eight. Reusing the full limit in both queries would silently double the work per step.

scan_after is a discovery position, while terminal_watermark proves a contiguous prefix has terminal ACKs. An unresolved possible delivery can hold the watermark at zero while later events complete and discovery advances. The query excludes retained ACKs but does not hide unresolved display-tombstoned events. This design gives later work useful progress without inventing completion for the old gap or adding a second accepted-work scheduler.
questions.alternatives: Inferred trade-off: a single cursor is smaller API surface and easy to paginate. It cannot express an unresolved early event plus useful later completions truthfully. A full rescan is also simpler but violates bounded work as history grows. Separate cursors and one budgeted wrap preserve both properties.
questions.counterfactual: Pass limit rather than limit - len(rows) to the wrapped query. A caller requesting eight rows could examine sixteen, expanding dependency calls and response work beyond the documented step bound under precisely the unresolved-gap workload.

challenge.symptom: A supposedly bounded processing call does more work when it wraps, or later results never progress behind one unknown delivery. A single happy-path page does not expose either defect.
challenge.diagnosis: Freeze a gap before the discovery cursor and useful work after it. Compare total examined rows across both queries, then inspect individual ACKs and the contiguous terminal prefix instead of trusting the scan position.
challenge.handling: Existing tests use a one-row total limit across repeated wraps and retain an unknown first event while the second progresses. The real store independently computes the earliest unACKed gap before advancing its terminal watermark.

followups.question: Can the scan skip an unknown event forever?
followups.answer: It can move past it for discovery but wraps within explicit bounded calls. The event remains retained and unACKed. Skipping it terminally or deleting its identity would make the watermark claim knowledge the system does not have.

followups.question: Why reject True as a limit?
followups.answer: The call requires an integer from one through eight, with exact primitive checking. Python would otherwise accept a boolean as one. Resource limits are public protocol values and should not depend on language-specific numeric subtyping.

followups.question: Does processing ACK the P1 source?
followups.answer: No. It records that this P3 delivery policy finished handling one exact event. P1 result-feed reads remain observation-only. The local ACK neither grants execution nor authorizes an action or human acknowledgement.

questions.watch_for: The total examination bound includes the wrapped page, and discovery is not terminal knowledge.

test.name: test_bound_total_limit_includes_wrap_and_rejects_invalid_limits
test.assertion: The test leaves an old possible delivery unresolved, repeatedly processes with limit one and requires one outcome each time. It also rejects zero, nine and True. The separate unknown-A/current-B test asserts distinct scan and terminal positions.

evidence.label: Public maximum eight and exact integer limit
Terminal watermark derives from the earliest unACKed gap
Wrapped query belongs to one read-only coherent page

questions.title: Replay a refresh before consulting the world again
questions.question: Why is the command receipt lookup before current source reads, revision caps and dependency checks?
answer: A refresh command identifies one already committed derived observation, not a request to recompute forever. The first lookup checks whether that exact command has a receipt. If it does, the receipt is validated against original work, attempt and expected revision, then returned without reading today's source, case or capacity state.

A new command follows the longer path: inspect the current metadata head, enforce expected local revision and caps, verify the exact source event and historical result, then collect separate as-of observations and commit through CAS. That order preserves an old successful command when the source is later unavailable or the profile reaches capacity. It also prevents a replay from silently changing its answer after a case revision. Changed target or expected revision still conflicts rather than borrowing another command's receipt.
questions.alternatives: Inferred trade-off: rerun validation on every call looks fresher and uses one path. It breaks exact replay by turning a previously committed command into a new availability or capacity check. Freshness should be an explicit new command, with a new observation and its own local revision.
questions.counterfactual: Move the receipt lookup after source validation or the revision cap. An original successful refresh would then fail when the source ID changes, the source is down or the head reaches its cap, making acknowledgement-loss recovery depend on unrelated later state.

challenge.symptom: A retry of a previously successful command returns a new error or a different applicability view after the case changes. The command is behaving like a mutable query instead of an immutable receipt.
challenge.diagnosis: Check whether command replay occurs before current observations and growth checks. Compare the original receipt bytes with the replay, and count dependency reads and writes rather than merely comparing a final badge.
challenge.handling: Existing tests make the source unavailable, change its ID, fail the case reader and fill the local head after the first commit. The same command still returns identical bytes with no new reads or writes.

followups.question: What if the caller wants a fresh answer?
followups.answer: Use a new explicit command with the expected current local metadata revision. That creates a separately timed observation while preserving the old receipt. It still cannot make P1 and case reads atomic or grant new action authority.

followups.question: Why validate expected revision on replay?
followups.answer: It is part of the command semantics. Reusing a command ID with a different target or expected revision is a changed-payload conflict, even if the old command already succeeded. Otherwise a retained receipt could be misrepresented as another operation.

followups.question: Does local CAS solve stale case reads?
followups.answer: It orders competing metadata writes only. It cannot turn separately timed source, execution and case observations into one atomic snapshot. Retained invalidation witnesses and final action guards remain necessary despite a successful local compare-and-set.

questions.watch_for: Replay returns the original observation; a fresh read needs a fresh explicit command.

test.name: test_known_command_replays_before_new_source_case_reads_or_caps
test.assertion: After one refresh the test changes source identity, makes source/case reads fail and fills the head. Exact replay must retain canonical receipt equality, unchanged feed read count and one total commit, independently proving the ordering contract.

evidence.label: New command revision and capacity checks follow replay
Changed expected revision conflicts under a known command

questions.title: Hide a card without freeing its protected identity
questions.question: Why write a display tombstone into applicability_heads rather than delete the result or decrement capacity?
answer: hide first loads the original projected result and existing applicability view under the refresh-control lock. An existing tombstone replays unchanged. Otherwise it constructs a tombstone bound to the exact event, projection digest, request digest and refresh policy, then stores it in the head. The operation does not delete the projection or refresh command history.

The visible card can disappear while original inspect and replay still work. Its protected capacity remains consumed, and processing must continue to discover unresolved events regardless of display state. This avoids a delayed replay becoming a new operation after someone tidies the UI. The deliberate cost is finite lifetime admission under the local profile; production reclamation would need an explicit replay horizon, retained protection and a tested restore contract.
questions.alternatives: Documented retention policy with inferred trade-off: deleting hidden rows immediately saves storage and appears to solve capacity. It also discards replay and receipt identity. Keeping a compact tombstone alongside the retained history makes the presentation decision permanent without inventing safe deletion semantics.
questions.counterfactual: Delete projected_results and old refresh commands, or decrement command_count when hide runs. An old command could become unknown or a new refresh could be admitted past the protected cap, contradicting lifetime identity protection after display pruning.

challenge.symptom: Hiding an old card unexpectedly frees admission, an original command loses its receipt, or an unknown delivery stops appearing in processing. Presentation retention has leaked into authority and replay lifetime.
challenge.diagnosis: Compare original projection, latest receipt, retained counts and processing visibility before and after hide. A disappearing UI card alone does not show whether protected identities or unresolved obligations were also removed.
challenge.handling: Existing unit assertions preserve original read bytes after hiding. The real applicability fixture hides at full capacity, successfully replays the old command and still rejects a new command with capacity. No automatic identity reclamation is implemented.

followups.question: Why bind the tombstone to digests?
followups.answer: It prevents a display decision for one event or request from being applied to another retained row with a similar identifier. The marker preserves exactly which immutable projection and policy were hidden, supporting replay and restore validation.

followups.question: Does hidden mean processing complete?
followups.answer: No. A possible delivery can remain unresolved even when its card is hidden. Discovery and ACK logic must continue to see that event; otherwise a display preference would erase an accepted recovery obligation without a terminal receipt.

followups.question: How would production reclaim this storage?
followups.answer: First define acceptable replay horizons and which compact identities must survive beyond them. Specify old-command rejection, backup/restore and source-incarnation behavior, then qualify those transitions. A business deadline or UI TTL alone does not supply that contract.

questions.watch_for: A hidden result is not an expired command identity or reclaimed execution capacity.

test.name: test_display_hide_replays_tombstone_without_changing_original_reads
test.assertion: The test hides twice, requires the same tombstone and unchanged projection/latest receipt bytes through original inspection. The real retained_capacity schedule additionally proves hiding does not free a protected command slot while original replay remains available.

evidence.label: Real cap remains full after hide and old replay
Protected command count validated independently of display
Tombstone writes the head without deleting original rows

questions.title: Allocate feed order inside the result transaction
questions.question: Why increment a locked scope-local head instead of using a global pre-commit sequence?
answer: append_result_event is called after result insertion under P1's existing admission guard in the same transaction. It locks the scope head, increments its retained sequence with a conditional update and appends the event before commit. A result replay returns its original body before this append path, so replay emits no additional event.

The important property is visibility order, not prettier numbering. With an independent global sequence, transaction A can reserve one and stall while B commits two; a consumer advancing past two may never see A's later commit. The protected local head prevents that gap from becoming visible as a committed higher event first. P3 consumes the public scoped result feed and verifies source/event/result identities; it does not create its own accepted-work stream or source acknowledgement.
questions.alternatives: Documented ordering requirement with inferred trade-off: a database sequence is fast and familiar but allocates independently of commit visibility. A transactional per-scope head serializes admission and can add contention. The local POC chooses a correct cursor contract before optimizing throughput or partitioning the authority.
questions.counterfactual: Allocate event sequence with nextval before the protected result transaction and let consumers advance to the maximum visible value. A stalled lower commit can then appear behind an already advanced cursor and be permanently skipped.

challenge.symptom: A feed consumer occasionally misses a committed result despite monotonically increasing IDs. The loss occurs when a lower-numbered transaction commits after the consumer already observed and checkpointed a higher number.
challenge.diagnosis: Reproduce with a held precommit result and a competing completion. Observe actual database lock contention, read the feed before release and compare final scoped event order; timestamps and single-threaded fixtures cannot expose the visibility race.
challenge.handling: Existing PostgreSQL tests hold the first completion before commit, prove the second is blocked and show no visible event until release. The final feed contains both original work IDs in order. This review did not rerun that gate.

followups.question: Why not use recorded_at_ms as the cursor?
followups.answer: Timestamps can tie and need not provide a safe committed order. The sequence contract makes pagination explicit within one source and scope. Time remains evidence about an observation, not the authority for deciding which committed rows a cursor may skip.

followups.question: Does the per-scope sequence imply a global order?
followups.answer: No. Cursors bind source and tenant/account scope. Events in different scopes have no promised common sequence. Imposing a global order would add contention and semantics the current consumer does not require.

followups.question: What about old results adopted during upgrade?
followups.answer: They are labelled adopted_history and retain original result bytes and timestamps. Their new feed sequence is an adoption order, not proof of the original chronological commit order. Consumers must keep that historical qualification visible.

questions.watch_for: Monotonic allocation is weaker than a cursor order safe under concurrent commits.

test.name: test_uncommitted_lower_event_cannot_be_skipped_by_later_completion

questions.title: Bound image cost before copying and decompression
questions.question: Why validate encoded size before Uint8Array.from and dimensions before constructing the decoder worker?
answer: The parent checks that body is a bounded Uint8Array before copying it. It then freezes reference metadata, copies owned bytes and verifies exact media type, byte length and digest. Reading the actual PNG header rather than trusting registry dimensions rejects oversized or mismatched images before a worker starts.

The fixed worker repeats structural checks and bounds decompression to the exact expected scanline length using inflateSync(maxOutputLength). It rejects extra compressed input and extra decoded rows before allocating the final pixel buffer. These layers bound different costs: encoded copy size, worker count, decoded dimensions and expansion. None proves extracted text is factual; the document provider runs only after validated decoding and still requires output validation and clarification handling.
questions.alternatives: Inferred trade-off: delegating every check to an image library is shorter and supports more PNG variants. It can allocate or decompress before applying application limits. This implementation deliberately supports a narrow RGB/RGBA subset and rejects unsupported forms rather than claiming full-format compatibility.
questions.counterfactual: Move the size check after Uint8Array.from or remove maxOutputLength from inflation. The first edit allocates an oversized caller buffer before rejection; the second lets a small compressed image expand far beyond its declared rows and memory budget.

challenge.symptom: A small screenshot input causes a large memory spike or stalls conversational processing, while a generous encoded-byte cap appears satisfied. Another symptom is provider work beginning for an image whose actual header contradicts its reference.
challenge.diagnosis: Measure allocation and worker startup order, not only the final rejection code. Compare actual header dimensions with trusted metadata and calculate expected scanline bytes before inflation; compressed byte length alone does not bound decoded cost.
challenge.handling: Existing tests reject encoded overflow and excessive or forged dimensions before workers start, and reject expansion/trailing compressed input in the fixed worker. Provider invocation is checked only after decode and a fresh deadline check.

followups.question: Why copy only after the bound check?
followups.answer: The caller owns mutable input bytes. A bounded copy establishes stable evidence across awaits, but copying first would let rejected input consume unbounded memory. Validation order must protect both ownership and resource limits.

followups.question: Does a 2 MiB PNG cap bound memory to 2 MiB?
followups.answer: No. Decoded pixels, scanlines, compressed buffers, worker runtime and provider state add separate costs. Dimensions and maximum expansion constrain some of them, while actual RSS measurement is still needed before any production capacity claim.

followups.question: Can a valid decoded region prove the extracted booking value?
followups.answer: No. Format and region structure are separate from factual extraction. The test-only literal image oracle can catch a schema-valid wrong value; arbitrary real-model OCR quality remains a separate evidence requirement and cannot supply mutation authority.

questions.watch_for: Bound before allocation; compressed size is not decoded cost or factual truth.

test.name: rejects encoded oversize before copying or starting a worker
test.assertion: The test supplies 2,097,153 bytes and requires evidence_mismatch with workersStarted=0. Separate dimension and expansion cases prove rejection before worker/decompression and bounded inflation; a matching source digest does not excuse malformed image structure.

evidence.label: Actual dimensions checked before fixed worker creation
Expected scanline length and maximum inflate output
Provider follows decode and fresh deadline check

questions.title: Select a closed codec through an explicit facade
questions.question: Why keep DelegationRunner, FixedPolicyRunner and ChannelPolicyRunner instead of auto-detecting every envelope version?
answer: The shared runner engine handles bounded ownership and P1 execution, while an explicit codec fixes the accepted request/result semantics. The original facade injects V1_CODEC, fixed-policy facades inject FIXED_CODEC, and ChannelPolicyRunner injects CHANNEL_CODEC plus an adapter that speaks nested fixed-policy v2. This reuses lifecycle machinery without silently broadening an old public contract.

An original v1 consumer therefore rejects v2 before issuance or completion. Origin-bound v3 retains source metadata in its durable envelope while the specialist sees only its supported nested request. Delivery support is separately versioned; the original projector and guarded-action adapter do not automatically become v2/v3 consumers. The current audit even records v2/v3 quarantine by the v1 projector, an honest compatibility limitation rather than a reason to reinterpret those bytes permissively.
questions.alternatives: Documented explicit-version policy with inferred trade-off: one auto-detecting facade reduces class names and appears future-proof. It can silently add authority, evidence requirements or persisted semantics to old consumers. Explicit facades keep defaults stable while sharing a private generic engine and narrow typed adapters.
questions.counterfactual: Replace V1_CODEC with a parser that accepts every known request version in the old runner. A previously v1-only consumer could now issue or complete v2/v3 work without supplying the evidence inventory or downstream semantics that those versions require.

challenge.symptom: Upgrading the library changes which persisted payloads an unchanged application executes, or new v3 results are assumed to support old projection/action features merely because invocation works. Version acceptance has leaked across independent boundaries.
challenge.diagnosis: Follow the facade constructor into its selected codec and invocation adapter. Check acceptance, specialist transport, durable result, delivery, projection and action separately; sharing a capability name does not make all versioned semantics interchangeable.
challenge.handling: Existing tests make the original facade inspect and run v2 bytes, then require rejection before any issue, completion or specialist call. Dedicated v2/v3 facades preserve their own explicit source and result contracts without changing v1 defaults.

followups.question: Why share the generic runner engine at all?
followups.answer: Ownership, capacity, issuance and exact completion have common mechanics. Sharing those reduces drift while a closed codec preserves the supported semantics. The generic implementation is private; consumers opt into a typed public facade instead of arbitrary runtime plugins.

followups.question: Can v3 reach a specialist that understands only v2?
followups.answer: Through the explicit channel invocation adapter. Trusted composition retains the original outer origin and validates the inner source-bound result before wrapping it back into v3. The specialist does not choose or rewrite the originating channel receipt.

followups.question: Does supporting v3 delivery complete integration?
followups.answer: No. Projection, action and broader release qualification remain separate capabilities and evidence gates. A delivery facade accepting one envelope does not authorize an older projector to reinterpret it or a controller to act without the correct exact confirmation contract.

questions.watch_for: A shared execution engine is not blanket compatibility across persistence, delivery, projection and action.

test.name: test_default_v1_runner_rejects_v2_before_issue_or_completion
test.assertion: The test calls both inspect and run_once on the original runner with retained v2 work. Both must fail invalid_stored_state and leave issue_count, complete_count and specialist request count at zero, proving rejection precedes authority use.

evidence.label: Original v3 bytes survive nested v2 transport
Original projector still uses the closed v1 parser

questions.title: Require complete equality when the port claims creation
questions.question: Why compare full canonical bytes on created=true before applying the looser replay identity rule?
answer: Replay matching deliberately ignores changing transport attempt metadata, and origin acceptance can return an earlier valid generated proposal for the same retained source operation. Those rules are correct only for an existing winner. When the execution port claims created=true, the coordinator must prove that the returned record contains exactly the complete proposal this call submitted.

The full canonical comparison includes attempt, generated deadline, sources and the origin envelope before _same_input applies replay semantics. It catches a port that substitutes another structurally valid request or returns stale metadata while claiming creation. A later exact original-origin lookup may still recover the true stored winner. The distinction protects acceptance integrity without renewing a retained deadline or choosing a new source configuration under an old operation.
questions.alternatives: Inferred trade-off: using the same logical comparison for both creation and replay is concise and avoids duplicate validation. It lets intentional replay flexibility conceal a lying or buggy creation response. The extra full-byte comparison is cheap within the fixed wire bound and verifies what this caller actually accepted.
questions.counterfactual: Remove the accepted.created canonical comparison and rely only on _same_input. A created record with a substituted attempt or a different valid generated proposal can then pass the replay rule, falsely acknowledging bytes this caller never submitted.

challenge.symptom: A new submit returns a valid-looking record with unexpected attempt, deadline or evidence while reporting created=true. Later replay may still appear consistent because its deliberately weaker equality rule hides the original substitution.
challenge.diagnosis: Separate the creation contract from retained-winner replay. Compare exact returned canonical bytes with the frozen submitted snapshot before using semantic replay matching, and inspect the port response rather than trusting its created flag alone.
challenge.handling: Existing tests substitute attempt bytes across all three facades and substitute an entire valid origin proposal. Creation must reject invalid_stored_state; a later replay can still return the genuine retained first winner without another acceptance.

followups.question: Why not require full bytes on every replay?
followups.answer: A new transport attempt is intentionally allowed to discover original accepted work, and the origin path may regenerate non-authoritative proposal details. Requiring full equality there would break safe reconciliation. Creation and replay answer different questions and need different comparisons.

followups.question: Does first-origin accept allow changing the user request?
followups.answer: No. Stable original source, scope, case, revision and conversation route remain bound. It returns the original winner for that same operation. A different user input or business revision requires a separate accepted operation, not a rewritten old request.

followups.question: Why snapshot before the first await?
followups.answer: Otherwise caller mutation could change the proposal between preflight, submit and returned-byte comparison. Canonical reparse fixes the accepted meaning before concurrency begins. Frozen outer types alone do not protect arbitrary nested mutable objects supplied by callers.

questions.watch_for: Replay flexibility must not weaken the exact proposal acknowledged on first creation.

test.name: test_created_true_full_canonical_guard_includes_attempt_for_all_versions
test.assertion: A test port returns created=true with substituted attempt bytes for v1, v2 and v3 facades. Every creation must reject invalid_stored_state after one submit. A separate valid-origin substitution case proves generated proposal changes cannot bypass the same guard.

evidence.label: Whole valid generated origin proposal substitution rejected
Snapshot is frozen before the first await
Exact submit and first-origin accept are explicit

limits: These are source-and-test defenses, not fresh executions or a claim that any unrun gate passed.
Current P3 complete acceptance remains three registered lab rows with fourteen planned full rows; selected deeper gates retain their own recorded local scope.
No source change, runtime migration, paid inference, new NATS service or new execution scheduler was introduced by this review.
The PNG path supports a declared static RGB/RGBA subset and a separate standalone document capability; it does not imply durable image-policy execution or general real-model OCR qualification.
The original v1 projector/action adapter does not automatically consume v2/v3 results. Explicit delivery and nested transport support are separate capabilities.
Current local ownership and synthetic principal checks do not establish production IAM, global capacity, multi-region recovery or termination of arbitrary remote work.

chapters.title: Code decisions in the joined application
chapters.subtitle: Reentrancy reads browser lifetime and the real SDK
intro: These decisions sit between the three libraries: a background read must share work without leaking it, a browser must retain original input through an ambiguous reply, and an SDK stream must survive the real framework lifecycle. The snippets are literal excerpts from the recorded repository commit.

Read the code page first. Predict the effect of the proposed edit before turning to the answer. Tradeoff analysis explains consequences visible in code and tests; it does not claim to reconstruct an undocumented design meeting.

concepts.title: A two page code review
concepts.body: The left page supplies a question, exact source and a tempting change. The facing page supplies the mechanism, alternatives, common challenge, three answered probes and a representative assertion.

concepts.title: Scope of evidence
concepts.body: A component test can establish a local lifetime or ordering property. It does not certify the full joined shutdown, physical microphone path, provider quality or production scale.

questions.title: Publish ownership before starting the task
questions.question: Why reserve a publication Future before calling _spawn, and complete it in finally?
answer: The task factory may start the coroutine before create_task returns its Task object. During that interval the scan can reenter the producer or race a close observer while self._scan is not yet assigned. _scan_publication represents an owner being transferred, so a reentrant reader cannot assume the producer is empty and close can wait for publication before draining the real scan.

The finally resolves the barrier for both successful creation and failed scheduling. _spawn separately closes an unscheduled coroutine. This is a local handoff protocol, not a durable work receipt. The implementation comment documents the eager-task concern; the tests drive that exact reentrancy rather than depending on the ordinary scheduler to expose it. A future refactor must preserve the reservation, publication and rollback as one lifecycle.
questions.alternatives: Assigning self._scan only after creating the task is shorter, but leaves a gap under eager execution. An async lock can serialize ordinary awaits, yet it must also define behavior during synchronous task-factory reentrancy. The current Future explicitly represents that transfer interval.
questions.counterfactual: Move self._scan_publication assignment below _spawn. A close invoked by eager execution can miss the admitted scan and finish before its actual work is visible.

challenge.symptom: A shutdown appears complete, then a late scan allocates an inspection owner. The bug may disappear under the default scheduler and reappear after an eager-task configuration change.
challenge.diagnosis: Inject a task factory that reenters read or close before returning. Observe the publication reservation and the actual scan count; do not infer absence from a temporarily missing Task reference.
challenge.handling: Preserve the existing publication barrier and test allocation failure separately. A failed allocation must leave no unowned coroutine, while a started task stays observable through close.

followups.question: Why is a boolean busy flag insufficient?
followups.answer: A flag can reject admission, but close also needs a completion event for the ownership transfer. The Future tells it when the Task reference or creation failure is published so it can observe the right object.

followups.question: Does this make the operation durable?
followups.answer: No. The barrier exists only inside one event loop. Durable accepted work remains in P1; process recovery still uses the original persisted identity rather than this Future.

followups.question: Why finally rather than the success branch?
followups.answer: If creation fails, a close observer must not wait forever for an event that only success would signal. Finally completes the publication phase while the failure path preserves correct ownership cleanup.

questions.watch_for: Do not remove a publication barrier merely because ordinary create_task appears to return before the coroutine runs.

test.name: test_eager_reentrant_close_waits_for_task_publication_and_actual_scan
test.assertion: The reentrant close must wait for publication and the actual held scan, then finish without an invisible late owner. Inspect the paired reentrant-read test for the one-scan assertion.

questions.excerpt:
# Eager task factories may run/reenter before create_task returns. This
        # reservation is also a publication barrier: close cannot miss the
        # already-started scan while its Task reference is being transferred.
        try:
            publication: asyncio.Future[None] = loop.create_future()
        except Exception:  # noqa: BLE001 - no reservation/owner exists on allocation failure
            raise CurrentResultProducerError() from None
        self._scan_publication = publication
        try:
            scan = self._scan = _spawn(self._run())
        except Exception:  # noqa: BLE001 - finite public boundary
            raise CurrentResultProducerError() from None
        finally:
            # Covers ordinary setup failure and cancellation/control flow. The
            # unscheduled coroutine was closed by _spawn; no actual owner hides.
            publication.set_result(None)

questions.title: Abandon the scan only after the last waiter leaves
questions.question: Why does _abandoned become true only when the departing observer is the last waiter?
answer: Concurrent reads join one published scan. Each observer has its own timeout, and shield prevents that observer from cancelling the underlying scan. A departing observer should not abandon useful work still needed by another reader. _waiters counts current observers, and the branch tests the count before finally decrements it.

When the last observer leaves, the scan is marked abandoned so its subsequent stages cannot start fresh reads as though a user were still waiting. Actual in-flight work remains owned until settlement, so a new read may still receive capacity. This deliberately separates interest in the result from ownership of the work. The returned error is also an observer outcome, not a business cancellation command.
questions.alternatives: A per-reader scan avoids reference counting but multiplies bounded database and transport work. Cancelling a shared scan on any timeout is simpler, yet one impatient caller would destroy another caller useful result. The current contract shares only a published, active, unabandoned scan.
questions.counterfactual: Set _abandoned unconditionally in either cancellation branch. The first canceled reader can now prevent the second reader from obtaining an otherwise valid result.

challenge.symptom: Two UI polls overlap. One is aborted during navigation and the other unexpectedly fails, or a new poll starts while the old actual read still occupies capacity.
challenge.diagnosis: Hold discovery, attach two readers, cancel them one at a time and compare observers with actual scan ownership. A reduced waiter count does not prove the discovery call settled.
challenge.handling: Keep the existing last-waiter rule and retained scan. Expose capacity honestly until abandoned work drains; allow a fresh scan after actual ownership is released.

followups.question: Why test _waiters == 1 before decrement?
followups.answer: At the exception branch the departing reader is still included. A value of one means it is the final observer. Moving the decrement earlier changes the condition and can introduce an off-by-one cancellation bug.

followups.question: Can the second reader get a full fresh budget?
followups.answer: It has its own observer timeout when it joins. That does not renew the scan business applicability or restart its work. Request waiting budgets and result deadlines remain distinct.

followups.question: Why refuse a new read after all waiters leave?
followups.answer: The abandoned scan or inspection can still use resources. Releasing its slot on observer abandonment would violate the actual capacity bound even though no caller wants its answer.

questions.watch_for: A shared promise needs a documented observer-cancellation policy.

test.name: test_joined_waiter_keeps_the_scan_after_the_first_waiter_cancels
test.assertion: With discovery held, two readers share one scan. Canceling the first must not stop the second from receiving current, and only one inspection owner is constructed.

questions.title: Expiry after a successful read
questions.question: Why check the selected result deadline again after inspection cleanup?
answer: The producer can select a current result, then spend time draining the inspection resource. That cleanup is real owned work and can be delayed. A deadline check before the read or before cleanup would allow a body selected before expiry to be returned as current after expiry.

The final branch replaces only the outward applicability observation with not_applicable. It does not delete the retained result or undo known delivery evidence. The selected deadline belongs to the original request; the implementation does not manufacture a new deadline from the caller timeout. This is a final local disclosure observation, not an atomic cross-store fence and not a guarantee about when the user will eventually read already transmitted bytes.
questions.alternatives: Returning the prepared observation immediately reduces latency but separates successful completion from resource cleanup and can publish stale applicability. Keeping a timestamp on the observation helps explain history; it does not replace the explicit final rule for a response labeled current.
questions.counterfactual: Delete the post-cleanup check because _select already checked expiry. A close held across the deadline can now return an expired current body.

challenge.symptom: A result looks eligible when selected, but a slow close makes the displayed answer arrive after its permitted deadline. A clean happy-path test never holds that stage.
challenge.diagnosis: Hold inspection close, move the controlled clock past the original deadline, then release close. Compare returned applicability with the durable historical result; the two should have different meanings.
challenge.handling: Retain the final applicability check and immutable historical truth. Do not solve a stale display by erasing P1 result or delivery identities.

followups.question: Why use an absolute result deadline?
followups.answer: It was part of the original accepted semantics. Replacing it with a new per-read duration would silently extend applicability whenever a reader retries.

followups.question: Is this business cancellation?
followups.answer: No. The producer suppresses a current display body. It neither requests cancellation of P1 work nor claims the specialist or supplier stopped.

followups.question: Can it expire after this check?
followups.answer: Yes. The response is as of a particular check and bytes take time to transmit. The claim must state that observation boundary rather than promise permanent future applicability.

questions.watch_for: A successful early read is not enough for a later response labeled current.

evidence.label: Drain inspection before the final applicability check

test.name: test_expiry_while_close_is_held_suppresses_prepared_current_output
test.assertion: Select a result while valid, hold cleanup and advance beyond its deadline. On release, state is not_applicable and result is None despite the earlier successful selection.

questions.title: Pacing without a shadow queue
questions.question: Why reread every discovered item even when a prior run is paced?
answer: Eligibility, original prepared identity and stored work are reread before the pacing gate. The in-memory _reruns map delays another local start of the same work; it does not own acceptance, terminal completion or an acknowledgment cursor. Existing actual owners and the two-job cap are checked independently.

This lets the process reduce repeated startup work without replacing durable P1 authority. A restart can lose advisory pacing and legitimately inspect again; only a new P1 issuance can authorize a new invocation. The full page scan and rotating admission priority also let later work progress. This is not production-wide retry scheduling, and the latest audit still records separate scan-loop failure backoff and shared-startup contention gaps.
questions.alternatives: Persisting a local done set could reduce reads but creates another authority that can diverge from P1. A durable scheduler would need an explicit redesign. The current bounded rescan trades extra read work for simple recovery and truthful discovery.
questions.counterfactual: Skip all previously observed work before reading stored state, or persist _reruns as completed. A later result or changed authoritative observation can now be hidden permanently.

challenge.symptom: Polling repeatedly reconstructs runners for the same task, or a quick optimization makes new work appear stuck behind previously seen identities.
challenge.diagnosis: Measure jobs_paced separately from stored reads and new-work starts. Verify that a paced work item is still revalidated and that work this process has never started is not delayed by another item pacing.
challenge.handling: Use the existing advisory per-work pacing and preserve full bounded scans. Any new persistent scheduler must explicitly define ownership and reconciliation instead of being introduced as a cache.

followups.question: Does losing pacing on restart duplicate an effect?
followups.answer: Pacing is not the effect guard. The runner must ask P1 for execution permission under original identity, and replayed issuance cannot invoke. Loss of this advisory map may add reads but must not create authority.

followups.question: Why record dispatched work in a set?
followups.answer: It bounds retained pacing metadata to the currently discovered dispatched window. Pruning advisory entries does not delete source identities or acknowledge the business work.

followups.question: Could one long-running job occupy every slot?
followups.answer: It should occupy its actual owned slot through closure. Fairness and admission for other slots are separate, and unresolved close must not be hidden by pretending the job completed.

questions.watch_for: An optimization map must not quietly become a second recovering queue.

test.name: test_rerun_of_the_same_work_is_paced_while_every_scan_still_rereads
test.assertion: A second paced scan performs another stored read but starts no job. After the configured delay it may run again using the same original command identity.

questions.title: Preserve a decoded acknowledgment
questions.question: Why decode a complete response before attempting writer cleanup?
answer: A valid complete response can already establish a known application receipt even if closing the transport later raises. _perform decodes the framed bytes before entering cleanup and preserves both knowledge and the primary validation or network failure. Failed close leaves the writer and capacity slot retained; it cannot turn a known receipt into an automatic resend.

The distinction is visible in the tests: the successful decoded receipt is returned, succeeded increments, and one pending owner remains until explicit close is retried. Conversely, malformed bytes retain their primary failure even if close also fails. The decoder is a trusted synchronous boundary with its own validation restrictions; arbitrary async user work is not allowed to hide inside response decoding.
questions.alternatives: Treating every close exception as request failure is simpler but can erase known receipt truth and provoke duplicate commands. Ignoring close completely leaks ownership. This design preserves the outcome while reporting and retaining cleanup separately.
questions.counterfactual: Move decoding after await _close_writer, or let a cleanup exception replace the decoded value. A valid accepted response can become unknown solely because socket teardown failed.

challenge.symptom: An API returned a receipt, but the caller retries the business action after a socket close exception. Alternatively the UI succeeds while the process slowly leaks connection capacity.
challenge.diagnosis: Record the order of complete framing, domain decode and actual close. Independently inspect the receipt and pending owner count; successful business observation can coexist with incomplete cleanup.
challenge.handling: Keep known bytes and original identity. Retry observation of the retained close owner without resubmitting the request, and preserve malformed-response errors as the primary failure.

followups.question: Is successful decoding enough to free the slot?
followups.answer: No. The writer can still be owned. Outcome truth and resource truth are independent, so pending_count may remain nonzero after a successful decoded operation.

followups.question: Why require a pure synchronous decoder?
followups.answer: Purity and bounded CPU cost are trusted caller obligations. FunctionType and code flags exclude coroutine and async-generator functions, but cannot prove purity or stop an ordinary function returning an awaitable. The wrapper must honor the narrower decoder contract.

followups.question: Can cleanup failure justify a fresh command?
followups.answer: Not by itself. If the receipt is known, preserve it. If the outcome is unknown, use the original operation reconciliation contract rather than inventing a replacement identity.

questions.watch_for: Business success and completed socket cleanup must not share one boolean.

test.name: test_valid_complete_ack_survives_actual_writer_close_failure
test.assertion: The test asserts decoded occurs before close_failed, the exact receipt survives, succeeded is one, pending_count is one, and a later close drains without another request.

questions.title: Recognize a reset as observed closure
questions.question: Why catch OSError from wait_closed but preserve other close failures?
answer: A transport reset can store a connection_lost error in the close waiter. Awaiting wait_closed again then raises the same OSError even though the socket has already closed. The helper recognizes that specific terminal transport observation, allowing the writer reference and its real capacity slot to retire.

It does not catch every Exception. A different failed close observer can still mean closure was not established under the adapter contract, so the owner remains retained and a later explicit close retries observation. That narrow distinction fixed permanent slot exhaustion after peer resets without converting arbitrary cleanup faults into success. The code comment documents this mechanism; the socket test verifies useful calls after reset rather than only asserting an exception was swallowed.
questions.alternatives: Catching nothing wedges a slot on a terminal reset. Catching every exception hides unresolved ownership. The chosen error family is narrow and depends on the specific asyncio stream close semantics being observed, not a universal rule for all client libraries.
questions.counterfactual: Replace except OSError with except Exception: pass. An injected nonterminal close failure can now falsely release the slot and permit new work while closure remains unresolved.

challenge.symptom: After a peer restart, two requests fail and the small client permanently reports capacity despite the sockets being gone. A broad catch appears to fix it but also hides unrelated close errors.
challenge.diagnosis: Separate a real peer reset from an injected close-observation failure. Inspect pending_count and demonstrate a later useful discovery call after the reset path.
challenge.handling: Use the narrow existing reset handling and retain other failures for explicit retry. Do not generalize that a stopped waiter or every I O error proves socket closure.

followups.question: Does OSError prove the remote action failed?
followups.answer: No. It describes the observed transport closure. The peer may have accepted the request before resetting; operation result reconciliation still follows its original identity.

followups.question: What should diagnostics contain?
followups.answer: A finite safe error code and bounded counters. Private peer error text is not needed to preserve the distinction between unavailable transport and incomplete cleanup.

followups.question: Why test a useful call afterward?
followups.answer: A test that merely expects unavailable can pass while every slot is leaked. Later useful discovery demonstrates the negative path did not destroy reusable capacity.

questions.watch_for: Observed transport closure does not establish absence of a business effect.

test.name: test_failed_close_observation_keeps_owner_but_peer_reset_closure_releases_it
test.assertion: An injected ordinary failure retains one owner until retried close. Two real reset failures leave zero pending owners, and a later discovery succeeds on the same client.

questions.excerpt:
async def close_writer(writer: asyncio.StreamWriter) -> None:
    writer.close()
    try:
        await writer.wait_closed()
    except OSError:
        # connection_lost stored the transport's error in the close waiter, which
        # re-raises it on every await; the socket is already closed by then.
        pass

questions.title: One user intention through double click
questions.question: Why keep #textInputId until durable acceptance rather than mint on each Send?
answer: Repeated Send can occur even when the first transport call completed: the durable acknowledgment may still be delayed. The nullish assignment retains one input UUID until acceptance is observed. Explicit Retry also finds the latest unknown text input and resends its frozen body and ID rather than whatever the textarea contains now.

The controller deduplicates the displayed user row by input identity, while the backend remains responsible for durable idempotency and changed-payload conflicts. Disabling the button improves interaction but is not the safety authority. A later accepted input can clear the pending identity and allow a genuinely new request. The test drives repeated programmatic sends to avoid relying solely on a disabled DOM control.
questions.alternatives: Minting a UUID for every click makes each click easy to track but turns accidental repeats into new obligations. Hashing text would collapse two intentional identical messages. An explicit retained input identity expresses intention independently of wording and transport attempts.
questions.counterfactual: Replace #textInputId ??= crypto.randomUUID() with crypto.randomUUID(). Two sends before the first durable ACK can create two accepted requests and duplicate the user history.

challenge.symptom: A quick double click or repeated Enter creates duplicate background work, while Retry after a network drop uses edited text and receives a conflict.
challenge.diagnosis: Compare original input IDs, frozen bodies, acknowledgment timing and source history. Count logical accepted inputs separately from sendText calls and UI click events.
challenge.handling: Retain the existing pending identity and replay the frozen unknown input. Keep keyboard and click admission consistent, and rely on server checks for durable safety.

followups.question: Why not deduplicate by text hash?
followups.answer: Two identical questions can be intentional at different times, and the same intention can be retried. A user-operation identity distinguishes those cases; the digest only binds bytes to that identity.

followups.question: What if the user edits while unresolved?
followups.answer: Do not silently change the bytes under the old key. The product needs a visible choice to retry the original or create a separately identified intention when the existing contract permits it.

followups.question: Does sendText resolving clear the ID?
followups.answer: It should not imply durable acceptance. The accepted acknowledgment is the separate observation that resolves the retained input under this controller contract.

questions.watch_for: A successful transport promise is not a durable acceptance receipt.

test.name: reuses one frozen input for a repeated Send until it is accepted, then mints a new one
test.assertion: Two sends before the durable ACK use equal frozen inputs and produce one user row. After acceptance, a subsequent intention receives a distinct ID and history entry.

questions.title: Do not fall back to an older green answer
questions.question: Why does the newest recorded but unusable result return no_delivery or not_applicable instead of continuing to an older result?
answer: The producer scans retained inputs newest first. A pending input without a recorded result may be skipped, but once a newer recorded result is selected, its failed applicability or missing delivery is itself meaningful. Continuing to an older green result would present historical information as the current best answer and hide the newer recorded state.

The code distinguishes not-yet-recorded from recorded-but-unusable. It preserves old facts in storage while refusing the misleading fallback. After the potentially delayed native read, it also rechecks execution and delivery identity before disclosure. This is a scoped selection policy, not a complete global ordering guarantee across arbitrary sources or a permission to apply the displayed result.
questions.alternatives: Choosing the newest usable result maximizes the chance of showing some answer, but can conceal that a newer result superseded it and is now expired, stale or undelivered. If a product wants historical fallback, label it explicitly and keep it outside the current-result contract.
questions.counterfactual: Change return not_applicable to continue. The UI can now display an older eligible result while a newer recorded answer is known to be inapplicable.

challenge.symptom: An old answer remains green after a newer check expired or lost delivery. Operators see apparent progress while the latest recorded state is hidden.
challenge.diagnosis: Construct two retained results with distinct original identities. Compare the newest recorded result with a newer pending input that has no result; those schedules should intentionally select differently.
challenge.handling: Keep the existing no-fallback policy for a current view. A separate historical view may expose older facts with their original time, identity and applicability limitations.

followups.question: Can a newer pending input hide every old result?
followups.answer: The implemented policy skips a not-yet-recorded result so earlier useful truth can remain visible. It stops fallback after selecting a newer recorded result, where a different semantic boundary has been crossed.

followups.question: Does no_delivery mean no result was computed?
followups.answer: No. It describes missing delivery evidence for the selected result. Execution result truth, delivery and display applicability are separate observations.

followups.question: Is discovery order business authority?
followups.answer: No. It is part of this bounded current-view selection. The original case revision, accepted work and public guards still control business applicability and action.

questions.watch_for: A helpful-looking fallback can turn an honest missing current answer into a stale claim.

test.name: test_latest_recorded_undelivered_never_falls_back_to_older
test.assertion: A newer recorded result without delivery yields no_delivery rather than returning the older current body. Inspect the paired expired test and the newer-pending test to explain the contrast.
