execution = self._execution(await self._result_read(), winner)
            self._check()
            if execution.result is None:
                await self._drain_inspection()
                self._check()
                continue
            self._selected_deadline = winner.request.deadline_at_ms
            if execution.applicability not in {"candidate", "clarification"}:
                return self._observation("not_applicable")
            before = self._delivery(await self._delivery_read(), execution)
            self._check()
            if before.receipt is None or before.intent is None:
                return self._observation("no_delivery")
            native = await self._native_read(delivery_id=before.intent.delivery_id)
            self._check()
            # A body remains withheld until fresh public P3 and P1 observations
            # after the potentially delayed, generation-bound P2 read.
            after_execution = self._execution(await self._result_read(), winner)

questions.title: Own media before publication awaits
questions.question: Why assign the source to #fixture before awaiting publishTrack and check admitted again?
answer: Source creation can finish after the caller observation times out or End begins. The code first retains the actual returned source, then checks whether the original operation is still admitted and the room is ready. A late source is stopped and closed before it can be published.

If publication itself stalls, the retained #fixture lets timeout or shutdown stop the track. The post-publication check prevents a late acknowledgment from reviving the expired operation. The five-second observer budget includes source acquisition in this path; that is a concrete limitation for user-controlled permission delays, not proof that a physical microphone was captured. The checked test uses a late fixture factory and establishes lifetime behavior rather than hardware qualification.
questions.alternatives: Storing the source only after publishTrack succeeds looks tidy but leaves a resource invisible during a stalled publish. Aborting the factory may help cooperative implementations, yet actual late results still need adoption and cleanup when abort is ignored.
questions.counterfactual: Move this.#fixture = source below await publishTrack. Timeout can no longer stop the newly acquired track while publication is unresolved.

challenge.symptom: End is clicked while audio setup waits, then a late stream starts capturing or publishing into a room that the user believes ended.
challenge.diagnosis: Hold the source factory and advance past the observer deadline, then resolve the source. Verify no publication occurs, stop and close run, and the actual pending owner is retained until settlement.
challenge.handling: Retain the existing late-source fence and owned cleanup. Any larger permission budget should be a deliberate product change with tests for both early cancellation and late completion.

followups.question: Why stop the track before await close?
followups.answer: Stopping reduces ongoing capture or media production immediately. The asynchronous close still needs observation for remaining source resources; neither operation substitutes for the other.

followups.question: Why check after publish as well?
followups.answer: Admission can change during that await. An acknowledgment from an old lifecycle cannot make the room ready again or imply the user still wants to send audio.

followups.question: Does this test prove microphone capture?
followups.answer: No. It tests the source ownership contract with a controlled fixture. Physical permission, capture quality and actual returned audio require their separately scoped browser or media evidence.

questions.watch_for: A late resource must be adopted and closed even when its caller has disappeared.

test.name: never publishes a source that arrives after its5s observer deadline
test.assertion: After the observer times out, the late source is stopped and closed, publishTrack was never called, and voicePrepared remains false while actual ownership is properly drained.

questions.title: Propagate the actual call budget
questions.question: Why pass the bridge timeout into ExternalOperationClient instead of leaving its default?
answer: A five-second dispatch step cannot help if an inner client silently times out at two seconds. The bridge passes its configured timeout as callTimeoutMs so the external accept can use the intended joined budget. A later check still verifies the call lifecycle before starting the operation.

The joined configuration uses a five-second dispatch step and an eight-second claim lease for new profiles; the origin hosts use the matching selected budget. Those numbers coordinate layers rather than making a universal latency guarantee. The regression holds a real local accept for 2.3 seconds and verifies success when the bridge budget allows it. That test does not prove every slow operation is safe or that a timed-out mutation can be resent.
questions.alternatives: Increasing only the outer timer masks inner deadline mismatches. Giving every nested stage a fresh full timeout can exceed the total request budget. Propagate a deliberate step budget and keep the authority lease long enough for the selected bounded operation and reconciliation policy.
questions.counterfactual: Delete callTimeoutMs because ExternalOperationClient has a default. A valid 2.3-second local accept can again become an ambiguous ACK before the five-second bridge step expires.

challenge.symptom: Requests fail around the same short threshold despite a longer configured application timeout, and retries observe that the original operation was actually committed.
challenge.diagnosis: Inventory every wrapper, network call and lease budget. Measure the cutoff at each layer and reconcile the original operation; do not infer nonacceptance from the earliest timer.
challenge.handling: Preserve explicit joined timeout propagation and default compatibility elsewhere. When changing limits, rerun the selected slow-accept regression and inspect claim expiry behavior separately.

followups.question: Why keep the old default elsewhere?
followups.answer: Changing an opt-in composition should not silently change every standalone consumer. The new optional call timeout lets the joined adapter select its budget while preserving the established default contract.

followups.question: Does an eight-second lease cancel a five-second call?
followups.answer: No. Lease eligibility and a caller or network timeout are different controls. A request may still have crossed an external boundary and require original-identity reconciliation.

followups.question: Can attestation consume budget too?
followups.answer: Yes. A complete design must account for earlier validation and attestation work and total remaining time. Passing this option fixes the documented nested cap, not every possible end-to-end scheduling delay.

questions.watch_for: Timeout configuration must be traced through every nested owner rather than inferred from the largest number.

test.name: lets a slow committed accept finish within the bridge budget rather than a 2 s client cap
test.assertion: With a 3.5-second bridge budget and a 2.3-second delayed local accept, the original operation receipt is returned and the remote retained receipt exists.

questions.title: Two handles for one logical recognizer
questions.question: Why does the scripted recognizer allow two stream handles?
answer: The real SDK clear_user_turn lifecycle opens a replacement STT stream before the old stream finishes closing. A strict one-handle cap therefore rejects the replacement and the first scripted voice turn can produce no transcript. Two handles accommodate the active and closing generations without allowing unbounded recognizer resources.

The resource bound counts actual retained handles, not the number of logical conversational turns. The genuine AgentSession regression clears and commits two fixture turns, checks exact recognized snapshots and observes one stable stream after replacement. It then explicitly opens two streams, rejects a third and demonstrates capacity recovery after closure. That is stronger than increasing a constant until a smoke test looks green; it explains both the required overlap and the continuing bound.
questions.alternatives: A cap of one is intuitively attractive for one active recognizer but incompatible with this replacement order. An unlimited set avoids rejection but loses resource bounds. Serializing replacement externally would require owning or changing the SDK lifecycle rather than assuming its close order.
questions.counterfactual: Change _Streams(2) back to _Streams(1) because the room has only one speaker. The replacement can fail before the closing old stream retires and the first real SDK voice turn can be lost.

challenge.symptom: Text works and later turns seem healthy, but the first scripted voice turn produces an empty transcript after clear_user_turn. A direct recognizer unit test may not reproduce it.
challenge.diagnosis: Exercise the real AgentSession replacement sequence and inspect live plus closing stream counts. Distinguish logical active turns from retained SDK handles and from physical microphone evidence.
challenge.handling: Keep the two-handle bound and genuine SDK regression. Reject a third handle and require actual close before reclaiming capacity; do not relax the cap without a lifecycle explanation.

followups.question: Does two handles mean two accepted user inputs?
followups.answer: No. Resource overlap is not intake identity. The original caller-bound turn and durable operation remain singular under their separate contract.

followups.question: Why test the framework instead of just stream()?
followups.answer: The failure comes from ordering between SDK replacement and closure. A direct stream test can establish a numeric cap while completely missing that integration sequence.

followups.question: Does scripted recognition prove ASR quality?
followups.answer: No. It proves the declared fixture path and lifecycle through the genuine runtime. Live recognition quality and provider media qualification need their own evidence.

questions.watch_for: One logical consumer can require overlapping physical resources during replacement.

test.name: test_sdk_clear_user_turn_replacement_commits_first_voice_turn
test.assertion: A real AgentSession clear/commit cycle yields the expected first and follow-up transcripts. Two retained streams are allowed, a third is rejected, and closing restores usable capacity.

questions.excerpt:
def __init__(self, profile: ScriptedModelProfile) -> None:
        super().__init__(
            capabilities=stt.STTCapabilities(
                streaming=True, interim_results=False, offline_recognize=False, manual_flush=True
            )
        )
        self.profile = profile
        # SDK clear_user_turn opens a replacement before its old stream finishes closing.
        self.streams = _Streams(2)
        self.current: str | None = None
        self.seen: set[str] = set()
        self.open: set[str] = set()
        self.pending: set[str] = set()
        self.finals: dict[str, CommittedTranscript] = {}

questions.title: Recheck at response admission
questions.question: Why repeat the current-room check immediately before sending an already prepared response?
answer: The exchange task can complete with valid current bytes, then yield before the HTTP handler sends them. End can run in that gap. The earlier checks in exchange cannot protect the later response admission, so the override repeats the captured room predicate immediately before calling the base response writer.

This prevents an old room response from starting a successful write after the local room fence has changed. The comment also states the limit: bytes already admitted to TCP are an earlier as-of observation. It is not a cross-store atomic revocation fence and cannot retract data already sent. The socket regression deliberately changes room state in an exchange-completion callback before the response handler resumes, exercising a narrower race than ending the room during the database read.
questions.alternatives: Checking only before the read avoids repeated predicates but misses lifecycle changes during and after it. Holding a global lock across the whole read and send would increase contention and still needs a clear external disclosure boundary. The local final check is explicit and bounded.
questions.counterfactual: Remove the _response override because exchange checked is_current three times. End after exchange completion can now allow the old room body to begin transmission.

challenge.symptom: A canceled or replaced room receives a late successful response even though all read-time permission checks passed. Ordinary End-during-read tests still pass.
challenge.diagnosis: Pause between exchange completion and first response send. Change the captured room state before the handler resumes and observe whether a 200 body is admitted.
challenge.handling: Preserve the final existing response fence and separate its scope from the producer drain. If bytes were already sent, retain the honest earlier observation rather than claiming they were revoked.

followups.question: Why check only successful responses here?
followups.answer: The protected disclosure is the successful current-result body. Failure responses follow their finite safe error contract; the code does not need to expose private result content to report closure.

followups.question: Does HTTP host close drain all P1 reads?
followups.answer: No. The host owns its calls and sockets, while the application separately owns producer and deeper public-client drainage. Closing one wrapper cannot certify every borrowed dependency is settled.

followups.question: What if the room closes after the check?
followups.answer: Bytes admitted after the local check still represent that earlier observation boundary. The design explicitly declines a claim of instantaneous global revocation or future human authorization.

questions.watch_for: Many preflight checks do not replace the final check at the actual disclosure boundary.

test.name: test_room_end_after_exchange_settles_is_fenced_at_actual_response_admission
test.assertion: The exchange returns encoded bytes, then a registered completion callback closes the room before response admission. The client receives closed, no successful read is counted, and a later current-room read progresses.

questions.excerpt:
async def _response(self, connection: _Connection, status: int, body: bytes) -> None:
        if status == 200:
            # The exchange task may settle before this handler resumes. Fence
            # again at response admission, immediately before the first send.
            # Bytes already admitted to TCP are an earlier as-of observation.
            self._application._check()
        await super()._response(connection, status, body)

chapters.title: WebRTC from first principles
chapters.subtitle: Understand the transport before diagnosing the agent
intro: WebRTC is a suite of browser APIs and protocols for interactive media and data. Learn the establishment path and the steady state media path separately. The questions below connect each mechanism to a symptom you could observe in this POC.

Protocol explanations describe the standards. Local application guarantees come from the repository. ICE success, an active track or a browser energy meter never proves durable acceptance, a business result or human consent.

concepts.title: Connection establishment
concepts.body: Capture permission, application signaling, SDP negotiation, candidate gathering and connectivity checks and DTLS establishment produce a usable encrypted path.

concepts.title: During the call
concepts.body: Media packets, loss recovery, congestion control, buffering and playback continuously trade latency against quality.

questions.title: The complete stack
questions.question: Explain WebRTC without saying it is just a peer to peer socket.
answer: WebRTC exposes capture, peer connection, media track and data channel APIs. The application supplies signaling to exchange descriptions and connectivity information. ICE finds a working path, while the media and data transports provide encryption and realtime delivery semantics. In this application the browser communicates with a LiveKit SFU and a programmatic agent participant.

For a whiteboard answer I draw a control path and a media path. An HTTPS or WebSocket request that successfully joins a room is control evidence. Audio must still be captured, published, forwarded, decoded and played. Keeping the two paths separate explains why a user can see captions while hearing nothing. [W1, W3]

followups.question: Where is signaling standardized?
followups.answer: The WebRTC API does not require one application signaling protocol. Applications must exchange the required negotiation information using their chosen signaling channel. LiveKit supplies that channel and its room protocol.

followups.question: Is WebRTC always browser to browser?
followups.answer: No. Servers, SFUs and native SDKs can be endpoints. The local agent is a participant that consumes and publishes media; it is not JavaScript running in the caller browser.

questions.watch_for: Do not put STT, LLM or durable workflow state inside the WebRTC transport layer.

questions.title: Offer answer and candidates
questions.question: What do SDP negotiation and ICE each contribute?
answer: Offer and answer negotiate media and transport parameters. ICE candidates describe possible network paths, and connectivity checks test candidate pairs. Trickle ICE can exchange candidates as they are discovered instead of waiting for all gathering to finish. A description does not prove that a candidate pair is reachable. [W1, W2]

In a debugging interview I would ask whether negotiation completed, whether candidates were gathered and exchanged, and which pair was selected. I would also check the SDK lifecycle before adding custom negotiation code: a second independent connection owner can race the SDK. The application should observe the transport and retain business identity through reconnect rather than reconstructing work from SDP.

followups.question: Why can a private candidate be unusable?
followups.answer: It may identify an address that the other endpoint cannot route to through its network. Candidate discovery and successful connectivity are separate observations.

followups.question: What changes during an ICE restart?
followups.answer: ICE credentials and candidate checking are renewed to establish a path. It does not grant permission to replay an application mutation or create a new business work identity.

questions.watch_for: Never infer reachability from a nonempty SDP blob.

questions.title: STUN TURN and restrictive networks
questions.question: How do STUN and TURN help a caller behind a firewall?
answer: STUN helps discover a mapped address and supports connectivity checks. TURN provides a relay allocation when a direct candidate path is unavailable. ICE evaluates available paths. A relay is a genuine media path with bandwidth, availability and operational cost; it is not merely a signaling fallback. TURN can use several client to relay transports. [W2, W4]

For this POC I would first establish the actual configured local exposure, then test a restrictive network explicitly. A passing loopback audio test does not demonstrate corporate firewall traversal. A production design would measure connection success and setup time by selected candidate type and transport, while redacting network addresses in shared diagnostics.

followups.question: Does TURN decrypt the conversation?
followups.answer: TURN relays packets; it does not inherently become the media decryption endpoint. The endpoint encryption arrangement determines who can read content. The SFU has a separate trust role.

followups.question: Would you force TCP immediately?
followups.answer: I would diagnose first and keep the supported fallback sequence. Reliable byte transport can increase delay when loss stalls later bytes; a reachable UDP path is often preferable for interactive media.

questions.watch_for: Do not claim local test success qualifies every NAT and firewall environment.

questions.title: Transport encryption and endpoint trust
questions.question: How are media protected, and what does end to end encryption change?
answer: DTLS SRTP establishes keys used to protect RTP media; data channels use SCTP over DTLS. Transport encryption protects the hop between endpoints. In a normal SFU deployment, the SFU is part of the trust boundary. Additional media end to end encryption changes which participants can decrypt. [W5, W6]

A voice agent needs authorized access to audio to transcribe or reason over it. I would draw where encryption terminates, where PCM exists and which provider sees it before making a privacy claim. In this repository I would point to scoped grants and provider isolation as application protections, without claiming that the current local showcase implements an E2EE design.

followups.question: Does HTTPS encrypt the audio path?
followups.answer: HTTPS protects the HTTP connection. WebRTC media has its own negotiated protection. Both matter, but observing an HTTPS URL proves neither successful media encryption negotiation nor end to end content privacy.

followups.question: Can an agent process encrypted audio without a key?
followups.answer: A normal speech pipeline cannot transcribe ciphertext. An E2EE architecture must deliberately authorize the agent as a decrypting endpoint or introduce a different processing design.

questions.watch_for: Hop encryption and end to end encryption are different guarantees.

questions.title: Packets time and intelligibility
questions.question: What do RTP, RTCP and the jitter buffer do for audio?
answer: RTP carries timestamped, sequenced media. RTCP supplies associated control and reception feedback. Arrival times vary; a jitter buffer delays playout enough to absorb some variation. Waiting longer can improve continuity but adds conversational delay. Late audio may have little value even if eventually delivered.

I would diagnose choppy speech with packet loss, arrival variation, concealment and buffer delay together, using interval deltas rather than lifetime counters alone. The W3C statistics specification defines jitter and jitter buffer observations. An application should connect these transport observations to actual returned audio and perceived turn timing instead of treating generated TTS bytes as proof of playback. [W7]

followups.question: Why not retransmit everything?
followups.answer: Recovery that arrives after a playout deadline cannot repair what the listener already missed. Loss recovery must fit the media deadline and the codec or receiver strategy.

followups.question: How do you estimate average jitter buffer delay?
followups.answer: For a consistent inbound stream, divide the interval increase in jitterBufferDelay by the interval increase in jitterBufferEmittedCount. Check units and a nonzero denominator; do not confuse the cumulative counter with milliseconds per packet.

questions.watch_for: A lower buffer target can reduce delay while making audible glitches worse.

questions.title: Data channels and durable messages
questions.question: If a data channel is reliable, why does P2 need an inbox?
answer: A data channel can provide ordered or unordered and reliable or partially reliable message delivery within a live connection. Those transport modes do not define a durable cross session business inbox. A process crash, a reconnect or an ambiguous application acknowledgment still needs an application identity and recovery contract. [W6]

P2 adds the missing boundary: authenticate the source, persist the accepted message under its original identity, detect changed payload conflicts and only then drive dispatch or generation. Reliable delivery of bytes and durable acceptance of a user operation are both useful, but they answer different questions. A browser retry must reconcile the original identity rather than infer failure from disconnection.

followups.question: What should be unreliable?
followups.answer: A transient cursor or live level indicator may tolerate loss. A business request should use a protocol with durable acceptance and explicit identity even if its underlying transport is reliable.

followups.question: Does ordering solve duplicate work?
followups.answer: Ordering only sequences messages within its defined transport context. It does not deduplicate a replay from another connection or atomically bind an input to accepted work.

questions.watch_for: Do not treat a transport send promise as a business commit receipt.

questions.title: Mesh SFU and MCU
questions.question: Why use an SFU for an agent application?
answer: A mesh sends media among endpoint pairs. An SFU forwards selected encoded streams to subscribers. An MCU mixes or transforms media into new output streams, incurring different compute and layout tradeoffs. LiveKit supplies an SFU; applications work with rooms, participants and track subscriptions. [L1]

For this POC the SFU lets a browser and a native agent exchange media using supported SDKs while the application focuses on business continuity. It does not make every participant free: track count, forwarding bandwidth and receiver decode work still matter. I would discuss a multi participant room separately from the many independent one caller rooms used by a voice service.

followups.question: Is SFU cost constant per room?
followups.answer: No. Publishers, subscribers, track selections and bitrates determine forwarding work and bandwidth. Room count alone hides very different workloads.

followups.question: What about simulcast?
followups.answer: A publisher can offer multiple independent quality encodings so an SFU can forward an appropriate layer per subscriber. That mainly addresses video distribution; it does not accelerate a slow supplier or repair lost business state.

questions.watch_for: Do not use an SFU diagram to imply mixed audio recording or a distributed business scheduler.

questions.title: Diagnose with getStats
questions.question: Which measurements would you inspect before blaming the model?
answer: I would identify the selected candidate pair, its transport and available RTT observations, then compare outbound and inbound RTP bytes and packets, loss, jitter and concealment on the relevant audio streams. I would inspect the actual audio element state, output routing and permission failures as well. The W3C statistics model gives the field meanings and links among reports. [W7]

Next I correlate that timeline with capture, STT final, durable input acceptance, LLM first token, TTS first audio, publication and browser playout observations. The repository deliberately separates those observations. If media never arrives, changing the model prompt is unlikely to fix the problem; if media is healthy but generation stalls, a network only diagnosis is incomplete.

followups.question: Why sample deltas?
followups.answer: Most counters accumulate. Bytes over an interval estimate bitrate as 8 times the byte delta divided by elapsed seconds. Use stable stream identity and reset the calculation after a counter or stream reset.

followups.question: Can stats prove the human heard the quote?
followups.answer: No. They establish scoped technical observations. Even a browser playout or energy observation does not establish human understanding or authorize a mutation.

questions.watch_for: RTT, jitter, model latency and user perceived delay have different definitions.

chapters.title: Inside a LiveKit agent session
chapters.subtitle: Rooms workers turns and the application boundary
intro: Read the pinned repository baseline separately from current online documentation. This snapshot records livekit-agents 1.8.11, the Python RTC SDK 1.2.0, LiveKit server 1.13.11 and browser client 2.23.0. These are repository selections, not a claim that they are the newest releases.

The public docs may evolve. Explain the architectural role before quoting an API signature. The POC deliberately owns manual input admission and durable execution without redefining the media runtime.

concepts.title: Objects with different lifetimes
concepts.body: A room carries participants and tracks. An agent server receives jobs. A job hosts a session. A case and its accepted work survive those conversational lifetimes.

concepts.title: The voice loop
concepts.body: Capture to STT to turn admission to generation to TTS to publication and playout is observable as multiple stages, not one success flag.

questions.title: Core runtime objects
questions.question: How do Room, Agent, AgentSession and an agent server differ?
answer: A room is the shared realtime transport context for participants and tracks. An Agent supplies instructions, tools and conversational logic. AgentSession orchestrates input, the voice pipeline, model invocation and output. An agent server registers for jobs and runs application entrypoints. [L4, L6]

The application must decide which object owns each resource and callback. Session shutdown should release session resources, while durable work remains in P1. A model handoff changes conversational control; it does not automatically transfer database lease authority. I would ground exact API usage in the pinned adapter rather than reciting a current quickstart from memory.

followups.question: Is an Agent a durable worker?
followups.answer: Not by that name alone. A conversational Agent defines behavior. Durable work execution in this repository uses explicit P1 records, grants and recovery contracts.

followups.question: Can I use LiveKit without AgentSession?
followups.answer: The server infrastructure supports programmatic participants. AgentSession is the high level orchestration surface for a voice agent, not a requirement for every media processing job. [L7]

questions.watch_for: Do not confuse a class name with a persistence guarantee.

questions.title: Dispatch and process isolation
questions.question: How does an agent become a participant in a room?
answer: Dispatch assigns an agent to a room. With explicit dispatch, the application targets a registered agent name and supplies job metadata. The agent server receives the job and executes the application entrypoint. The documented job lifecycle isolates jobs in separate processes. [L5, L7]

I would authenticate the application that requests dispatch and validate metadata before using it as a trusted binding. Room participant identity and business identity need an explicit relationship. A successful dispatch is not readiness for inference, durable input or playback. The POC waits for mode consistent readiness and retains the case independently of whether that room worker survives.

followups.question: Why explicit dispatch?
followups.answer: It makes the intended agent and launch point visible, and avoids automatically starting an unintended worker for every room. Exact routing and options should follow the selected SDK and server contract.

followups.question: Does process isolation provide crash recovery?
followups.answer: It limits the blast radius of a job crash. It does not restore application memory or reconcile an uncertain supplier call; those require durable state and an explicit recovery path.

questions.watch_for: Dispatch acknowledgment, connected participant and ready business agent are separate milestones.

questions.title: Trace the voice pipeline
questions.question: What happens from a spoken request to an audible answer?
answer: The client publishes audio and the agent receives it through the room. A cascaded pipeline produces speech recognition, decides the user turn boundary, invokes the language model and streams synthesized audio back. The repository adds durable admission before generation, then records distinct generation and playback observations.

I would show the correlated input and operation ID at the durable boundary, then the generation identity and output evidence. Some stages overlap, so summing arbitrary component durations can double count. A business check can run in the background while the conversation gives a truthful pending response. No stage permits the model to approve the exact supplier mutation.

followups.question: Where do you measure responsiveness?
followups.answer: Choose a concrete start and finish, such as actual end of user speech to first rendered agent audio, and keep pipeline metrics as supporting breakdowns. State capture and measurement limitations. [L12]

followups.question: What if TTS succeeds but the browser is silent?
followups.answer: That is an output path failure. Inspect publication, subscription, received packets, decode and audio playback. Preserve generated output as a fact without labeling it heard.

questions.watch_for: A text transcript or TTS completion is insufficient media evidence.

questions.title: Turn taking and durable intake
questions.question: Why does the native adapter use manual turns?
answer: The project wants one durable input before one conversational generation. Competing SDK text consumption, preemptive generation or automatic turn ownership could begin a reply before the accepted input is fixed. The native adapter therefore uses an explicit admission path and preserves the original caller bound final recognition before awaits.

Manual mode is an application correctness choice with a latency and integration cost. It is not a claim that the framework default is broken. LiveKit provides multiple turn detection strategies; VAD activity, final transcription and semantic end of turn answer different questions. The important project invariant is that the selected turn source and durable input have one owner. [L9]

followups.question: Is a final transcript permission to mutate?
followups.answer: No. Recognition finality establishes an input observation. The model, durable intake, exact quote consent and action commitment remain different boundaries.

followups.question: Could you enable preemptive generation later?
followups.answer: Only with a contract that keeps speculative output separate from accepted work and prevents speculative side effects. Measure the latency benefit and test changed transcripts, cancellation and repeated commit.

questions.watch_for: Do not promote interim recognition into a second durable operation.

questions.title: Interruption without losing truth
questions.question: What should happen when the user barges in?
answer: The conversational layer should stop or pause the previous output promptly and decide whether the new speech is a true interruption. LiveKit exposes interruption handling and tuning, including mechanisms for distinguishing brief backchannels from intentional barge ins. Those are conversational controls. [L10, L11]

The business layer must separately decide whether accepted work should continue or receive a cancellation request. Cutting off speech does not prove a supplier call stopped. The project should retain the original accepted operation, its known results and the newly recognized input. Reconnect or interruption history must represent the observed output boundary rather than asserting that the whole generated answer was heard.

followups.question: Does every okay interrupt?
followups.answer: Not necessarily; it can be backchannel feedback. Tune using representative audio and false interruption measurements, while keeping exact business confirmation outside inferred conversation semantics.

followups.question: Should barge in cancel background work?
followups.answer: That is a product decision expressed as an explicit command. Stop output first, then apply the documented cancellation boundary without erasing prior effect truth.

questions.watch_for: Do not equate session.interrupt with remote effect cancellation.

questions.title: Text is a full modality
questions.question: What changes when the same agent supports SMS and text?
answer: Text removes speech recognition and audio playback stages but retains identity, ordering, admission, authorization and result delivery questions. LiveKit text streams carry realtime text and have no long term message persistence. P2 supplies a durable channel history and dispatch boundary around that transport. [L8]

SMS introduces a different sender verification and callback model. A trusted association must bind it to the correct account and case; a string in a payload cannot supply that authority. A new SMS is a distinct input even if its wording matches a voice transcript. The product should preserve channel provenance while letting the case survive all of these interactions.

followups.question: Can late joiners read old streams?
followups.answer: Do not assume realtime streams provide historical replay. The application needs retained history and a scoped read contract for a fresh session. [L8]

followups.question: Does a phone number prove the account?
followups.answer: Only the application association and verified provider path define the permitted binding. The project distinguishes retained history access from current permission needed for selected new actions.

questions.watch_for: Supporting text means more than rendering transcriptions in a chat bubble.

questions.title: Reconnect and rehydrate
questions.question: What state should survive a network drop?
answer: The SDK should manage its supported transport reconnect path and the application should present a useful reconnecting state. The current LiveKit connection guide documents fallback transports and reconnect events. A full reconnect or fresh room can replace transport objects, so callbacks and subscriptions need explicit lifetime ownership. [L3]

P1 work and P2 accepted inputs survive independently. Rehydration loads current permitted context using retained channel state and public case observations; it does not resubmit every visible message. I would test a disconnect after acceptance but before ACK, and a fresh room after a completed result, then verify stable original identities and no new supplier effects.

followups.question: Should the UI disable all reads?
followups.answer: It should distinguish transport health from authenticated control API availability and freshness. Safe reads may remain useful; new authority changing actions need their own admission checks.

followups.question: Can the old transcript be the new case state?
followups.answer: No. A transcript is historical evidence. The session should obtain an authorized current case view with explicit as of boundaries.

questions.watch_for: Never use reconnect as permission to blindly replay all tool calls.

questions.title: Provider modes and observability
questions.question: How do you know a session actually used the configured inference mode?
answer: The repository defines scripted, local_real and provider_real as distinct trusted modes. The selected mode must agree through grants, worker readiness and safe telemetry. A configured badge or healthy provider process does not show that actual inference occurred. There is no silent cross mode fallback.

For a qualified run I would inspect actual usage observations, the selected model or provider identifiers and correlated session traces, alongside the required returned audio evidence. Numeric usage supports what was invoked; it does not prove model quality. Current LiveKit observability documentation describes per component, turn and session surfaces, but exact use must match the pinned code. [L12, L13]

followups.question: Why no silent fallback?
followups.answer: It can change latency, cost, privacy and behavior while making test evidence misleading. If fallback is desired, its policy and identity must be explicit and observable.

followups.question: Does scripted testing still matter?
followups.answer: Yes. Deterministic faults can establish invariants and useful progress. Actual inference and media qualification remain separate requirements that scripted providers cannot satisfy.

questions.watch_for: Never say local_real is qualified merely because weights were downloaded.

chapters.title: Failure diagnosis and production recovery
chapters.subtitle: Find the failing boundary and recover without inventing success
intro: Production questions reward a sequence of discriminating observations. Start with the user symptom, separate control, media, inference and business state, and choose a recovery action that preserves original identities.

The incidents below are constructed interview scenarios. Proposed production mitigations are design reasoning, not claims that this local POC has been deployed at production scale. Where a current repository finding is relevant, it is named explicitly.

concepts.title: Four diagnostic planes
concepts.body: Control and authentication; media connectivity and playout; inference and turn taking; durable business execution.

concepts.title: A recovery rule
concepts.body: A timeout changes what the caller knows. It does not necessarily change what the remote system did.

questions.title: Connected but silent
questions.question: The room is connected and captions update, but the user hears nothing. How do you debug?
answer: First establish which direction is silent. For agent to user audio, verify that a response was scheduled, that TTS produced audio, that the agent published the intended track, that the browser subscribed, that inbound packets and decoded samples advanced, and that output playback was permitted. Check the audio element, device routing, muted state and user gesture requirements.

Use one correlated turn and avoid mixing counters from old tracks after reconnect. The project has separate text, SDK and browser evidence precisely because a successful earlier stage is insufficient. Preserve a useful pending or failed audio state in the UI, without marking the response heard or retrying any business effect. Transport diagnostics follow standard connection and statistics observations. [L3, W7]

followups.question: What if only the microphone direction fails?
followups.answer: Check permission and the captured track first, then local publish bytes and agent input. A working agent output path does not prove the microphone was captured or forwarded.

followups.question: Would you regenerate the answer?
followups.answer: Only after deciding the conversational retry contract. Regeneration can be useful for audio failure, but it must not repeat the accepted business operation or invent a second input.

questions.watch_for: Captions and a connected icon cannot establish returned audio.

questions.title: Latency climbed overnight
questions.question: How would you investigate a p95 response latency regression?
answer: Define the metric and population before changing settings. Compare the same inference mode, turn type and measurement boundary. Separate time spent recognizing the end of speech, durably admitting the turn, waiting for a model, producing first audio, transporting it and playing it. Look for a changed distribution, not just an average.

In this POC I would examine event loop lag, connection establishment, read slot contention, database locks, worker startup and provider usage. The latest audit names shared startup slots and dispatch work that includes current result reads and playout, which can couple unrelated latencies. I would reproduce one constrained case, capture the timeline and change the bottleneck with an explicit invariant check. [L12, L13]

followups.question: Why not lower endpointing immediately?
followups.answer: It may reduce delay while cutting the user off. A latency fix must preserve turn quality, durable input ordering and the intended interruption behavior.

followups.question: Is sub 500 ms guaranteed?
followups.answer: No universal target follows from the JD or this repository. State a proposed SLO with a measurement boundary, percentile, load and mode, then measure it.

questions.watch_for: Do not add overlapping streaming stage durations and call the sum measured end to end latency.

questions.title: A dependency times out
questions.question: When is retry safe and when should the outcome remain unknown?
answer: I classify the operation before retrying. A side effect free read can often retry within one bounded budget. An accepted command with a stable receipt replays its original identity. A supplier mutation or outbound send that may have crossed its reservation boundary requires the operation specific reconciliation contract; a timeout alone cannot establish nonexecution.

The repository retains possible effect markers and known results, and distinguishes ordinary ambiguous sends from an operation with an explicitly frozen idempotency capability. P1 v5 persists selected predispatch unavailable retry due times, but the current audit leaves outages after reservation outside that pacing coverage. I would present that limitation and avoid claiming one generic retry policy handles every phase.

followups.question: Does exponential backoff ensure safety?
followups.answer: It reduces pressure; it does not identify whether the previous call took effect. Stable identity, receiver or supplier semantics and current permission decide whether another call is allowed.

followups.question: Should every layer retry three times?
followups.answer: No. Nested retry policies multiply load and exceed deadlines. Give one owner the total budget and define which lower layer outcomes it may repeat.

questions.watch_for: Transport failure is not reliable evidence of business failure.

questions.title: Crash after a possible effect
questions.question: The worker dies after a supplier call but before saving its result. What next?
answer: The next worker must inspect the durable original effect state, current grant and supplier capability. If a possible effect marker exists, it cannot assume the call never happened. For a cooperating supplier, lookup by the frozen operation identity can establish the known result. For an ordinary supplier with no reliable reconciliation, the outcome may remain unknown and require explicit operator handling.

The recovery test should kill a real owned process at a controlled boundary, then independently inspect supplier identity and call or effect counts. Merely raising an exception before the call does not test the dangerous window. Reaping the old worker also matters: an abandoned waiter is not proof that the original process or external request stopped.

followups.question: Can the takeover issue a new supplier key?
followups.answer: That would discard the uncertainty protection. The original logical operation identity must remain fixed through reconciliation.

followups.question: What if the old worker finishes late?
followups.answer: A stale lease must fail protected writes, while known supplier truth is still reconciled under the current authority. The supplier needs its own cooperation to prevent duplicate effects.

questions.watch_for: Database fencing cannot independently fence a remote request.

questions.title: Duplicate SMS and contradictory callbacks
questions.question: A carrier retries a webhook and later sends conflicting delivery statuses. What should happen?
answer: Authenticate the raw callback before replay lookup or expensive admission. Match the immutable provider scope, attempt key and request digest. A replay with the same identity and bytes returns the original observation; changed payload identity conflicts stay explicit. A current association must not silently retarget an old attempt.

Contradictory callback facts should be retained and reduced by the documented provider rule. They are evidence about the exact old attempt, not permission for a new send. A NEW reservation rechecks earlier operations, callbacks and current route or suppression under shared admission. A callback arriving after an admitted external call cannot retrospectively fence that already possible call.

followups.question: Can you just keep the latest timestamp?
followups.answer: No general contract authorizes timestamp arbitration. Provider timestamps can be delayed or conflicting, and the original immutable attempt binding is more fundamental.

followups.question: Does delivered mean acknowledged?
followups.answer: Carrier delivery evidence does not establish that the human read or understood the message. Receiver acceptance, carrier observations and human acknowledgment stay separate.

questions.watch_for: A callback is evidence, never an implicit resend command.

questions.title: An old result appears current
questions.question: The specialist says eligible after the customer changes the request. How do you prevent a stale action?
answer: Keep the original result as truth about its submitted snapshot and record applicability as a separate observation against current case state. A result can be validly produced and still be stale for the revised case. Display metadata should expose as of context instead of replacing the current authority.

Before action, use the public guard that atomically checks current work and case eligibility and exact confirmation, then commits intent and its receipt. A separate preflight read is vulnerable to a race. The existing race tooling demonstrates revision first and intent first schedules; a later revision cannot silently undo a committed original intent. Semantic validity and human permission still require their own checks.

followups.question: Could a refreshed green badge authorize action?
followups.answer: No. Refresh is derived metadata from separately timed reads. Only the current guarded action transaction can decide permission at commitment.

followups.question: Should the stale result be deleted?
followups.answer: No. It remains useful historical truth and may be needed for audit and replay protection. Display pruning must preserve protected identities and unresolved processing.

questions.watch_for: Stored result truth, current applicability and action permission are three different claims.

questions.title: Shutdown consumes the final input
questions.question: How would you investigate the gateway normal stop findings?
answer: The latest audit records a high severity possibility that dispatch keeps claiming attempts while the Parent endpoints close, permanently exhausting pending inputs. It also records a last input lifecycle risk when a worker stops before gateway room closure and binding revocation. These are current open findings, not solved behavior to claim.

I would draw the shutdown dependency graph: stop new admission at the right boundary, quiesce dispatch before its endpoints close, retain every admitted owner until settled, observe child closure, then close shared readers. I would prove the revised order with a final input accepted during stop and with an endpoint blocked at the write boundary, checking useful progress after restart and preserving original receipts.

followups.question: Why not suppress all close errors?
followups.answer: That can conceal unresolved owners and delete evidence too early. Preserve the primary failure and report incomplete cleanup while retaining the objects needed to observe eventual closure.

followups.question: Can a timeout justify deleting room files?
followups.answer: No. First establish that the exact owned process or group exited and was reaped. A canceled waiter alone does not establish that state.

questions.watch_for: Describe the proposed repair as future work until its source and gates exist.

evidence.label: GW A1 GW A2 and DEMO A6

questions.title: Provider outage and reconnect storm
questions.question: How do you keep one outage from overwhelming the service?
answer: Separate rejection of new work from preservation of accepted work. Bound new admission, in flight requests and reconnect attempts; apply a single total retry budget with backoff and jitter where the operation permits it. Give the user a truthful degraded state rather than starting unbounded generations or repeating uncertain commands.

For a production design I would isolate provider capacity from read and control paths, add fair admission and observe pending age and useful completion. In this POC, bounded slots and persisted retry pacing already illustrate part of that design, while the audit documents remaining shared pool and failure scan backoff issues. Those limits prevent me from claiming fully isolated failure domains today.

followups.question: Would you switch providers automatically?
followups.answer: Only under an explicit mode and fallback contract that preserves visibility, privacy, budget and semantic constraints. The current repository has no silent inference mode fallback.

followups.question: What do you alert on?
followups.answer: User impact: connection success, pending age, end to end response or completion SLOs, unknown effect growth and cleanup failure. Raw reconnect counts are supporting signals rather than the entire incident definition.

questions.watch_for: A healthy process is not proof of available inference or useful business progress.

chapters.title: Designing for scale and durable progress
chapters.subtitle: Capacity reliability availability and durability have different contracts
intro: The repository qualifies selected local workloads. The following scaling exercises deliberately change the constraints and ask what would need to be designed and measured next. They do not convert local throughput or sampled memory into a global service capacity claim.
Always separate the media plane, inference capacity, durable authority and notification path. Each scales on a different unit and fails at a different boundary.

concepts.title: Reliability and availability
concepts.body: Reliability concerns correct sustained behavior; availability concerns being able to serve the defined operation. A service can answer quickly and incorrectly.

concepts.title: Durability and recoverability
concepts.body: Durability concerns retained committed state under a stated fault model. Recovery additionally needs readable compatible state, identity preservation, ownership and an executable procedure.

questions.title: Scale the right subsystem
questions.question: How would you evolve this local POC for ten thousand concurrent conversations?
answer: I would start with a workload definition: active audio ratio, turn rate, call duration, specialist fan out, model and provider mix, message size and retention. Then size media forwarding, agent jobs, inference and database admission independently. Ten thousand silent connections and ten thousand simultaneous spoken turns are different systems.

The POC runs one local SFU and does not claim production media scale. A production design would use supported deployment and routing patterns, independent agent capacity, bounded database connections and a measured admission plan. Public self hosted LiveKit documentation uses Redis for distributed room routing and currently requires a room to fit on one node. LiveKit Cloud has a different mesh offering; I would not conflate the two. [L2]

followups.question: What is the first load test?
followups.answer: One representative room and turn workload with a frozen manifest, then a controlled ramp. Retain raw results, queue age, errors, actual resource use and independent reconciliation.

followups.question: Why not add more workers immediately?
followups.answer: Workers can increase contention or overload a provider and database. Measure the bottleneck and retain ownership and admission invariants at each new concurrency level.

questions.watch_for: Never extrapolate local samples into production capacity without a workload and failure model.

questions.title: Capacity arithmetic
questions.question: How do you estimate concurrency and backlog?
answer: For a stable system, Little law relates average in system work L to arrival rate lambda times average time W. As an illustrative design exercise, 20 accepted tasks per second with a mean residence time of 3 seconds imply about 60 resident tasks. This is an assumption based estimate, not a repository measurement.

A dependency outage breaks steady state assumptions and grows backlog until admission or storage limits intervene. Separate active slots, pending work and retained identities. P1 and P2 preserve identity protections at capacity; evicting a display row does not create room for another protected operation. I would size retention and replay horizons as part of the design rather than just multiplying worker count.

followups.question: Why is p95 not substituted for W?
followups.answer: Little law uses averages over a stable system. Percentiles help bound user experience and burst planning, but substituting them blindly changes the calculation meaning.

followups.question: What if arrivals exceed service capacity?
followups.answer: Backlog and waiting time grow. Apply bounded admission and explicit rejection or deferral rather than letting memory and deadlines become the accidental queue policy.

questions.watch_for: Distinguish an illustrative estimate from measured throughput.

questions.title: Backpressure that reaches admission
questions.question: Where should concurrency limits live?
answer: Limits belong at the resource boundary they protect and at the authority that accepts durable obligations. The HTTP body, queued requests, actual remote calls, database connections, retained identities and result consumers each need a bound. A semaphore around a waiter is inadequate if timed out calls continue using resources after their slots are released.

In the joined application, ChannelPolicyExecutor limits owned jobs and retains runner ownership through closure. Shared reader capacity is reserved so background inspection cannot occupy every dispatch slot. This is a concrete useful pattern, but the latest audit still records other shared startup and read pool contention. A production extension would define tenant fairness and budget policy above these mechanism limits.

followups.question: What does the user see at capacity?
followups.answer: An explicit bounded failure or pending state with stable original identity. Replays and reads should remain available under the documented contract instead of being rejected like new obligations.

followups.question: Why bound bytes as well as requests?
followups.answer: Ten small inputs and ten large images can have very different memory, CPU and downstream cost. Per request count limits alone do not constrain total resource use.

questions.watch_for: Retain actual I O ownership after a caller abandons waiting.

evidence.label: Discovery readers preserve a dispatch slot

questions.title: High availability without lost truth
questions.question: How do database replication and backups affect the design?
answer: Define which acknowledged commits must survive which failures. A replica can improve availability and recovery options, but asynchronous replication may lose recent commits on promotion. Backups need a tested restore procedure, compatible schema and retained application identities. A successful health check does not establish any of those contracts.

This local POC uses isolated PostgreSQL and explicit migrations, not a demonstrated HA deployment. Before production promotion I would specify recovery point and recovery time objectives, test failover and restore, and reconcile committed cases, work results and external effect keys against the supplier. Losing an idempotency record while an external effect survives can be more dangerous than losing a display history row.

followups.question: Can reads go to any replica?
followups.answer: Only if the operation tolerates that freshness. Permission checks and exact commitment must use the authoritative guard; an asynchronously lagging read cannot authorize a current action.

followups.question: Why preserve tombstones?
followups.answer: A replayed old identity must not become new merely because detailed history was pruned. Tombstones or an explicit supported replay horizon protect that boundary.

questions.watch_for: Availability, replication and backup are complementary mechanisms with different failure coverage.

questions.title: Fairness and useful progress
questions.question: How do you stop one account or one unresolved result from blocking everyone?
answer: Use bounded admission by the relevant scope, separate control and read capacity from expensive work, and define a fair discovery policy. In a result consumer, an unresolved old result must not force the system to stop examining later useful events. P3 keeps its discovery scan separate from the contiguous terminal ACK watermark and bounds each examination pass.

That does not authorize skipping unknown results forever or ACKing them to free capacity. Preserve their identities and expose pending age. A production extension could apply per tenant shares and starvation detection while leaving the source authority unchanged. I would test both the negative case, where an unresolved event stays unACKed, and the positive case, where later valid work completes.

followups.question: Why separate scan and ACK cursors?
followups.answer: The scan cursor supports discovery and fairness. The contiguous watermark represents terminal processing knowledge. Advancing the latter over an unknown event would falsely assert completion.

followups.question: Can you drop old unresolved rows?
followups.answer: Display retention cannot remove protected processing identities or silently free durable capacity. Cleanup needs a separate replay and ownership contract.

questions.watch_for: Useful progress must be demonstrated alongside rejection and safety assertions.

questions.title: Deploy while sessions are active
questions.question: How should a rolling deployment stop taking work?
answer: Drain new admission before tearing down the resources serving accepted work. For the media plane, the LiveKit self hosting guide documents draining existing rooms while rejecting new rooms. That is different from the application gateway draining accepted dispatch and from a durable worker relinquishing an explicit lease. [L2]

I would define a dependency graph and a deadline for each tier: front door, dispatch, per room workers, business runners, then shared readers. Observe actual termination before releasing a lease or deleting files. The current POC audit exposes shutdown order and budget inversions, so I would use those findings as the starting point for a tested repair rather than claim a production safe rolling deployment.

followups.question: Can SIGKILL be a normal drain?
followups.answer: It can be part of an enforced upper bound, but it leaves recovery obligations and possible external calls. A later owner must reconcile original state instead of assuming cancellation.

followups.question: Can old and new schema code overlap?
followups.answer: Only under an explicitly compatible migration and capability contract. Runtime roles must not perform opportunistic DDL while serving traffic.

questions.watch_for: Media room drain and durable business drain are distinct lifecycles.

questions.title: SLOs for a voice and work system
questions.question: Which objectives would you define?
answer: I would define separate user centered objectives for connection setup, completed turn responsiveness, accepted input durability, business work completion and result disclosure. Each needs a denominator, percentile or success ratio, time window and inclusion policy. A fast apology response should not count as successful business completion.

Then map supporting metrics to causes: event loop lag, pending age, lease takeovers, unknown effects, provider first byte time, slot saturation and cleanup incompleteness. The repository retains numeric usage and explicit observations; production alert thresholds would need measured baselines. Correlation identifiers should connect a case and its attempts while low cardinality metrics avoid unbounded labels.

followups.question: What would you page on?
followups.answer: Sustained user impact or imminent exhaustion, such as accepted work aging beyond its objective or growing unresolved effects. A single retry counter increment may be a diagnostic signal rather than a page.

followups.question: What if privacy limits transcripts?
followups.answer: Keep identifiers, timing, safe result classes and bounded structured diagnostics. Rich content should follow explicit access and retention rules rather than being copied into every metric or trace.

questions.watch_for: An exporter being reachable does not prove that useful sanitized traces were exported.

questions.title: Multi region and a single owner
questions.question: What changes if a business case can run in two regions?
answer: Choose where the case authority lives before drawing active active workers. A single writer or globally coordinated authority must order revision, exact consent, execution eligibility and intent. A regional room can be transient while durable work remains anchored elsewhere. Network partitions require an explicit availability versus coordination tradeoff.

The POC has no qualified multi region business failover. I would first support region independent authenticated reads and controlled session routing, then design authority failover with original identities, database time assumptions, lease epochs and supplier reconciliation intact. Introducing a regional broker does not by itself provide a globally ordered case or external effect fence.

followups.question: Can two regions both claim on local time?
followups.answer: That risks overlapping owners if their authorities are not coordinated. The existing design uses authoritative database time after locks; a multi region design must preserve an equally explicit eligibility contract.

followups.question: Would room migration move the business case?
followups.answer: Not automatically. Media placement and case ownership have different latency and consistency requirements, so bind them deliberately rather than making room location the authority key.

questions.watch_for: Label multi region designs as proposed extensions, not local POC accomplishments.

chapters.title: NATS from subjects to durable consumers
chapters.subtitle: Choose the messaging contract before choosing the API
intro: The interview value of NATS is understanding its boundaries: live routing, durable storage, consumer progress and application side effects. A fast message exchange does not automatically provide an accepted workflow, a safe retry or a committed supplier action.

These questions use original hypothetical examples inspired by the POC. NATS is study material and a possible future integration, not an installed service in this repository. Distinguish a broker mechanism from the business contract you would build around it.

concepts.title: Three acknowledgments to distinguish
concepts.body: The publisher may learn a message was stored, a consumer may tell the broker it handled a delivery, and an application may retain a business receipt. Those facts need distinct names and identities.

concepts.title: A failure first answer
concepts.body: Explain the happy path, then crash immediately before and after each acknowledgment. If the story loses a request or repeats an effect, name the missing recovery contract.

questions.title: Messaging without endpoint addresses
questions.question: What is NATS, and how do Core NATS and JetStream differ?
answer: NATS routes messages by subject between publishers and subscribers without requiring each publisher to know the receiving process address. Core NATS provides live at-most-once delivery to interested subscribers; it does not retain a backlog for an absent subscriber. JetStream adds streams and consumers for retained messages and tracked delivery. [N1, N2, N6]

For an original design example, I might use a live work-changed notification to wake an existing P1 poller. Losing that hint is acceptable only because durable eligibility remains discoverable. If I instead promise that a disconnected downstream audit consumer will later see every event, I need a retained event contract, storage limits and replay behavior. These are different requirements even if the messages share a subject prefix. I would first name the obligation and its owner, then select live messaging or durable consumption. Neither choice automatically makes a supplier mutation safe to retry.

followups.question: Is a successful Core publish a subscriber receipt?
followups.answer: No. It does not prove a handler processed the message or committed a business result. In an application that needs a receipt, define a response or durable read protocol with a stable original identity rather than inferring success from the publish call.

followups.question: Why not always enable durable storage?
followups.answer: Retention adds operational ownership, capacity and replay choices. Keep ephemeral hints cheap when a separate durable authority can recover missed notifications; require persistence when the messaging contract itself must bridge a consumer outage.

questions.watch_for: Core connectivity, JetStream storage and business acceptance are different facts.

questions.title: Design a subject space
questions.question: How do subjects and wildcards work, and how would you name subjects for this application?
answer: Subjects are case-sensitive, dot-separated token sequences. A subscription wildcard star matches one token; the trailing greater-than wildcard matches one or more remaining tokens. A producer should publish to a concrete subject, while consumers subscribe to the exact name or permitted pattern. For example, continuity.eu.work.ready matches continuity.*.work.ready and continuity.eu.>, but continuity.eu itself does not match the latter. [N14]

For a hypothetical integration I would keep stable service and event concepts in the subject and put bounded correlation IDs in the validated payload. I would avoid raw phone numbers, transcripts or bearer tokens in subjects because subject names can appear in operational surfaces. A tenant token in the subject is a routing convention, not authentication: trusted credentials and subject permissions still determine who can publish or subscribe. Version the payload contract explicitly, and decide whether a new semantic event needs a new subject rather than changing the meaning silently.

followups.question: Why avoid a subject for every token of generated text?
followups.answer: Subject count is not the only cost; subscriptions, permissions, observability and payload fan-out also need bounds. A coherent subject taxonomy makes routing reviewable. Streaming output can carry bounded sequence metadata without inventing a new authorization surface for every chunk.

followups.question: Can a wildcard subscription cross tenants?
followups.answer: Only if the authenticated principal is granted that subject range. A broad subscription pattern is a request, not proof of permission. Test a credential from tenant A against tenant B subjects and verify denial independently of payload labels.

questions.watch_for: A subject naming convention does not establish a trusted tenant boundary.

questions.title: Broadcast and worker selection
questions.question: How does a queue group differ from ordinary publish subscribe?
answer: Ordinary subscriptions each receive a matching live publication. Subscribers sharing a subject and queue group divide those deliveries: one member is selected for a message within that group. Separate groups can each receive their own selected copy. A Core queue group does not retain work or redeliver it after the selected member crashes. [N4]

In a hypothetical agent system, analytics and an operator dashboard might each need an independent notification, whereas interchangeable cache-refresh workers might share a group. I would not give three independent services the same group name if each must observe every event. I would also avoid treating the selected worker as the durable owner of the business operation. A member can die after receipt or perform an action before losing its response. The POC already expresses ownership through P1 grants and retained original identities. A queue group could choose who tries to wake or inspect work without replacing those authoritative checks.

followups.question: Does one selected member mean exactly one effect?
followups.answer: No. Selection describes routing of this delivery. It says nothing about a handler crash, an application retry, another publication or an external effect. Preserve the original business identity and use its authority to decide what can run.

followups.question: What if one worker is much slower?
followups.answer: Measure outstanding real work and useful completion, then choose bounded concurrency and an appropriate durable work model if needed. Group membership alone is not a fairness, deadline or backpressure policy for arbitrary handler runtimes.

questions.watch_for: A queue group is not a durable queue and does not make business execution exactly once.

questions.title: Request reply does not remove ambiguity
questions.question: How does NATS request reply work, and what does a request timeout tell you?
answer: Request reply layers a reply subject onto publish subscribe. The requester listens for a response, sends a request naming the reply destination, and waits under a deadline. Supported clients can distinguish a no-responders observation from a response timeout. That describes messaging visibility, not durable business execution. [N5]

Suppose a hypothetical specialist receives a request, stores a result and then loses its connection before replying. The requester times out even though useful work happened. Retrying with a fresh work ID could duplicate the operation. I would bind the original scoped command and payload digest, support lookup or original replay where the operation contract permits it, and keep uncertainty visible otherwise. A read-only advisory request may have a simpler retry policy than a supplier mutation. One total deadline should cover the allowed attempts; nested unconditional retries should not multiply work or hide which request identity remains unresolved.

followups.question: Does timeout cancel the responder?
followups.answer: It ends the requester wait. The responder might still be executing or might already have committed. A cancellation protocol needs a separate identity and defined semantics; it cannot be inferred from the disappearance of a reply inbox.

followups.question: Can no responders authorize a new operation key?
followups.answer: It can inform a retry policy for the original attempt, but cannot erase an earlier possibly delivered request. Reconcile the full original operation history. Treat one transport observation as evidence about that exchange, not a global proof of nonexecution.

questions.watch_for: A requester deadline is not a remote stop guarantee.

questions.title: The crash gap around consumer acknowledgment
questions.question: When should a durable consumer acknowledge a message?
answer: A JetStream stream retains messages under its configured policy, while a consumer tracks delivery progress. With explicit acknowledgments, an unacknowledged message can be redelivered after AckWait. A confirmed acknowledgment additionally lets the client learn that the broker recorded the acknowledgment. A broker ack is still separate from an application transaction. [N6, N7]

For a hypothetical projection handler I would atomically retain the original event identity and its derived state in the application database, then acknowledge the delivery. Crash before that transaction means the next delivery can do the work. Crash after commit but before acknowledgment means replay must find the retained identity and avoid another state transition. Acknowledging first creates a loss gap; doing an unprotected external mutation first creates a duplicate-effect gap. If a supplier is involved, use its existing stable effect and reconciliation contract rather than assuming the consumer acknowledgment participates in the supplier transaction.

followups.question: What does double acknowledgment solve?
followups.answer: It reduces uncertainty about whether the broker recorded the consumer ack. It does not atomically include a PostgreSQL write or external supplier call. Keep the application identity ledger so a redelivery remains safe across those separate boundaries.

followups.question: Should every failure be acknowledged?
followups.answer: Only under a defined terminal-handling contract. A malformed immutable event may be durably quarantined and then retired; a transient dependency failure should remain recoverable. Define retry limits, retained evidence and operator handling instead of dropping either case silently.

questions.watch_for: Acknowledge after a durable application disposition, while preserving idempotency for the commit-before-ack crash.

questions.title: Bound exactly once to the right boundary
questions.question: JetStream supports deduplication and confirmed acknowledgments. Why can the application still repeat a side effect?
answer: A stable Nats-Msg-Id can suppress repeat storage within the configured duplicate-tracking window. Confirmed consumer acknowledgments address whether the broker recorded delivery progress. Those mechanisms strengthen broker-level publish and consume behavior, but do not create one atomic transaction with an arbitrary supplier. [N15, N7]

Consider an original hypothetical booking change: the handler invokes the supplier, the supplier commits, and the handler dies before retaining the result or acknowledging. Redelivery cannot determine the supplier outcome from the broker state. The application must keep the original effect identity and use a cooperating supplier lookup or idempotency contract; otherwise unknown may be the truthful result. A second danger is replay after the broker deduplication window: the business protection may need to outlive that window. I would therefore state exactly which duplicate is suppressed, for how long, and which external boundary still requires application reconciliation. A marketing label cannot substitute for that failure analysis.

followups.question: Can the same message ID be reused with changed bytes?
followups.answer: The application should reject changed semantics under one logical identity using its canonical payload or digest. A broker duplicate identifier is not a replacement for a domain-level changed-payload conflict contract. Preserve the original bytes and stable receipt.

followups.question: When is a stronger end to end claim defensible?
followups.answer: When the effect and deduplication receipt commit atomically in the same authority, or every external participant enforces a documented compatible protocol. Name the fault model, retention horizon and proof; do not extend a broker feature beyond those participants.

questions.watch_for: Deduplicated storage is not exactly-once execution of an external business effect.

questions.title: Ordering has several meanings
questions.question: How would you preserve case ordering while processing messages concurrently?
answer: Distinguish stream storage sequence, delivery order and handler completion order. An asynchronously retried publish can be stored after later messages; concurrent handlers can finish in another order; redelivery can revisit earlier work. JetStream offers expected-subject-sequence publishing to reject an inappropriate append, but it does not decide the application case revision for you. [N9]
