For an original case example, revisions A and B should pass through the current authority expected-revision guard even if the notification bus presents B first. A worker can use sequence metadata to detect gaps or reconstruct a projection, but it should not infer business permission from the order in which callbacks ran. If strict per-case execution ordering is required, design a partition or serialized ownership policy and measure its head-of-line cost. Independent cases can still proceed concurrently. Do not manufacture a global ordering requirement merely because one case needs a local causal order; it would reduce throughput without solving supplier uncertainty.

followups.question: Would one worker solve ordering?
followups.answer: It can serialize its own handling, but only while that ownership and input protocol hold. Restarts, multiple producers and retries still require revision and identity checks. A single process also introduces capacity and availability limits that should be explicit.

followups.question: Can timestamps decide the winner?
followups.answer: Not safely by themselves. Producer clocks and delivery delays are not a serialized case authority. Use the actual expected revision or another explicit causal contract; retain timestamps as observations useful for diagnosis rather than mutation permission.

questions.watch_for: Storage order, business causality and completion order are separate contracts.

questions.title: Backpressure must bound actual work
questions.question: How would you handle a slow consumer without turning the broker into an unbounded memory buffer?
answer: Core NATS can disconnect a slow consumer whose pending data exceeds its limit. JetStream pull consumption provides bounded batch and expiry controls; MaxAckPending limits outstanding unacknowledged deliveries across a consumer. Broker and client limits are useful mechanisms, but the application still owns handler concurrency, bytes and downstream work. [N13, N8]

For a hypothetical policy worker, I would align fetch size with available execution slots, cap the complete payload bytes, and stop pulling before downstream requests accumulate. A handler timeout must retain the actual remote call until settlement instead of freeing a semaphore while the call still runs. Observe pending age, unacknowledged count, redelivery, processing time and useful completion together. On overload, stop admitting new obligations according to the product contract while keeping original receipts and recovery reads available. Simply increasing AckWait or pending limits may conceal a stuck handler and increase the crash-replay burst rather than improve reliability.

followups.question: Why cap bytes if batch size is small?
followups.answer: A batch of eight large images can consume far more memory than eight short status events. Bound both the encoded frame and validated content, and include retained results and downstream buffers in the resource model.

followups.question: What should a worker do during graceful shutdown?
followups.answer: Stop new pull admission first, retain and finish or truthfully abandon owned work under its protocol, then close subscriptions and connections. Observe actual tasks and external requests; an empty local queue does not prove every handler stopped.

questions.watch_for: A released waiter slot does not prove the real handler or external request stopped.

questions.title: Replication needs a stated fault model
questions.question: What does a three replica JetStream stream buy, and what does it not buy?
answer: JetStream replication uses consensus groups. For three replicas, a majority is two; a committed write can continue to be protected when one member is lost, while losing quorum prevents normal write progress. Placement and the underlying storage matter: three processes on the same machine do not establish host-failure tolerance. [N12, N16]

For a hypothetical production design I would specify the required recovery point and recovery time, the failure domains, storage assumptions, backup procedure and restore reconciliation. I would test an acknowledged publish followed by one node loss, then a quorum loss and controlled restoration, while comparing independently retained event identities. Replication is not backup: a mistaken authorized deletion can propagate, and operator identity or configuration loss can make good data unusable. It also does not preserve PostgreSQL case receipts if that separate authority loses data. The complete application recovery story must reconcile both stores and any external effects rather than treating the broker cluster as universal durability.

followups.question: Why not put replicas in distant regions immediately?
followups.answer: A wider failure domain can increase consensus latency and introduce different partition behavior. Choose placement against measured latency and availability objectives. Multi-region fan-out and a globally writable durable authority are different requirements that need separate design.

followups.question: How would you test durability honestly?
followups.answer: Start with a frozen topology and expected failure, wait for the actual storage acknowledgment, inject that failure, reopen through another live member and verify original bytes and identities. Keep restoration and cleanup evidence, and avoid substituting a health check for reconciliation.

questions.watch_for: Replica count alone does not establish a recovery objective or an end to end durability guarantee.

questions.title: Authenticate principals and restrict subjects
questions.question: How would you secure a NATS integration for multiple accounts and specialist services?
answer: NATS separates authentication, subject-level publish and subscribe authorization, and transport encryption. Accounts isolate subject spaces, with explicit sharing where configured. Appropriate credentials establish the connected principal; a tenant field in a payload does not. Permission design must include the required reply and acknowledgment paths without granting unrelated administrative subjects. [N10, N11]

For an original application design I would give the source publisher only its event subjects and give each specialist only its permitted request and response scope. Browser RTC credentials would not become broker credentials. The application would still validate scoped command bindings, closed payload shape, identity conflicts and exact human confirmation at P1. Rotating credentials should stop new unauthorized admission without pretending it cancels a request already accepted by a remote service. I would test cross-account denial, overly broad wildcard grants, forged tenant labels, stale credentials and safe diagnostics. Logs and metrics should reveal finite error classes rather than copying bearer material or private message contents.

followups.question: Does TLS replace authorization?
followups.answer: TLS protects a connection and can support authenticated identity, but it does not decide which business command the principal may perform. Restrict broker subjects and enforce the application case, work and confirmation guards independently.

followups.question: Why review reply inbox permissions?
followups.answer: Request reply needs a route back, and an overly broad reply grant can expose other traffic. Grant the supported narrow pattern and verify the actual client protocol. A working request is not proof that the surrounding permission set is least privilege.

questions.watch_for: A broker-authenticated service still needs scoped application authorization and cannot supply human consent.

walkthrough.detail: Publisher sends a concrete subject; matching subscribers receive according to ordinary subscription or queue-group routing. Ask what is lost if the receiver is offline.
Specify stream retention, bounded payloads, a stable event identity and consumer state. Distinguish publisher storage acknowledgment from consumer acknowledgment.
Commit the application disposition before consumer acknowledgment and prove replay finds the same identity. Preserve uncertainty for an external side effect outside that transaction.
Match fetch, bytes, acknowledgment wait and handler concurrency to actual downstream capacity. Test overload, useful progress, shutdown and restored replay.

limits: No NATS or JetStream service was started for this book. The examples are proposed designs and protocol study, not new measured implementation.
A broker stream retention window does not define a safe business idempotency horizon.
Exact APIs and security options are version-sensitive; the cited official documentation was checked for this edition.

chapters.title: NATS in the LiveKit ecosystem
chapters.subtitle: Separate a supported bus adapter from a deployed architecture
intro: The phrase LiveKit uses NATS needs a precise component and source. Public self-hosting documentation, the reusable PSRPC library, the inspected open-source server wiring and private Cloud infrastructure are different evidence domains.

This chapter corrects a common interview trap: a library supporting NATS does not prove every LiveKit deployment selects it. All proposed NATS additions to this POC remain hypothetical and preserve P1 as the durable execution owner.

concepts.title: Three claims to keep separate
concepts.body: A bus implementation exists; a public component constructs that implementation; a specific deployed service runs it. Evidence for the first does not establish the other two.

concepts.title: Transport is not the application authority
concepts.body: A messaging layer may route an RPC or wake a poller. Accepted work, exact confirmation, result truth and effect recovery still need their documented owners.

questions.title: What the self hosting guide actually says
questions.question: Does LiveKit require NATS to scale a self-hosted server cluster?
answer: The public self-hosted distributed guide specifies Redis as the shared store and message bus. It describes cluster-aware room placement, a signaling instance bridging to the room-hosting node, and the current constraint that a room fits on one node. That source does not establish a NATS requirement. [L2]

In an interview I would draw the documented architecture first and then ask which component the NATS question concerns. The media plane, agent worker dispatch, service RPC and durable application execution can use different mechanisms. For this repository, one local SFU is an explicit scope choice. More durable business workers do not turn that media deployment into a multi-node cluster. I would also keep private Cloud topology out of the answer unless there is a direct relevant public source. The useful engineering answer is not choosing a familiar broker name; it is identifying which state is shared, which process hosts a room, and what evidence supports the failure and routing claim.

followups.question: Would adding Redis make one enormous room unlimited?
followups.answer: No such conclusion follows. Many concurrent rooms and the limits of one room are different sizing questions. Define publishers, subscribers, track count and bitrates, then test the selected server topology rather than extrapolating from total room count.

followups.question: How much of this is demonstrated by the POC?
followups.answer: The POC demonstrates selected local media and application gates around one SFU. The distributed deployment described in the external guide is study material and a future design option, not a measured capability of this checkout.

questions.watch_for: Do not replace the documented Redis architecture with an assumed NATS architecture.

evidence.label: One local SFU and deferred distributed media

questions.title: PSRPC is an abstraction over a bus
questions.question: Where does NATS appear in LiveKit public code?
answer: LiveKit publishes PSRPC, a Go RPC library with generated Protobuf services and multiple message-bus implementations. Its current README lists localbus, natsbus and redisbus packages, selected by passing the constructed bus to generated clients and servers. It distinguishes single-handler RPC, fan-out RPC and subscription behavior. Supporting NATS at this reusable seam is a specific public fact. [B1]

The architecture lesson is dependency inversion: an RPC contract can be independent of one broker client. That does not make every transport semantically interchangeable. I would review deadlines, subscription lifetime, queue selection, payload limits, compression and close behavior at the selected adapter and generated service. Most importantly, the existence of a NATS adapter says nothing by itself about whether a particular server binary constructs it or whether any hosted product runs it. In a project discussion I would be explicit that this Python and TypeScript POC does not implement PSRPC merely because it uses LiveKit Agents.

followups.question: Should you memorize a historical NewNatsMessageBus call?
followups.answer: Understand the seam first and verify the selected library version. The current README moved NATS and Redis constructors into their bus packages while retaining a local compatibility alias. Reciting an older signature without checking it can obscure an otherwise correct architectural explanation.

followups.question: Does generated RPC add workflow durability?
followups.answer: It can standardize request and response handling, but durable accepted work requires retained identities, storage transitions and recovery semantics. A generated method over a live bus is not automatically a persistent workflow or an atomic external effect protocol.

questions.watch_for: A supported PSRPC NATS transport is not evidence of a specific deployment choice.

questions.title: Follow the construction path
questions.question: How would you verify which bus the open-source LiveKit server actually selects?
answer: I would inspect the public server construction path rather than infer it from dependencies. In the inspected master wire_gen.go, getMessageBus returns the local message bus when there is no Redis client and constructs redisbus when there is one. The public sample configuration includes Redis settings. These observations describe that inspected source path, not every LiveKit service or private deployment. [B2, B3]

A complete source-based investigation would record a commit or release, follow the configuration into construction, inspect the reachable consumers and compare runtime configuration without exposing credentials. A transitive NATS module in a dependency graph is weaker evidence: it may support tests or an unused adapter. Conversely, the selected local or Redis path does not prove that no other LiveKit component could use NATS. I would state both the supported conclusion and its scope. The same method applies to this POC: declarations, generated config and actual process ownership should agree before making a deployed-architecture claim.

followups.question: Why distinguish master from a pinned release?
followups.answer: A moving branch can change after the interview notes were written. Tie an implementation claim to the inspected revision when possible, and describe it as a source observation. The POC pinned server image is a separate artifact with its own selected baseline.

followups.question: What if a GitHub comment says Cloud uses NATS?
followups.answer: Treat it as a lead, not proof. Look for an official relevant architectural statement or a component construction path. Do not turn a user comment, an adapter package or a dependency into a claim about private Cloud internals.

questions.watch_for: Dependency availability is weaker evidence than a reachable, configured construction path.

questions.title: What this repository runs
questions.question: Where is NATS in your local POC, and why did you leave it out?
answer: There is no NATS service in the maintained local Compose topology. The POC uses PostgreSQL for durable application authority, one self-hosted LiveKit SFU, explicit local HTTP boundaries and bounded process ownership. Its fixed application scope deliberately avoids introducing another distributed queue or workflow platform. I would show the configuration and ownership map rather than imply that studying NATS means I deployed it here.

That is a scope decision, not a universal claim that a broker is unnecessary. The project is intended to make acceptance, uncertain effects, leases and recovery boundaries visible in a local environment. Adding an independent durable broker consumer as another owner of accepted specialist work would complicate the central invariant. If a later requirement demonstrates a notification-latency, fan-out or integration need, I would evaluate a bus against that specific requirement and include its lifecycle and failure gates. Until then, keeping deployment smaller makes the existing evidence easier to interpret and reproduce.

followups.question: Does omitting NATS weaken the job relevance?
followups.answer: The role values reasoning about state, concurrency, channels and developer abstractions. The repository demonstrates those mechanisms directly. NATS knowledge helps evaluate a future transport, but claiming an unimplemented broker would make the project explanation less credible.

followups.question: How would you demonstrate the absence?
followups.answer: Inspect the maintained service definitions, generated configuration contract and actual owned process inventory for the selected profile. State the scope of the check. Do not claim that a missing service in one file proves anything about unrelated hosted systems.

questions.watch_for: Clearly label NATS knowledge and proposed integration separately from implemented POC behavior.

questions.title: Add wake up hints without a second owner
questions.question: If you added NATS tomorrow, how would you preserve the existing durable-work contract?
answer: My first hypothetical integration would use notifications as hints that existing authoritative work may be eligible. A consumer would validate the event and ask P1 or the existing dispatcher for current eligible work; it would not execute solely because a message arrived. Periodic durable discovery would remain the recovery path for dropped hints. A duplicate, reordered or stale hint would therefore be harmless to business identity and permission.

If reliable event publication itself becomes required, I would design a transactional event outbox at the owning database boundary. A bounded relay would publish the original event identity and retain its publication outcome; a crash after publish but before relay bookkeeping would require deduplication at the receiver. This is a proposed extension, not a new table or service already present in the POC. P1 would still issue execution, retain results and guard action. The broker would not become a second accepted-work authority, and consumer acknowledgment would describe notification handling rather than business completion.

followups.question: Why retain polling when notifications are fast?
followups.answer: A wake-up hint can be lost during disconnect or before subscription becomes active. Durable eligibility is the completeness mechanism. A periodic bounded scan makes notification loss a latency issue rather than loss of an accepted obligation.

followups.question: Would you put every supplier request on JetStream?
followups.answer: Only after explicitly redesigning execution ownership and proving compatibility. The safer first extension keeps the existing P1 grant and effect protocol. Transporting an event must not bypass exact confirmation, current eligibility, original identity or supplier reconciliation.

questions.watch_for: A hypothetical event outbox must remain distinct from the existing business completion outbox and execution authority.

questions.title: Design the interview failure experiment
questions.question: How would you prove a proposed NATS integration did not lose work or repeat a business effect?
answer: I would freeze an original synthetic command, source identity, expected authority transitions and fault schedule before the run. Then test database commit before notification, publication before relay bookkeeping, consumer disposition before acknowledgment, broker reconnect, duplicate and changed payload, handler crash and shutdown while a message is in flight. The assertions would reconcile P1 work and effect identities against independent supplier evidence rather than merely count broker deliveries.

Useful progress is part of the proof: a missed notification must still be discovered, a duplicate must return the original outcome, and unrelated current work must complete while an old effect remains unknown. A retained result must survive late delivery or lease expiry without becoming new action permission. I would capture actual processes, storage and cleanup, and test source and isolated installed consumers separately. These are acceptance criteria for a future experiment. The book adds no NATS service, no broker benchmark and no production-capacity claim to the current repository.

followups.question: What would count as a failed experiment?
followups.answer: A missing original work record, a second supplier identity, changed semantics under one key, premature acknowledgment without retained disposition, a stuck real handler hidden by a released slot, or cleanup that cannot account for owned resources. Passing notification throughput would not excuse any of those failures.

followups.question: What would you say about the result in the interview?
followups.answer: Name the exact topology, source revision, declared fault cases and observed invariants. Keep an initial failure and later repair visible. Describe untested regions, failover modes and retention horizons as remaining work rather than generalizing a local passing run.

questions.watch_for: Count independently reconciled business identities, not just messages sent or callbacks received.

evidence.label: Frozen workload and actual ownership model

walkthrough.detail: Ask whether the question concerns the public media server, PSRPC, another service, private Cloud infrastructure or the local application. Avoid transferring facts between them.
Check the supported transport implementation, the reachable constructor and the selected configuration separately. Record the revision and disclose any inference.

walkthrough.step: Preserve authority in a proposed extension
walkthrough.detail: Keep P1 as accepted-work owner. Let a hint trigger bounded discovery, or design a distinct reliable event-publication contract with original identities and receiver deduplication.
Prove original business work and effects survive dropped, repeated and reordered messages, reconnect and real process death. Measure capacity only within a declared envelope.

limits: The inspected public PSRPC library supports NATS; this does not establish NATS use by every LiveKit component or any specific Cloud deployment.
The inspected public server construction path selects local or Redis messaging. A moving public branch is distinct from this repository selected server image.
The local POC has no NATS service. Every NATS application integration and its proposed verification in this chapter is future design material.

chapters.title: Questions behind the Agents role
chapters.subtitle: Python TypeScript APIs and framework judgment
intro: The job description centers on framework abstractions for realtime voice and text, state across long interactions, agent delegation and clear developer APIs. It also emphasizes Python, TypeScript, documentation and community feedback. The questions here are inferred from those responsibilities; they are not a verified interview loop. [JD]

Use the project as evidence, then reason about the changed constraint. The strongest answer names a concrete API behavior and a failure schedule. A correct definition without a usable developer contract is only the beginning.

concepts.title: Framework judgment
concepts.body: Make the safe path simple without hiding uncertainty. Preserve compatibility, disclose limits and explain who owns cleanup.

concepts.title: Practical fluency
concepts.body: Be ready to implement a bounded async component, validate untrusted input, design a typed result union and debug a resource leak without relying on memorized terminology.

questions.title: Async is not automatic parallelism
questions.question: What happens if a function marked async performs blocking database or CPU work?
answer: The async declaration does not move work away from the event loop. A blocking call can delay audio processing, cancellation, heartbeats and unrelated sessions sharing that loop. I would use an appropriate async client or a bounded offload boundary for unavoidable blocking I O, and a measured process or service boundary for substantial CPU work.

The hard part is ownership. Canceling an asyncio waiter around a thread does not forcibly stop that thread. The wrapper must retain the actual operation, its slot and its exception observation until settlement. The repository explicitly documents this contract and tests real process or thread boundaries where necessary. A faster timeout that releases the semaphore while work continues would make the advertised resource bound false.

followups.question: When does to_thread help?
followups.answer: It is useful for suitable blocking I O. It is not a universal way to parallelize Python CPU work, and cancellation of the awaiting task is not thread termination. [PY]

followups.question: How would you prove the bound?
followups.answer: Block the actual worker behind a controllable barrier, time out its waiter, try another admission, and assert the second cannot consume the still occupied slot. Then release and observe real settlement.

questions.watch_for: Do not describe async def as a thread or process boundary.

questions.title: Choose structured concurrency deliberately
questions.question: When would you use TaskGroup and when would you retain a task separately?
answer: TaskGroup fits related operations whose lifetime and failure policy belong to one scope. It waits for group completion and applies a coordinated cancellation policy when a child fails. A separately retained owner is appropriate when an already admitted external operation must outlive a particular observer timeout. These are different contracts, not competing style rules. [PY]

I would expose close or aclose on that owner, stop new admission during close and retain it if closure observation times out. The joined executor is an example of preserving runners and retrying closure. Shielding a task may protect a narrow observation boundary, but it does not make work durable and must not turn caller cancellation into silent success.

followups.question: What do you do with CancelledError?
followups.answer: Run necessary cleanup and propagate cancellation unless a narrow documented interface intentionally translates it. Do not map it to a successful result or an ordinary transient retry.

followups.question: Why retain a strong task reference?
followups.answer: It makes ownership and outcome observation explicit. Detached work that carries accepted business obligations cannot depend on a caller accidentally keeping a future alive.

questions.watch_for: Task cancellation, remote stop and durable business cancellation are separate operations.

questions.title: Immutable inputs and typed ports
questions.question: Why are dataclasses and Protocols useful, and where do they fail?
answer: Small immutable domain values make accepted semantics explicit, while Protocols define the narrow behavior expected of a store, supplier or reader. Constructor injection exposes lifetime and capability requirements and lets isolated tests use realistic adapters. This avoids importing sibling storage internals or hiding authority in a service locator.

Static typing cannot validate external bytes, and frozen=True does not recursively freeze nested dictionaries. I would parse and bound raw input, copy mutable nested data into an accepted snapshot and retain canonical bytes or a digest according to the contract. Then mutate the original caller object in a test and verify that replay semantics did not change. The repository uses typed public boundaries but does not claim whole repository strict typing.

followups.question: Why not accept dict everywhere?
followups.answer: It hides required fields, invariants and capabilities from both tooling and consumers. A raw dict is appropriate at decode time, before validation into a narrow domain contract.

followups.question: Can tests still violate a Protocol?
followups.answer: Dynamic composition can hide missing methods if types are erased. Assign the adapter to the public Protocol and exercise the actual invoked method through a contract test.

questions.watch_for: A type annotation is not runtime authentication or validation.

questions.title: Design a result API callers can use
questions.question: Which outcomes should submit and inspect distinguish?
answer: I would distinguish a new accepted operation, exact replay, changed payload identity conflict, invalid input, unauthorized scope, capacity or dependency unavailability, and an acknowledgment whose outcome is unknown. Those outcomes imply different caller actions. A caller should not parse exception strings to discover whether it may retry.

The API should preserve the frozen original request through ambiguous acknowledgment and provide a scoped reconciliation path. Do not automatically turn every timeout into a failed submission. Current service fixes explicitly replay the original submit before get or cancellation when its acknowledgment was lost. A simple happy path is good developer experience only if the error path is equally truthful.

followups.question: Would you throw or return a union?
followups.answer: Either can work if callers get stable typed categories and original identity. Use exceptions for the language natural failure boundary and result variants for expected states; document both clearly.

followups.question: How do you explain unknown to a product developer?
followups.answer: The service may have accepted the original operation, so preserve its key and inspect or replay according to its receipt contract. Do not create a replacement intention merely to remove a spinner.

questions.watch_for: Do not collapse unauthorized, unavailable and possibly accepted into one retryable error.

evidence.label: Frozen submit replay and definitive auth outcomes

questions.title: TypeScript at a trust boundary
questions.question: How would you make a channel result exhaustive and safe?
answer: Treat decoded input as unknown and validate it before narrowing to a closed domain union. Use a discriminant such as kind or state so callers handle accepted, conflict, unavailable and unknown outcomes explicitly. An exhaustive switch can make an unhandled variant a compile time error, while runtime parsing still rejects unsupported bytes. [TS]

The Python and TypeScript implementations also need matching bounds, supported versions, numeric constraints and canonical semantics. A cast from JSON.parse to the desired interface skips that work. I would test shared positive and negative fixtures and run an installed consumer built from the packed artifact, because a source tree import can conceal missing exports or undeclared dependencies.

followups.question: Does readonly make nested data immutable?
followups.answer: It constrains the typed use of values, not every external reference or runtime mutation. Copy or normalize accepted data into the contract representation and test mutation resistance.

followups.question: How do you add a new state compatibly?
followups.answer: Decide whether old consumers can safely interpret it. For closed authority envelopes, an explicit version or new facade may be safer than silently widening the same accepted bytes.

questions.watch_for: as SomeType changes the compiler view, not the runtime payload.

questions.title: Timeouts in JavaScript
questions.question: Why is Promise.race with a timer insufficient cancellation?
answer: It settles the observer race but does not inherently stop the losing operation. Fetch, a worker or a provider promise can continue after the caller receives a timeout. The adapter must retain ownership, use supported abort mechanisms where available and observe actual settlement before releasing a real capacity slot.

I would carry one absolute local request deadline through body read, validation, invocation and cleanup observation, rather than granting every stage a fresh full budget. Business deadlines remain persisted UTC facts at the authority. The repository bounded specialist and channel adapters exercise this distinction; an AbortSignal is a request to cooperate, not proof a remote supplier has undone an effect.

followups.question: What if abort is ignored?
followups.answer: Return the correct observer outcome while retaining the actual owner and its slot. Expose incomplete cleanup if necessary and keep a later observation path.

followups.question: What should a retry preserve?
followups.answer: The original operation identity and deadline semantics. A new attempt may exist only if the durable authority issues it and the external boundary contract permits another call.

questions.watch_for: A resolved timeout promise cannot certify stopped resource usage.

questions.title: Tests that establish a contract
questions.question: How would you test the hard parts rather than mirror the implementation?
answer: Start with independent observable assertions: one accepted identity, one supplier effect or explicit unknown, exact receipt bytes, no stale action and useful later progress. Control concurrency with barriers and database lock observations instead of arbitrary sleeps. Kill an owned process at the actual boundary when recovery is the claim.

Use deterministic contract fixtures for pure validation, real PostgreSQL for transaction and database time rules, sockets for transport close ownership, installed wheel or npm consumers for packaging, and real browser audio for media. A mocked timer cannot establish physical process exit or returned audio. Preserve failed artifacts and distinguish a targeted rerun from a clean full lane.

followups.question: Can LLM evaluation replace assertions?
followups.answer: It can supplement conversational quality assessment. Exact identity, effect counts, eligibility and cleanup need deterministic assertions against independent observations.

followups.question: What does a zero test runner mean?
followups.answer: It provides no passing behavioral evidence. Missing setup, skips and timeouts remain nonpassing when the selected requirement needs those assertions.

questions.watch_for: Test quantity and test realism are different dimensions.

questions.title: Design the minimal public SDK
questions.question: What should an application developer need to know to use one of these libraries?
answer: Expose the domain operation, required trusted binding, stable identities, expected result categories and lifecycle. Keep SQL schema details and internal polling machinery behind adapters. The developer still needs to know when an outcome is unknown and when exact human confirmation is required; hiding those is misleading abstraction.

I would start with an installed minimal example that submits, inspects and closes under normal and failure paths. It should use only declared exports and extras, work outside the checkout and show one conflict or unknown outcome. From that consumer, refine names and defaults. The project already treats independently built wheel and npm artifacts as a separate gate instead of assuming source tests establish usability.

followups.question: What belongs in a quickstart?
followups.answer: A small successful path, prerequisites, safe defaults, how to inspect the original operation after an ambiguous ACK, and the actual close procedure. Link deeper recovery detail without omitting its existence.

followups.question: Would you expose a generic execute callback?
followups.answer: Only if the authority and serialization contract can support it safely. This POC deliberately supports finite capabilities rather than caller selected worker code or a general workflow graph.

questions.watch_for: A smaller API is not better if it hides the only safe recovery action.

questions.title: Compatibility as a behavior contract
questions.question: How do you evolve persistence and APIs without rewriting history?
answer: Use explicit owner migrations and preserve legacy accepted bytes, identities and receipts. Runtime serving code should validate supported capabilities without doing DDL. A new semantic binding often requires a versioned proposal or facade instead of filling old missing fields from today state.

This repository has separate version families: the P1 business schema, P1 work schema, P2 inbox schema and P3 request envelopes. Their numbers are not interchangeable. I would test old state before and after an interrupted or repeated upgrade, verify backup recovery and run an installed old supported API against the new compatible store. Exact replay must retain its original meaning even after defaults change.

followups.question: Can you automatically populate legacy consent?
followups.answer: Not with new mutation authority. Legacy v1 consent stays readable and replayable, while a new v2 proposal supplies the required case and supplier revision bindings.

followups.question: Why not migrate during application startup?
followups.answer: It expands runtime privileges and creates concurrent DDL and availability risks. The design deliberately separates the owner upgrade from serving principals.

questions.watch_for: Schema version, contract envelope version and semantic policy version are different axes.

questions.title: Product and community judgment
questions.question: A developer says your API is correct but impossible to debug. What do you do?
answer: Ask for the concrete task, the misleading state and the information they needed at that point. Reproduce it with a minimal example and inspect whether the API distinguished pending, failed, unknown and known result states. Improve the error contract and documentation around the user journey, not just the internal implementation name.

For this project I would show the original operation ID, safe current status, what is known, and the next permitted action without exposing credentials or private payloads. Add a focused regression and an installed example. Share the design tradeoff and migration impact asynchronously so users can assess it. This is a proposed response pattern; any story about having done it should use your actual contribution.

followups.question: What if users demand automatic retries?
followups.answer: Explain the uncertain effect case with a concrete example and offer safe replay or reconciliation where the contract supports it. If new guarantees are needed, change the operation semantics explicitly.

followups.question: How would you measure the improvement?
followups.answer: Use time to first successful integration, ability to recover a simulated ambiguous acknowledgment, support confusion and retained correctness. A new name alone is not evidence of improved usability.

questions.watch_for: Do not invent customer feedback or personal ownership to make an answer sound experienced.

questions.title: Your contribution and AI assistance
questions.question: How should you discuss authorship of an AI assisted repository?
answer: Separate what exists in the artifact from what you personally designed, implemented, reviewed and can reproduce. Describe how AI assistance was used without inflating authorship. Pick a small critical path and explain the invariant, the exact code, the test schedule and the known failure boundary without reading a generated summary.

I would prepare one handwritten coding exercise and one live code reading path, then keep a list of decisions I independently validated. A strong claim is specific: I can explain why this zero row conditional update means lost authority and show the competing schedule. A weak claim is that the repository has many lines or tests. The documentation itself asks for accurate contributions and explainable evidence.

followups.question: What if you cannot explain a module?
followups.answer: Say so precisely, explain the interfaces you do understand and inspect the source. Do not turn a generated implementation into a claim of personal expertise.

followups.question: What would you code live?
followups.answer: A bounded async adapter with real ownership after waiter timeout, or an idempotent acceptance function with changed payload conflict. State the fault model before writing the happy path.

questions.watch_for: The book is rehearsal material, not a substitute for firsthand understanding.

questions.title: Choose the next coherent slice
questions.question: What would you work on next and how would you know it is done?
answer: Choose an existing high value gap and name the affected acceptance or task scope. For this snapshot, the normal stop input exhaustion and final input lifecycle findings are strong candidates because they threaten accepted work during an ordinary user action. Read the relevant plan dependencies and implementation before choosing a repair.

The slice should demonstrate a final accepted input during shutdown, correct dependency ordering, no exhausted retries caused solely by closing endpoints, preserved original identities and useful restart progress. Run the narrow regression, affected real process and database lanes and required shared checks. Keep unresolved full charter and provider gates open. This is a proposed next slice, not a claim that all remaining release work can fit into it.

followups.question: Would you add more features first?
followups.answer: I would justify the priority against user impact and current scope. A compelling new modality does not erase a known accepted work lifecycle risk.

followups.question: What would you ask LiveKit engineers?
followups.answer: How they want developers to observe uncertain long running work, how text channel identity should compose with sessions, and which framework boundary should own interruption versus business cancellation. These are technical discussion prompts, not assumptions about internal plans.

questions.watch_for: Definition of done must include safe rejection, useful progress and real cleanup evidence.

challenges.title: Connected room silent answer
challenges.symptom: The room connects and captions update, but the caller hears no returned audio from the agent.
challenges.first_check: Trace one turn through TTS output, publication, subscription, inbound packets, decoding, audio element state and output device.
challenges.handling: Diagnostic pattern: isolate the failed media stage; existing evidence separates generated text, SDK playout and browser playback observations.
challenges.avoid: Do not regenerate business work or claim successful playback because captions, a waveform or a connected badge appear.

challenges.title: First scripted voice turn disappears
challenges.symptom: Text works, but the first scripted voice turn produces no transcript after the SDK clears its user turn.
challenges.first_check: Inspect real AgentSession stream replacement order and count active plus closing STT handles during clear_user_turn.
challenges.handling: Implemented: retain two bounded recognizer handles for replacement overlap; the genuine SDK regression still rejects a third handle.
challenges.avoid: Do not equate one logical speaker with one instantaneous resource handle or relax the bound without understanding replacement lifetime.

challenges.title: Real providers stall before usage
challenges.symptom: Configured real providers report zero inference usage while the spoken response times out during a qualification attempt.
challenges.first_check: Check native TLS diagnostics, trusted inference mode and whether the explicitly selected approved certificate bundle reached the native runtime.
challenges.handling: Supported setup: select the approved certificate-only bundle and rerun P1-20; the current post-v5 provider requalification remains open.
challenges.avoid: Do not disable TLS verification, expose provider keys or infer actual inference from a healthy process or configured badge.

challenges.title: The inner timeout wins
challenges.symptom: Accept fails near two seconds even though the enclosing dispatch step allows five seconds and the original operation later exists.
challenges.first_check: Inventory bridge, client, endpoint and claim budgets; compare their actual cutoff times before interpreting the lost acknowledgement.
challenges.handling: Implemented joined fix: pass the bridge budget into ExternalOperationClient; new joined profiles separately retain a longer claim lease.
challenges.avoid: Do not enlarge only the outer timer, multiply independent retries or treat timeout as proof that acceptance never committed.

challenges.title: Signed SMS rejected by time checks
challenges.symptom: A correctly shaped SMS request is rejected despite an apparently valid signature and familiar sender identity.
challenges.first_check: Check canonical timestamp representation, seconds units, clock skew and the sixty-second transport window before inspecting durable sender association.
challenges.handling: Implemented: authenticate bounded raw bytes and canonical time before SQL; legitimate retries preserve original event semantics and refresh permitted transport authentication.
challenges.avoid: Do not widen the window silently, trust body scope or confuse provider HMAC authentication with customer account authorization.

challenges.title: An old interrupt stops new speech
challenges.symptom: A delayed interruption or recognition callback affects the next answer instead of the response or source turn that created it.
challenges.first_check: Compare immutable response tickets, actual speech handles and caller-bound turn IDs across each await and SDK replacement.
challenges.handling: Implemented: interrupt the original bound handle and freeze genuine final recognition before awaiting durable intake; preserve separate business cancellation.
challenges.avoid: Do not select mutable current speech after an await or treat stopping agent audio as cancelling accepted supplier work.

challenges.title: A grant expires behind a lock
challenges.symptom: A worker starts while its lease is live, waits for admission and reaches its protected write after expiry.
challenges.first_check: Observe the actual SQL lock wait and sample PostgreSQL time after locks; compare the retained owner, epoch and expiry.
challenges.handling: Implemented: use clock_timestamp after lock admission and reject expired authority; native bindings similarly recheck current grant time under protection.
challenges.avoid: Do not authorize writes from transaction-start timestamps, cached expiry or worker wall time, even when the epoch still matches.

challenges.title: Cancellation cannot prove prevention
challenges.symptom: A takeover lookup finds nothing, but an older reserved supplier request may still execute after cancellation or deadline.
challenges.first_check: Inspect original dispatch_count, reservation identity and supplier capabilities before interpreting a lookup miss as evidence of nonexecution.
challenges.handling: Implemented audit repair: retain UNCERTAIN with ambiguous_outcome when prior dispatch remains possible; cancellation requested remains a separate disposition.
challenges.avoid: Do not erase a possible old call, invent a new supplier key or promise reversal from a newer database lease.

challenges.title: Valid JSON unsupported conclusion
challenges.symptom: The specialist returns a well-formed result that contradicts supplied policy facts or claims an unsupported eligibility conclusion.
challenges.first_check: Check exact request and result bindings, policy version and independently validated factual support before considering current applicability.
challenges.handling: Implemented: validate factual support before expiry classification and retain only the contractually permitted result; exact human confirmation remains separate.
challenges.avoid: Do not promote schema validity, model confidence or a plausible citation into factual truth, current applicability or mutation permission.

challenges.title: One click becomes two inputs
challenges.symptom: Repeated Send or Enter creates duplicate background work before the first durable acceptance acknowledgement reaches the browser.
challenges.first_check: Compare original input UUIDs, frozen bodies, acceptance timing and retained user rows rather than counting only transport sends.
challenges.handling: Implemented: preserve the pending input identity through repeated sends and replay the original unknown body; backend acceptance enforces immutable semantics.
challenges.avoid: Do not mint a fresh UUID per retry or deduplicate by text hash, which conflates intentional identical messages.

challenges.title: An older answer stays green
challenges.symptom: The display shows an older eligible answer after a newer recorded result becomes expired, inapplicable or lacks delivery evidence.
challenges.first_check: Distinguish a newer pending input without results from a newer recorded result; inspect original delivery and current observation times.
challenges.handling: Implemented: stop fallback after selecting a newer recorded result and recheck applicability after cleanup; historical facts remain retained.
challenges.avoid: Do not hide newer unusable state behind an older green answer or let a cached badge authorize a booking action.

challenges.title: Capacity blocks receipt recovery
challenges.symptom: The retained store is full and clients cannot discover whether their earlier commands committed before acknowledgements were lost.
challenges.first_check: Verify original-identity lookup occurs before new-work capacity and expiry checks, while catalog and credential validation still run.
challenges.handling: Implemented: exact original submit and cancellation replay remain available at capacity; only genuinely new retained identities consume admission.
challenges.avoid: Do not delete protected identities to free display space or replace an unresolved original command with another business identity.

challenges.title: Timeout leaves unexpected capacity pressure
challenges.symptom: Clients time out, yet later requests still encounter capacity and underlying threads, sockets or remote work remain active.
challenges.first_check: Inspect actual retained tasks, process groups and writer owners; compare them with cancelled waiters before assuming a resource leak.
challenges.handling: Implemented: keep slots until actual work settles; retry incomplete close observations, with terminal peer-reset closure handled separately.
challenges.avoid: Do not release capacity in a waiter-level finally or assume cancelled await, elapsed timeout and reaped process mean the same thing.

challenges.title: Normal stop consumes pending inputs
challenges.symptom: A normal joined shutdown keeps dispatch claiming against closing Parent endpoints, potentially exhausting pending inputs or stranding the final room input.
challenges.first_check: Inspect dispatch admission, endpoint closure, room binding revocation and actual worker drainage in one shutdown dependency timeline.
challenges.handling: Open 0048 findings: quiescing dispatch before endpoint closure and correcting room retirement order are proposed repairs requiring implementation and fresh evidence.
challenges.avoid: Do not describe these lifecycle findings as solved or erase pending identities merely because launcher processes have exited.

challenges.title: A known receipt meets failed cleanup
challenges.symptom: A complete validated acknowledgement arrives, then writer cleanup raises and the caller is tempted to repeat the accepted command.
challenges.first_check: Check whether decoding completed before cleanup, preserve the exact receipt and inspect the retained writer and pending owner count.
challenges.handling: Implemented: return known decoded truth while retaining incomplete cleanup ownership; later close retries observe settlement without resending the request.
challenges.avoid: Do not let teardown failure overwrite a valid receipt or declare a resource free merely because domain decoding succeeded.

challenges.title: Eager scheduling hides a late owner
challenges.symptom: Shutdown appears complete before an eagerly started scan publishes its Task reference, leaving work or inspection resources arriving afterward.
challenges.first_check: Use the existing reentrant task-factory test to inspect publication reservation, actual scan count and close ordering before task creation returns.
challenges.handling: Implemented: reserve the publication Future before spawning and resolve it in finally; close waits for publication before draining actual owners.
challenges.avoid: Do not infer absence from an unset Task field or assume default scheduler ordering is guaranteed across task factories.

challenges.title: One unavailable result blocks later work
challenges.symptom: A transient feed, result or delivery read error prevents later useful events from progressing through completion processing.
challenges.first_check: Check per-row unavailable classification, separate discovery and terminal-ACK cursors, and the shared eight-row budget across cursor wrap.
challenges.handling: Implemented: leave transiently unavailable rows unacknowledged while bounded discovery examines later useful work; preserve identities and explicit pending observations.
challenges.avoid: Do not terminally acknowledge unknown rows to advance a watermark or reset the row budget when wrapping the cursor.

challenges.title: Schema validation itself causes effects
challenges.symptom: Opening a client evaluates unexpected metadata behavior, or an upgrade encounters unmanaged running work that cannot satisfy the new lease contract.
challenges.first_check: Inspect metadata relation kind before selecting its version, then verify owner role, ACTIVE state and unresolved legacy execution ownership.
challenges.handling: Implemented: catalog preflight rejects side-effecting metadata views; coordination upgrade refuses unmanaged running inquiries before DDL so original reconciliation can finish.
challenges.avoid: Do not adopt drifted metadata automatically, repair consent during startup or force an upgrade past unresolved legacy supplier work.

authority.title: Who owns each fact
authority.caption: Application composition borrows public ports. Dashed boundaries separate ownership. P3 uses public P1 grants/results; none of the three libraries gains permission to copy sibling storage.

commit.title: The two orders of revision and intent
commit.caption: Conceptual competing schedules. The guarded transaction defines the winner; a later observation or wall-clock timestamp cannot rewrite that commitment.

effect.title: A possible external effect stays possible
effect.caption: Conceptual knowledge states, not a literal enumeration of every storage value. Cancellation or deadline after a prior reservation cannot establish that a paused call never ran.

lease.title: A lease check after the lock wait
lease.caption: Illustrative ordering without measured durations. A request can start before expiry and acquire the lock after expiry; eligibility must use fresh authoritative time.

feedcommit.title: Feed sequence follows visible commit order
feedcommit.caption: Same source and scope under the shared work admission guard. The counterexample is an unimplemented alternative showing why an earlier sequence allocation alone is insufficient.

intake.title: One native input before one generation
intake.caption: Recognition, accepted input, generation and playback are separate observations. The two-handle SDK overlap is a resource lifecycle fact, not a second accepted turn.

context.title: Rehydrate without inventing an atomic snapshot
context.caption: P2 and public P1 observations occur at different times. The final permission check restricts disclosure but does not make the earlier reads a cross-store atomic transaction.

outbound.title: Reserve permission before carrier I O
outbound.caption: The reservation transaction shares admission with callback and current-permission checks. A later callback cannot fence an external call that was already admitted.

auth.title: Authenticate twice for two different questions
auth.caption: The cheap pass validates signed bytes before SQL. It uses signed time and cannot establish current freshness; the protected pass uses fresh database time after the lock.

delegation.title: Acceptance issuance result and action
delegation.caption: These gates answer different questions. The original v1 action path and the explicit newer policy delivery facades have separate support; the diagram grants no automatic version compatibility.

feed.title: Scan progress is not the terminal watermark
feed.caption: Illustrative eight-event window. Later useful terminal observations can progress while an earlier unknown prevents a contiguous terminal watermark from advancing.

facts.title: Valid bytes can still be unsupported facts
facts.caption: Independent gates, not one success flag. In fixed-policy verification, unsupported factual output remains invalid even when it is late; expiry must not mask the factual error.

singleflight.title: Shared scan and independent observers
singleflight.caption: One published scan can serve two observers. Canceling the first does not cancel the second; losing the last observer abandons interest while actual ownership remains until settled.

webrtc.title: Signaling and media use different paths
webrtc.caption: Protocol overview. A control connection is not proof of a working media path. TURN relays a path; it does not become application consent or a durable inbox.

pipeline.title: Where a voice answer can pause
pipeline.caption: A conceptual pipeline, not measured latency. Streaming stages may overlap; do not sum arbitrary component durations and call that observed end-to-end delay.

triage.title: Start with the missing observation
triage.caption: A diagnostic decision guide. Follow the evidence for the failing layer instead of treating every silence, delay or missing receipt as one retryable error.

lifetime.title: One timeout and three remaining lifetimes
lifetime.caption: Composite example for retained loopback/media owners, not every slot in the repo. Ordinal stages are not measurements. Each slot releases when its own protected actual resource settles; some require writer closure.

nats.title: Three acknowledgments with different meanings
nats.caption: Hypothetical messaging integration. A stream storage acknowledgment, consumer progress acknowledgment and retained application receipt are distinct facts.

planes.title: LiveKit transport bus and application authority
planes.caption: Public evidence supports Redis/local server wiring and a NATS-capable PSRPC library. It does not establish every LiveKit Cloud internal deployment or a NATS service in this POC.
